Discriminators: staging in Users\Public or Temp, password flag, document-folder scope at machine speed, off-hours timing, and an archiver launched as a descendant of the HUNT-02 process tree. A user zipping one folder at 14:00 from Explorer is not this hunt's target.

writeup.problem: Detection rules only catch what someone already knew to look for. Projects 1 to 3 built strong known-bad coverage, and the Projects 2/3 incident still contained behavior none of those rules fired on: no rule looked for living-off-the-land downloads, WMI persistence, process injection, discovery, jittered beaconing, or data staging. Project 4 is the hypothesis-driven layer that closes that gap: assume the endpoint telemetry (Sysmon process, network, registry, WMI, and file events) contains attacker behavior the rules missed, form a specific falsifiable hypothesis for each suspected behavior, and hunt the telemetry until each hypothesis is confirmed, explained benignly, or honestly left inconclusive.
writeup.methodology: Lab: the same environment as Projects 1 to 3 (WIN-LAB01, WIN-LAB02, DC-LAB01, FILE-LAB01, host-only network) with full Sysmon telemetry: Events 1 (process create with hashes and parent), 3 (network), 7/8/10 (image load, remote thread, process access), 11 (file create), 13 (registry), 19 to 21 (WMI), and 22 (DNS), forwarded to the SIEM. Method per hunt: (1) write the hypothesis before touching data, in if/then form tied to an ATT&CK technique, (2) baseline first (30 days of parent-child pairs, executable prevalence by hash, WMI consumer inventory, per-host destination rarity), (3) hunt with stack counting and rarity rather than signatures, ranking results rarest-first, (4) pivot every hit across the other telemetry types by ProcessGuid and timestamp, (5) record a verdict per hunt and graduate only the proven patterns into the Project 1 rule pack. Tools: Sysmon, Splunk Free, Sysinternals (Autoruns and Process Explorer for live verification), MITRE ATT&CK for technique framing. All activity is the same simulated lab intrusion from Projects 1 to 3, extended with the behaviors those projects did not cover; isolated lab only.
writeup.findings: 8 hunts run, 6 confirmed malicious, 1 benign-explained, 1 kept as a standing scheduled hunt. Confirmed: HUNT-02 found patient zero (WINWORD.EXE spawning cmd then encoded PowerShell from a macro lure, Invoice_Q3.docm, 14:58). HUNT-06 reconstructed the discovery burst (7 built-in tools in 5 minutes, including Domain Admins enumeration). HUNT-01 caught the certutil -urlcache download of stage2 from the known C2 IP, a genuine Project 1 gap. HUNT-04 found the persistence the rules missed: a WMI CommandLineEventConsumer (UpdaterHealth) re-running upd.exe daily at 03:00, created 3 minutes after the scheduled task. HUNT-05 found upd.exe injecting into explorer.exe (all-access handle plus a remote thread in unbacked memory), which explained HUNT-07: a jittered beacon to 198.51.100.23:8443 (26 connections, jitter ratio 0.41) that Project 2's fixed-interval search missed because the interval was randomized and the process name read as trusted explorer.exe. HUNT-08 changed the incident's nature: a password-protected 412 MB 7z archive of Documents and Desktop staged in Users\Public at 22:47 and assessed as exfiltrated before the Project 3 encryption — a double-extortion pattern. HUNT-03's prevalence stack ranked upd.exe and stage2 as the two rarest executables on the fleet, confirming stack counting as the fastest triage entry point. Net effect: the incident timeline now runs unbroken from the 14:58 lure to the 23:38 anti-recovery commands, and three hunts graduated into standing rules.
writeup.challenges: Hunting is slower and less certain than alerting, and the write-up has to say so. Baselines cost real time: the parent-child and prevalence baselines needed 30 days of telemetry before rarity meant anything, and a small 3-host lab makes rarity look cleaner than a real fleet of thousands, where the rare-executable queue would be far longer and mostly benign. Sysmon Event 8 (remote thread) and Event 10 are high-volume on a general fleet, so HUNT-05 only works scoped to unusual source processes, not as a blanket search. Jitter analysis (HUNT-07) needs hours of connections before the statistics separate a beacon from a chatty application, so it can never be a real-time control. One hunt stayed inconclusive on lab data alone: a single-host rare legitimate tool could not be fully cleared without the intel enrichment Project 5 provides, and it is recorded as inconclusive rather than forced into a verdict. Finally, telemetry gaps bound everything: anything the actor did before Sysmon forwarding started, or in the Project 2 log-gap window, is unhuntable and stays listed as unknown.
writeup.learned: The core lesson is the difference between hunting and alerting: a rule asks 'did this known-bad thing happen', a hunt asks 'if the attacker did X, what would the telemetry have to show' — and then accepts whatever the data answers, including 'no'. Writing the hypothesis first is what keeps a hunt honest; without it, hunting degenerates into scrolling logs until something looks odd. Prevalence and baselining did more work than any single query: rarest-hash stacking found the actor's binaries with no signature at all, and the parent-child baseline made one Office-to-shell chain decisive. Hunting also re-attributes evidence: the 'trusted explorer.exe' beacon was only malicious once the injection hunt explained it, which is a warning against clearing activity by process name. The practical output matters as much as the findings: three hunts (LOLBIN download, WMI consumer creation, unbacked remote thread) graduated into the Project 1 rule pack, the IOC list (stage2 hash, archive hash, C2 timing profile) goes to Project 5 for enrichment, and the memory-resident payload in explorer.exe is the direct handoff to Projects 6 and 7. Next: Project 5, Threat Intelligence Dashboard, enriches every indicator collected across Projects 1 to 4.

soc.title: Threat Intelligence Dashboard
soc.desc: Enrich suspicious IPs, domains, and file hashes.
steps: Choose enrichment sources for IPs, domains, and hashes
Build the dashboard layout: indicator in, verdict and context out
Test with known-bad and known-good indicators
Document example lookups and what the enrichment changed

Assemble the indicator list from Projects 1 to 4 (attacker IP, C2 IP and URL, tunneling domain, file hashes, ransom-note URL and wallet) and normalize formats: defanged for sharing, full hashes recorded
Enrich every indicator in at least two independent sources and record the fields, not just the score: first/last seen, ASN and owner, passive DNS, detections, related samples
Give every indicator a written verdict (malicious, malicious-associated, attribution-supporting, benign-explained) with its evidence and confidence, including the benign control lookup
Feed verdicts back: blocks at the firewall, hashes and imphash into the hunt list, the inconclusive Project 4 hunt closed, and preserved samples queued for Project 6

items.title: IP: 203.0.113.87 — attacker source (scan, SSH and RDP brute force)
items.src: AbuseIPDB · VirusTotal · GreyNoise · Shodan · RDAP (ASN/owner)
items.logic:
INDICATOR: 203.0.113[.]87 (IPv4, from INV-04/INV-07, Projects 2 and 4)
LOOKUP ORDER: 1) AbuseIPDB — abuse confidence score, report categories, distinct reporters, last reported 2) VirusTotal — detection ratio, passive DNS resolutions, communicating files, ASN 3) GreyNoise — scanner classification: internet background noise vs targeted 4) Shodan — open ports and services on the host itself 5) RDAP — allocation, ASN, hosting provider
FIELDS RECORDED: first seen, last seen, abuse confidence, report categories (port scan, SSH, brute force), hosting ASN, reverse DNS
VERDICT RULE: malicious requires two independent sources agreeing AND matching local telemetry (scan at 01:58, brute force 02:03-02:14). A reputation score alone never convicts.
items.ev:
Enrichment result (lab capture):
AbuseIPDB: confidence 100%, 214 reports in 30 days, categories: Port Scan, SSH, Brute-Force, Hacking. Last reported inside the incident window.
VirusTotal: 11/94 vendors flag the IP; passive DNS shows it previously resolving a throwaway dynamic-DNS hostname; ASN: budget VPS hosting provider, no reverse DNS.
GreyNoise: classified as a mass scanner BUT also flagged for SSH and RDP brute-force behavior — background-noise label does not explain the targeted follow-through in INV-07.
Shodan: the host itself runs SSH and an open proxy port — a rented attack box, not a compromised home router.
VERDICT: MALICIOUS, high confidence. This is the actor's infrastructure, not shared egress.
items.triage:
1. Block at the perimeter firewall in both directions and log any further hits (blocked hits after containment = other victims or retries).
2. Retro-hunt the IP across all log sources for 30 days, not just the incident window — INV-07's timeline method, wider.
3. Pivot on the ASN + passive DNS hostnames: list sibling IPs the actor may rotate to and pre-stage them as watchlist IOCs.
4. Reset every credential the IP touched (jsmith, deploy) even if a given attempt failed — see INV-01/INV-02.
5. Record the full field set in the incident record; 'IP was malicious' without the fields is not reusable intel.
items.fp: Caveats: reputation data goes stale — an IP flagged today may be reallocated to an innocent customer next month, so blocks carry a review date (90 days here). Shared VPN/proxy egress and CGNAT can put legitimate users behind a flagged IP; that is why the verdict required the local telemetry match, not the score alone. GreyNoise's scanner tag is the classic trap: most mass scanners are noise, this one followed through, and only the local logs could tell the difference.

items.title: IP: 198.51.100.23:8443 — command and control destination
items.src: VirusTotal · Shodan · URLhaus · Passive DNS · Certificate Transparency (crt.sh)
items.logic:
INDICATOR: 198.51.100[.]23, port 8443 (from INV-05 beaconing and HUNT-01/HUNT-07)
LOOKUP ORDER: 1) VirusTotal — detections, hosted URLs, downloaded/communicating samples, passive DNS 2) Shodan — service banner on 8443, other open ports, TLS certificate details 3) URLhaus — malware URLs hosted on the IP 4) Passive DNS — every domain that has resolved to this IP, with first/last seen 5) Certificate Transparency — certificates issued for the IP/domains
FIELDS RECORDED: first seen in intel, hosted URL paths, cert issuer/subject/validity, sibling domains, related sample hashes
VERDICT RULE: a destination with hosted malware URLs or communicating samples in intel, plus local beaconing evidence (INV-05/HUNT-07), is confirmed C2 — block and hunt, do not debate the score.
items.ev:
Enrichment result (lab capture):
VirusTotal: 9/94 flag the IP; relations list the exact URL the actor used — http://198.51.100.23:8443/stage2.dat (the HUNT-01 certutil download) — submitted to URLhaus as a malware distribution URL.
Shodan: only port 8443 open, serving a self-signed certificate (subject = the IP itself, issued 6 days before the incident, 90-day validity). No web content, no hostname.
Passive DNS: one short-lived domain resolved here for 3 days overlapping the incident, then moved — fast-flux style rotation.
First seen in intel: 8 days before the incident — the infrastructure was stood up for this campaign.
VERDICT: MALICIOUS — confirmed C2 and payload host. The cert creation date and first-seen date together bound the campaign's preparation window.
items.triage:
1. Block IP and port at the firewall; also block the sibling passive-DNS domain and watch for the actor rotating to a new IP (cert transparency and passive DNS alerts on the same cert/domain pattern).
2. Hunt the whole fleet for any connection to this IP or its sibling domain, any port, 30 days back — beaconing hosts are compromised hosts (HUNT-07 method).
3. Pull the hosted URL list into the hunt: any host that fetched /stage2.dat or a sibling path gets the Project 6 sandbox treatment for what it downloaded.
4. Isolate WIN-LAB01 (already done in Project 2) and treat explorer.exe's injected payload as live until the memory image is examined in Project 7.
5. Share the indicator set (IP, domain, cert fingerprint) as the incident's exportable IOC package — this is the entry other teams would consume.
items.fp: Caveats: bare-IP hosting with a self-signed cert also describes legitimate admin panels, VPN endpoints, and IoT dashboards — the conviction here comes from the URLhaus payload URL plus local beaconing, not the cert alone. Non-standard ports are weak evidence by themselves. Passive DNS has coverage gaps: absence of a domain in passive DNS does not prove the IP never hosted one, which is why the local DNS logs (Sysmon 22) were checked too — they showed no lookup at all, matching a hard-coded IP.

items.title: Domain: tunnel.example.net — DNS tunneling parent domain
items.src: Passive DNS · RDAP/WHOIS (registration age) · VirusTotal · urlscan.io
items.logic:
INDICATOR: tunnel[.]example[.]net and its high-entropy subdomains (from Project 1's DNS tunneling rule)
LOOKUP ORDER: 1) RDAP/WHOIS — registration date, registrar, registrant privacy, nameservers 2) Passive DNS — full subdomain history, resolution targets, first/last seen per record 3) VirusTotal — detections, subdomains, communicating samples 4) urlscan.io — any observed web activity (expected: none, this is a DNS-only domain)
FIELDS RECORDED: domain age at incident time, nameserver history, A/NS records, subdomain count and entropy profile, resolution IP history
VERDICT RULE: a young domain (registered days before use), privacy-shielded, whose only traffic is high-volume unique subdomains resolving to one IP, is a tunneling/C2 domain — sinkhole it, do not just block one subdomain.
items.ev:
Enrichment result (lab capture):
RDAP: domain registered 11 days before the incident, privacy-protected registrant, budget registrar, nameservers changed twice in the first week.
Passive DNS: 1,900+ unique subdomains ever observed, all high-entropy labels, all resolving to one IP for TXT/NULL-style query bursts; zero subdomains a human would type. Record types dominated by TXT — the tunneling signature.
VirusTotal: 7/94 flag the domain; one communicating sample in relations is a known DNS-tunneling tool family.
urlscan: no web observations at all — consistent with a DNS-only channel.
VERDICT: MALICIOUS — purpose-built tunneling domain. Registration age (11 days) is the single strongest field: the business has no reason to talk to an 11-day-old domain at 640 unique subdomains per 15 minutes.
items.triage:
1. Sinkhole the parent domain at the resolver (blocking subdomains one by one is unwinnable — they are generated). Log sinkholed queries: any internal host still asking is infected or misconfigured.
2. Retro-search DNS logs fleet-wide for the parent domain and for the pattern (unique-subdomain volume per parent) — other hosts may tunnel through different parents.
3. Bound the exfiltration: subdomain label length x query count gives a rough ceiling on data volume; record the estimate and its uncertainty honestly in the incident record.
4. Watch the registration pattern: alert on internal DNS queries to domains younger than 30 days — this graduates into a standing enrichment check on DNS logs.
5. Keep the domain on the watchlist after sinkholing; re-registration by a new owner later is common and the block needs a review date.
items.fp: Caveats: legitimate services also use long subdomains and TXT records — DNS-based AV lookups, anti-spam checks, CDN steering, and some software-update schemes all look tunnel-shaped at a glance. The discriminators are domain age, subdomain uniqueness/volume per host, and the querying process (Project 1's rule carries the Image). Young-domain alerting will fire on every new SaaS tool a user tries; tune by pairing age with volume, never age alone.

items.title: Hash: upd.exe (SHA-256 9f2c…a41b) — the actor's main binary
items.src: VirusTotal · MalwareBazaar (abuse.ch) · Hybrid Analysis report · Internal prevalence (HUNT-03)
items.logic:
INDICATOR: SHA-256 9f2c…a41b (full hash in the incident record), file C:\Users\Public\upd.exe (from Projects 1, 3, and 4)
LOOKUP ORDER: 1) VirusTotal — detection ratio and vendor labels, first/last submission, signer, imphash, section hashes, behavior summary 2) MalwareBazaar — family tags, distribution history, related samples 3) Public sandbox reports (Hybrid Analysis) — ATT&CK behaviors other analysts already observed 4) Internal — prevalence stack from HUNT-03 (hosts, executions, first seen)
FIELDS RECORDED: detection ratio, consensus family label, first seen in the wild vs first seen locally, signer status, imphash (for variant hunting)
VERDICT RULE: multi-vendor detection with a consistent family label, plus this lab's own behavioral record (persistence, injection, encryption), is confirmed malware. Local behavior outranks a low detection ratio for fresh samples.
items.ev:
Enrichment result (lab capture):
VirusTotal: 48/72 engines detect; labels converge on a ransomware-loader family; first submitted 19 days before the incident; unsigned; imphash shared with 6 sibling samples.
MalwareBazaar: hash listed, tagged with the same family, distribution method noted as malicious document attachments — matching the Invoice_Q3.docm lure from HUNT-02.
Hybrid Analysis (public report on a sibling imphash sample): behavior includes vssadmin shadow deletion, Run key persistence, and process injection — the exact Project 1/3/4 behavior chain, observed independently.
Internal prevalence: 1 host, first seen 2026-11-20T14:58, the rarest executable on the fleet (HUNT-03).
VERDICT: MALICIOUS — confirmed, family-attributed. Enrichment's real value here is the imphash and sibling samples: six more hashes to hunt before they are used.
items.triage:
1. Hunt all 7 hashes (this one plus the 6 imphash siblings) across the fleet and in email-gateway and proxy logs — the lure was a document, so check who else received it.
2. Add the hash and imphash to the blocklist/detection pack; imphash catches rebuilds that change the file hash.
3. Preserve this exact sample for Project 6: detonate it in the sandbox and compare its live behavior against the public sandbox report — agreement validates the lab method.
4. Use the family label for scoping, not storytelling: family attribution guides which IOCs to expect (wallet format, note text), it does not change containment.
5. Record first-seen-in-the-wild (19 days before) in the timeline — the actor used a current, circulating build, not a bespoke one-off.
items.fp: Caveats: hash verdicts are exact-file only — one byte changed, one packer run, and the hash is unknown again, which is why imphash and behavior carry the hunt. Detection ratios move over time (engines add signatures), so the recorded ratio is dated. A clean hash result is the weakest verdict in this project: it means 'not known', never 'safe' — ENR-05 is the proof case. Never submit internal or user files to public sandboxes without checking what the file contains; this sample was an attacker binary, but the habit protects the next case.

items.title: Hash: stage2 payload (SHA-256 44d0…c9e2) — the hash intel cannot clear
items.src: VirusTotal · MalwareBazaar · Internal prevalence and behavior chain (HUNT-01/HUNT-03)
items.logic:
INDICATOR: SHA-256 44d0…c9e2, file downloaded as stage2.dat then renamed (from HUNT-01/HUNT-03)
LOOKUP ORDER: 1) VirusTotal — any record at all? detection ratio, submission history 2) MalwareBazaar — listed or unknown? 3) Internal — where did it come from (URL, parent process), what loaded it, what did it do
FIELDS RECORDED: presence/absence in each source, first submission dates if any, internal delivery and execution chain
VERDICT RULE: when external intel is empty, the verdict comes from provenance and behavior: a file fetched by certutil from a confirmed C2 IP (ENR-02) and loaded within the hour is malicious by chain of custody, whatever the hash databases say. Record the verdict as 'malicious — local evidence, no external corroboration' so the confidence is honest.
items.ev:
Enrichment result (lab capture):
VirusTotal: no detection record — the hash returns a bare file page, 0 detections, first submitted by this lab's lookup (i.e., nobody had reported it).
MalwareBazaar: not listed.
Internal chain (HUNT-01/HUNT-03): downloaded 2026-11-20T15:22 by certutil -urlcache from 198.51.100.23:8443/stage2.dat — the ENR-02 confirmed C2 — renamed to a .dll, 1 host, 2 executions, loaded in the window between the discovery burst (HUNT-06) and the injection (HUNT-05).
VERDICT: MALICIOUS on local evidence alone. This is the entry that teaches the project's core lesson: enrichment confirms the known; it cannot clear the new.
items.triage:
1. Treat the sample as the highest-value sandbox candidate: Project 6 detonates this one first, because its behavior is the least documented.
2. Block by hash internally and hunt the delivery URL path (/stage2.dat) in proxy logs — the URL is a more durable indicator than this hash.
3. Check what the .dll was loaded into and what it did between load and the HUNT-05 injection; that gap is its undocumented behavior window.
4. Submit the sample to intel sources through the lab's normal channel so the next analyst gets a record — enrichment is also contribution.
5. Keep the verdict wording precise in the incident record: 'no external corroboration' stays attached, so nobody later upgrades it to 'intel-confirmed'.
items.fp: Caveats: zero detections also describes every brand-new legitimate file — a developer's fresh build would look identical in the hash sources. What separates this file is provenance (a LOLBIN download from a confirmed C2) and company (the HUNT-02/05/06 chain), not the empty intel result itself. Acting on 'unknown hash' alone would FP constantly; acting on 'unknown hash + malicious delivery chain' is the tuned rule, and it graduates to Project 4's hunt queue rather than a paging alert.

items.title: Hash: docs.7z (SHA-256 c4a8…2f19) — the staged exfiltration archive
items.src: VirusTotal · Internal file auditing (archive contents list) · DLP-style scoping
items.logic:
INDICATOR: SHA-256 c4a8…2f19, file C:\Users\Public\docs.7z, 412 MB, password-protected (from HUNT-08)
LOOKUP ORDER: 1) VirusTotal — expected result: no record or clean (an archive of the victim's own documents is not malware) 2) Internal — the archive's file list from file auditing: exactly which folders and files were staged 3) Network — the outbound session that followed (HUNT-07 destination)
FIELDS RECORDED: archive hash (for tracking and dedup, not verdict), source folder list, file count, size, creation time, destination of the follow-on transfer
VERDICT RULE: for collection artifacts the enrichment question is not 'is it malware' but 'what does it contain and where did it go'. Verdict: malicious-associated — a breach-scoping artifact, handled as evidence of theft, not as a detection target.
items.ev:
Enrichment result (lab capture):
VirusTotal: no record for the hash; a forced scan of the (encrypted) archive structure reports clean — expected and meaningless for verdict: the contents are the user's own documents.
Internal file auditing around 22:47: the archiver read 1,140 files across Documents and Desktop (the HUNT-08 command line scope) — that read list, not the archive, is the exposure inventory.
Network: outbound session to 198.51.100.23 (ENR-02) at 22:52 from the injected explorer.exe, size consistent with the archive leaving.
VERDICT: MALICIOUS-ASSOCIATED — data assessed as exfiltrated. The hash's job in the dashboard is tracking: if this exact archive appears anywhere else (another host, a leak site sample), the hash is how you recognize it.
items.triage:
1. Scope the breach from the archiver's read list: those 1,140 files define notification and impact, not the encrypted set from Project 3.
2. Preserve the archive and its hash as evidence; do not delete it during cleanup — it is the definitive 'what was staged' record.
3. Search other hosts for the archiver pattern and for this hash (a second staging point means a second foothold).
4. Brief the double-extortion position plainly: encryption recovery (Project 3) does not close this incident while a copy of the data sits with the actor.
5. Feed the destination + timing back to ENR-02's record so the C2 entry carries the exfiltration finding.
items.fp: Caveats: hash intel is structurally useless for verdicts on user-data archives — every victim's archive is a unique file no database has seen. Analysts waste time 'checking the hash' here; the check that matters is the contents inventory. Password protection on the archive also blocks content scanning, which is itself a (weak) signal — legitimate user archives in this lab were never password-protected, but that baseline is environment-specific and must be re-proven elsewhere.

items.title: URL + wallet: ransom note .onion URL and BTC address
items.src: URLhaus · VirusTotal (URL) · Blockchain explorer (wallet history) · Ransomware payment trackers
items.logic:
INDICATORS: the .onion payment URL and BTC wallet address from the Project 3 ransom note (YARA-01)
LOOKUP ORDER: 1) URLhaus / VirusTotal — is the URL or its clearnet infrastructure already reported, and under which family? 2) Blockchain explorer — wallet first-seen, transaction count, total received, clustering (is this wallet per-victim or shared across the campaign?) 3) Ransomware trackers — does the note text + wallet pair match a tracked family's known infrastructure? 4) Cross-check against ENR-04's family label — independent agreement or not?
FIELDS RECORDED: wallet first seen, payments received before this incident (were there earlier victims?), URL report history, family cross-references
VERDICT RULE: note indicators enrich attribution and victimology; they never change containment. A wallet with prior payments proves an active campaign; an empty wallet proves nothing (fresh per-victim wallets are standard).
items.ev:
Enrichment result (lab capture):
Note: the wallet in the lab note is a documented test address (1A1zP1...DivfNa, the address Project 3 planted), so the on-chain fields below are the method recorded against the lab's simulated tracker data, not a live payment history.
URLhaus/VirusTotal: the .onion service itself is not directly scannable; the family's known clearnet staging URL pattern matches ENR-04's imphash siblings.
Wallet method result: check first-seen and inbound history — a wallet funded/receiving before this incident indicates earlier victims and a running campaign; per-victim fresh wallets show zero history by design.
Tracker cross-reference: note phrasing + extension (.lockbit marker from YARA-02) + wallet format agree with ENR-04's family attribution from two independent directions.
VERDICT: ATTRIBUTION-SUPPORTING — three independent lines (hash family, note/extension markers, tracker pattern) converge on one family. Recorded as supporting evidence, not as a block target: you cannot block a wallet.
items.triage:
1. Never interact with the .onion URL from a work system: no visiting, no 'checking if it is up' — note indicators are enriched from trackers and intel, not by browsing.
2. Record wallet, URL, note text hash, and extension together as the family fingerprint; hand to whoever handles the ransom decision discussion with the legal/HR context it needs.
3. Use prior-victim evidence (wallet history method) in the impact briefing: an active multi-victim campaign changes leak likelihood assessments.
4. Hunt the note hash and filename fleet-wide one more time with the tracker data in hand — families reuse note templates across victims in the same org.
5. Do not let attribution work delay containment: this entry is deliberately last in the lookup order during a live incident.
items.fp: Caveats: on-chain data is public but easy to misread — address reuse, mixers, and exchange deposit addresses can make an innocent service look like a campaign wallet, and a fresh wallet's emptiness is not exculpatory. Family attribution from note text alone is unreliable (notes are copied between groups); here it only counts because the hash evidence (ENR-04) arrived at the same label independently. The lab's test wallet means amounts and dates in a real case must be pulled live at briefing time, never quoted from this dashboard.

items.title: Hash (control): ~update.exe — closing Project 4's inconclusive hunt
items.src: VirusTotal · Publisher/signature verification · Internal prevalence over time (HUNT-03 method)
items.logic:
INDICATOR: SHA-256 61bd…77e0 (as logged in HUNT-03), file C:\Users\jsmith\AppData\Local\Temp\~update.exe — the rare, unsigned, single-host executable Project 4 recorded as INCONCLUSIVE because intel context was missing
LOOKUP ORDER: 1) VirusTotal — detections, signer/publisher metadata, first seen in the wild, prevalence (how many submitters worldwide have this file?) 2) Signature and metadata check — original filename, product name, version resource vs the renamed-looking '~update.exe' 3) Internal — re-run prevalence after 7 more days: does the 'rare' file recur on a schedule (updater behavior) or never again?
FIELDS RECORDED: worldwide prevalence, wild first-seen date, product metadata, recurrence pattern
VERDICT RULE: benign requires positive evidence, not absence of detections: a wild first-seen years old, high worldwide prevalence, product metadata matching a real application, and scheduled recurrence together clear a file. Any one alone does not.
items.ev:
Enrichment result (lab capture):
VirusTotal: 0/72 detections; first seen in the wild 3 years ago; submitted by thousands of users; version resource names a real, widely used application's updater component — the '~update.exe' Temp filename is that product's normal update staging pattern.
Internal re-check: the file recurred on the host on a weekly cadence matching the application's update schedule, always written by the application's own service process — not by explorer, Office, or a shell.
Prevalence contrast with ENR-04/ENR-05: upd.exe was rare locally AND rare globally AND new; this file is rare locally but common globally and old. That contrast is the whole lesson of the prevalence method.
VERDICT: BENIGN-EXPLAINED. Project 4's inconclusive hunt is closed with evidence, and the file joins the known-benign hash list so future hunts start cleaner.
items.triage:
1. Close the HUNT-03 queue item with this verdict and its evidence fields attached — 'benign' without the fields would have to be re-proven next quarter.
2. Add the hash to the known-benign list used by the prevalence hunt, with a review date (a product update changes the hash; expect a new rare-hash queue item then, and clear it the same way).
3. No blocking, no user contact needed: the parent process and schedule are the application's own.
4. Keep the entry on the dashboard as the standing control: any future enrichment process that cannot reproduce this benign verdict on a known file is not trusted on unknown ones.
5. Note the residual risk honestly: a signed-or-known file can still be abused (living-off-the-land), so benign here means 'this file, this behavior' — a future odd behavior from it reopens the question.
items.fp: This entry IS the false-positive lesson: rarity plus unsigned plus a Temp path — the exact surface traits of ENR-05's malicious stage2 — described a legitimate updater. The discriminators were all contextual: global prevalence, wild age, product metadata, parent process, and recurrence. Tune every prevalence queue with a known-benign list and this four-field clearing standard, or the queue fills with updaters and the real stage2 gets cleared by an analyst in a hurry.

writeup.problem: Projects 1 to 4 produced a pile of indicators and a pile of questions. The firewall knows 203.0.113.87 scanned the lab, but is it a known attacker or shared infrastructure? VirusTotal-style intel exists for upd.exe, but the stage2 payload returns nothing at all. One rare executable from the Project 4 prevalence hunt sat formally inconclusive because nobody could say whether it was a threat or an updater. Project 5 builds the threat intelligence layer that answers those questions properly: an enrichment dashboard where every indicator collected across the incident — IPs, a domain, file hashes, a URL and a wallet — is looked up in multiple independent sources, the useful fields are recorded (not just a score), and each indicator leaves with a written verdict, a confidence level, and the actions that verdict drives. Enrichment is what turns one lab's incident into reusable intelligence, and turns 'we saw an IP' into 'we know what this IP is, when it was stood up, and what else it has done'.
writeup.methodology: Indicator set: everything Projects 1 to 4 collected — attacker source IP 203.0.113.87, C2 destination 198.51.100.23:8443 and its /stage2.dat URL, tunneling parent domain tunnel.example.net, SHA-256 hashes for upd.exe, the stage2 payload, the docs.7z staging archive, and the inconclusive ~update.exe, plus the ransom note's .onion URL and BTC wallet. (Lab indicators use documentation IP ranges and a documented test wallet, per Projects 1 to 3.) Sources by indicator type: IPs — AbuseIPDB, VirusTotal, GreyNoise, Shodan, RDAP; domains — passive DNS, RDAP/WHOIS for age, VirusTotal, urlscan.io; hashes — VirusTotal, MalwareBazaar, public sandbox reports, internal prevalence; URL/wallet — URLhaus, ransomware trackers, blockchain explorer. Method per indicator: (1) normalize and defang, (2) look up in at least two independent sources, (3) record fields — first/last seen, ASN and owner, registration age, passive DNS, detection ratios, related samples, imphash — never just a verdict score, (4) weigh external intel against local telemetry, with local behavior as ground truth when they disagree, (5) write the verdict in a fixed vocabulary (malicious, malicious-associated, attribution-supporting, benign-explained) with confidence and the actions it triggers, (6) feed results back: firewall blocks, hunt-list hashes, watchlist entries with review dates. All lookups are passive — nothing here touches the attacker's infrastructure directly.
writeup.findings: 8 enrichment lookups completed: 2 IPs, 1 domain, 4 hashes, and 1 combined URL/wallet entry. Five malicious verdicts: the source IP 203.0.113.87 (AbuseIPDB confidence 100% with port-scan/SSH/brute-force categories, VPS hosting, GreyNoise scanner-plus-brute-force profile — targeted, not background noise); the C2 198.51.100.23 (URLhaus lists the exact /stage2.dat payload URL, Shodan shows only 8443 with a self-signed cert issued 6 days before the incident, first seen in intel 8 days prior — infrastructure stood up for this campaign); the tunneling domain tunnel.example.net (registered 11 days before use, 1,900+ high-entropy subdomains, TXT-heavy — sinkholed at the parent); upd.exe (48/72 detections, consistent ransomware-loader family label, imphash linking 6 sibling samples, public sandbox behavior matching this lab's observed chain); and the stage2 payload — malicious on local evidence alone, with zero external detections, recorded honestly as uncorroborated. The docs.7z archive is malicious-associated: hash intel is meaningless for a victim-data archive, and its value is the 1,140-file exposure inventory from HUNT-08. The ransom-note wallet/URL entry is attribution-supporting: note markers, extension, and tracker patterns converge with the hash family label from an independent direction. And the control case closed the loop: ~update.exe, Project 4's inconclusive rare executable, is benign-explained — globally common, 3 years old in the wild, a real product's updater with a weekly recurrence — proving the enrichment process can clear a file with positive evidence, not just convict. Net actions: both IPs and the domain blocked/sinkholed with review dates, 7 hashes (upd.exe plus imphash siblings) added to the hunt list, and the incident's IOC package is now exportable.
writeup.challenges: Four honest difficulties. First, sources disagree and scores hide it: GreyNoise's 'scanner' classification was technically true and operationally misleading for the source IP, and only the recorded fields plus local telemetry resolved it — a dashboard that shows scores instead of fields would have waved the actor through as background noise. Second, freshness cuts both ways: the most dangerous indicator (stage2) had no intel footprint at all, while stale reputation on a reallocated IP would falsely convict an innocent host — every verdict here is dated and the blocks carry 90-day review dates for exactly that reason. Third, some indicator types resist enrichment structurally: victim-data archives are unique files no database knows, .onion services cannot be scanned directly, and per-victim wallets are empty by design, so those entries document method and limits instead of pretending to a verdict the sources cannot support. Fourth, source limits are real: free tiers rate-limit lookups, passive DNS coverage is partial, and several fields (full sandbox reports, historical WHOIS) sit behind paywalls — the dashboard records which source each field came from so gaps are visible. Lab limitation: indicators use documentation ranges and a test wallet, so the on-chain and live-reputation fields demonstrate the recorded method and the lab's captured results rather than a live internet pull.
writeup.learned: Enrichment answers 'where else has this been seen, and in what company' — it never answers 'guilty' by itself. The verdicts that held up in this project all paired external fields with local telemetry: the C2's cert date mattered because it preceded the local first-seen by days, and the source IP's reputation mattered because the local timeline showed follow-through. Recording fields instead of scores is what makes intel reusable: scores change silently, but 'registered 11 days before, TXT-heavy, 1,900 subdomains' is still evidence next quarter, and the imphash outlived the file hash as a hunting pivot. The benign control was as valuable as any conviction — a process that cannot clear ~update.exe with positive evidence will eventually clear a stage2 by fatigue. Finally, enrichment is a loop, not a lookup: verdicts fed firewall blocks, hunt lists, a sinkhole, a closed hunt, and the Project 6 sandbox queue (upd.exe and the undocumented stage2 detonate next, in that order), and the sandbox's behavior report will come back here as new intel. Next: Project 6, Malware Analysis Sandbox, takes the two preserved samples into an isolated environment.

soc.title: Malware Analysis Sandbox
soc.desc: Study suspicious file behavior in an isolated environment.
steps: Build a fully isolated analysis VM (host-only networking, snapshots)
Set up behavior monitoring: processes, files, registry, network
Analyze a safe practice sample and record its behavior
Write the behavior report: IOCs, persistence, network calls
Verify isolation before any detonation: host-only network, no shared folders or clipboard, simulated internet only (FakeNet/INetSim), and the clean snapshot's hash checked
Run static triage on every sample first (hashes, strings, imports, capa) and log the behavior predictions before executing anything
Detonate each sample under the full monitoring stack (Sysmon, Procmon, Regshot before/after, Wireshark) on the hardened, aged profile, and export the behavior timeline for every run
Extract IOCs and ATT&CK behaviors from each run, compare them against the Projects 1 to 5 telemetry and intel records, and revert to the clean snapshot after every sample

items.title: Static triage: upd.exe before detonation (hashes, strings, imports, capabilities)
items.src: Static analysis: SHA-256 / imphash, Detect It Easy, capa, strings, PE import review (no execution)
items.logic:
SAMPLE: upd.exe, SHA-256 9f2c…a41b, C:\Users\Public\upd.exe (preserved in Project 3, enriched in ENR-04)
STATIC METHOD (always before any run): 1) Hash the sample on receipt and confirm it matches the incident record — a hash mismatch means the wrong file, stop. 2) File profile: PE32+, unsigned, 1.8 MB, entropy 7.61 (matches YARA-03's packed profile). 3) Strings: ransom-note fragments, the .lockbit extension marker, vssadmin/wbadmin command fragments, and the C2 IP 198.51.100.23 as a plain string — the sample barely hides anything. 4) Imports: BCryptEncrypt / BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey (encryption), VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread (injection kit), RegSetValueEx + task-related COM strings (persistence), WinINet InternetOpenUrl (network). 5) capa capability mapping: encrypt-data, inject-process, persist-via-registry, delete-shadow-copies — the static picture already predicts the Projects 1 to 4 behavior chain.
RULE: static triage writes the detonation checklist — every predicted capability becomes a behavior to confirm or refute in SBX-02/03/06.
items.ev:
Static triage record (lab capture):
SHA-256 9f2c…a41b — matches ENR-04 record exactly. Imphash matches the 6 sibling samples from Project 5.
Detect It Easy: PE32+ executable, packed (high-entropy .text-adjacent section), no authenticode signature, linker timestamp 6 days before the incident — consistent with ENR-02's certificate date: same preparation window.
capa highlights: 'encrypt data using BCrypt', 'create process in suspended state / write process memory', 'set registry run key', 'delete volume shadow copies', 'query DNS / connect to remote host'.
Strings of note: 'RESTORE_FILES.txt', '.lockbit', 'vssadmin Delete Shadows /all /quiet', '198.51.100.23', 'stage2.dat', a BTC address matching the Project 3 note (1A1zP1...DivfNa lab test address).
PREDICTION LOGGED: persistence (Run key + task), injection into a shell process, C2 to the hard-coded IP, anti-recovery, then encryption. Dynamic runs grade this prediction.
items.triage:
1. File the static report with the sample's chain of custody (source host, who preserved it, hash on receipt) — Project 7's forensics will need it.
2. Turn every capa capability into a watch item for the dynamic run; a predicted behavior that does NOT appear is itself a finding (dormant capability or sandbox evasion, SBX-07).
3. Cross-check strings against existing detections: the note text and extension extend YARA-01/YARA-02; the hard-coded IP confirms ENR-02 without any network contact.
4. Do not 'test run' the sample on the analysis host to see what it is — static triage exists precisely so the first execution happens inside the isolated VM (SBX-02).
5. Queue the imphash siblings for the same static pass when time allows; rebuilds usually keep imports and capabilities even when strings change.
items.fp: Caveats: static traits are circumstantial by themselves — BCrypt imports, packing, and high entropy also describe legitimate installers and protectors (YARA-03's FP lesson). What convicts statically here is the combination plus the strings: no legitimate updater ships ransom-note text and a shadow-delete command line. Packers can also hide imports entirely (one LoadLibrary/GetProcAddress pair), so a quiet static result never clears a sample — it only means the dynamic run carries the verdict, which is exactly the stage2 situation in SBX-04.

items.title: Dynamic run: upd.exe process tree and persistence (Run key + scheduled task reproduced)
items.src: Sandbox VM telemetry: Sysmon (1, 11, 13), Process Monitor, Regshot before/after, Autoruns diff
items.logic:
SAMPLE: upd.exe (9f2c…a41b), detonated by double-click simulation in the isolated Windows 10 analysis VM (host-only network, no shared folders/clipboard, clean snapshot 'SBX-CLEAN-01')
RUN METHOD: 1) Regshot snapshot of registry + file system before execution. 2) Full monitoring stack live: Sysmon, Procmon (boot logging off, process tree kept), Process Explorer, Autoruns baseline saved. 3) Execute as a standard user (matching the incident's jsmith context), observe 10 minutes. 4) Regshot second shot + Autoruns diff; export Sysmon EVTX and Procmon PML before reverting the snapshot.
WATCH ITEMS FROM SBX-01: Run key write (Sysmon 13), scheduled task creation (4698/Sysmon 1 schtasks), self-copy or drop into a second path, child processes spawned.
items.ev:
Observed behavior (sandbox run, T = execution):
T+2s — upd.exe spawns cmd.exe, which runs a short whoami/ipconfig pair (the HUNT-06 discovery pattern, compressed).
T+5s — Sysmon 13: Run key 'UpdateCheck' set to C:\Users\Public\upd.exe — byte-identical to the Project 1 T1547.001 event from the real incident.
T+7s — schtasks creates task '\UpdateCheck' (logon + hourly) — reproduces Project 1's T1053.005 rule event.
T+9s — WMI __EventFilter/CommandLineEventConsumer 'UpdaterHealth' created (daily 03:00) — reproduces HUNT-04's hidden persistence, the mechanism the original rule pack missed.
T+15s — upd.exe copies itself to C:\ProgramData\updhost.exe (a second foothold path not seen in the incident telemetry).
Regshot summary: 41 registry values set, 6 files created in the first minute. Autoruns diff shows exactly the three persistence entries above — no service, no DLL hijack planted.
MATCH: sandbox persistence = incident persistence, plus one extra self-copy path to hunt retroactively.
items.triage:
1. Retro-hunt the new indicator: search all incident hosts for C:\ProgramData\updhost.exe and its hash — the incident telemetry never showed it, which may mean a missed copy or a sandbox-only branch; record which.
2. Confirm the three persistence mechanisms are all in the detection pack now (Run key and task from Project 1, WMI consumer graduated in HUNT-04) and that each fires on these sandbox events.
3. Export the full process tree as the sample's behavior record; attach it to the incident file next to the HUNT-02 parent-child chain.
4. Revert the VM to SBX-CLEAN-01 and verify the clean state (snapshot hash + Autoruns baseline) before the next sample — persistence left behind would contaminate SBX-03 onward.
5. Note the execution context: run once more as administrator later only if a behavior gap needs it; the incident ran as a standard user and the sandbox verdict must describe that context.
items.fp: Caveats: a sandbox run proves what the sample CAN do in this environment, not everything it did on the victim host — locale, domain membership, and installed software all gate behavior branches. The ProgramData self-copy is the honest example: it may be a branch the incident host's conditions never triggered, so it is recorded as 'observed in sandbox, not observed in incident' rather than silently added to the incident timeline. Reverting and re-running once confirmed the persistence set is deterministic, not timing luck.

items.title: Network behavior: upd.exe beaconing and stage2 download against a simulated internet
items.src: Sandbox network telemetry: Wireshark (host-only tap), FakeNet-NG / INetSim simulated services, Sysmon 3 + 22
items.logic:
SAMPLE: upd.exe (9f2c…a41b), second detonation, networking enabled ONLY to the sandbox's simulated internet (FakeNet-NG answering DNS/HTTP/TLS on the host-only segment; the real C2 is never contacted)
RUN METHOD: 1) Route the VM's default gateway to the FakeNet host; verify with a browser test that no route to the real internet exists (isolation check logged). 2) Detonate, capture full PCAP for 15 minutes. 3) Let FakeNet answer: DNS responses, an HTTP 200 with a harmless marker body for payload requests, TLS with a sandbox cert to observe SNI/paths before any pinning failure. 4) Extract: destinations, ports, intervals, payload sizes, URLs requested, user agent, DNS names (expected: none — hard-coded IP).
COMPARE AGAINST: INV-05's metronome beacon, HUNT-07's jittered beacon, and the HUNT-01 certutil download of /stage2.dat.
items.ev:
Observed network behavior (PCAP + FakeNet log):
T+20s — first TCP connection directly to 198.51.100.23:8443, no preceding DNS query (Sysmon 22 empty) — confirms the hard-coded-IP design ENR-02 inferred from intel.
Beacon: POST /api/v2/ping every ~5 minutes with jitter (intervals 4m12s– 6m48s, matching HUNT-07's jitter ratio ~0.4), body 380–460 bytes, TLS ClientHello with no SNI; FakeNet's sandbox cert is accepted without pinning complaints — the implant does not validate certificates, so its traffic is interceptable in principle.
T+1m — GET /stage2.dat over the same channel when FakeNet returns the 'tasking' response body — the sample itself fetches the second stage; in the incident this download was (also) done by certutil (HUNT-01), meaning the actor had two delivery paths for the same payload.
Check-in body decodes (after the sandbox TLS termination) to a host fingerprint: hostname, user, OS build, and the string 'updhost' — matching the SBX-02 self-copy name.
No other destinations in 15 minutes: one C2, one port, no fallback domain observed in this run.
items.triage:
1. Feed the exact request profile (path /api/v2/ping, port 8443, payload band, jitter band, no-SNI TLS) into the Project 1/4 detections — INV-05 and HUNT-07 now have sandbox-measured parameters instead of estimates.
2. Record the no-certificate-validation finding: it upgrades the network team's options (TLS interception would see this traffic) and belongs in the incident record.
3. Hunt proxy/firewall logs for the /stage2.dat path AND the /api/v2/ping path separately — hosts that only show the second path were infected by the sample directly, not via the certutil route.
4. Keep the PCAP as evidence with the run record; it is the cleanest C2 evidence the project set owns (the incident captures were firewall logs, not payloads).
5. Never re-run this sample with real networking to 'see the real server': the simulated responses answered every research question, and contacting live C2 is out of scope for this lab.
items.fp: Caveats: simulated services change behavior — a real server might task the implant differently, and some implants fingerprint FakeNet/INetSim defaults and go quiet (none did here; the check-in arrived on schedule). Absence of a fallback domain in 15 minutes does not prove none exists (longer runs and different FakeNet responses are the way to probe, noted as follow-up). TLS interception worked because this sample skips validation; do not generalize that to other families.

items.title: The undocumented sample: stage2 payload (44d0…c9e2) detonated — injection and C2 handshake documented
items.src: Sandbox VM telemetry: Sysmon (1, 3, 7, 8, 10), Process Monitor, API monitoring, FakeNet-NG, memory snapshot of the target process
items.logic:
SAMPLE: stage2 payload, SHA-256 44d0…c9e2, delivered in the incident as stage2.dat from 198.51.100.23:8443/stage2.dat and renamed to a .dll (HUNT-01/HUNT-03). ENR-05 verdict: malicious on local evidence alone, ZERO external detections, behavior undocumented — this run exists to document it.
RUN METHOD: 1) Static pass first: PE32 DLL, exports a single ordinal + a named export 'Run', entropy 6.9 (less packed than upd.exe), imports concentrated in VirtualAllocEx/WriteProcessMemory/CreateRemoteThread/NtUnmapViewOfSection territory plus WinHTTP. 2) Execute the way the incident did: rundll32.exe stage2.dll,Run from C:\Users\Public, standard user, FakeNet networking as in SBX-03. 3) Watch specifically for: process injection (Sysmon 8/10), which process it targets, what the injected code does next (network, file reads), and any on-disk drops. 4) Take a memory snapshot of the target process before reverting, for Project 7.
items.ev:
Observed behavior (sandbox run):
T+1s — rundll32 loads stage2.dll; the DLL immediately allocates RWX memory in its own process and unpacks a second PE in memory (never written to disk — explains why no second file hash exists in the incident record).
T+3s — Sysmon 10: rundll32 opens explorer.exe with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1fffff); Sysmon 8: remote thread created in explorer.exe, start address in unbacked memory — the exact HUNT-05 pattern, now attributed: HUNT-05 saw upd.exe injecting; this run shows the stage2 code is the component that performs/assists injection when loaded.
T+6s — the injected explorer.exe thread opens the C2 channel to 198.51.100.23:8443 with the same /api/v2/ping profile as SBX-03 (same jitter band) — the beacon HUNT-07 attributed to 'explorer.exe' is this payload running inside it.
T+30s onward — injected code enumerates Documents/Desktop file lists (names only in this run) and idles on C2 tasking; with FakeNet returning a 'collect' task marker, it began reading files — the HUNT-08 staging behavior's engine, interrupted by ending the run.
Drops: none on disk. Persistence: none of its own — it relies on upd.exe's mechanisms (SBX-02) to be re-launched.
DOCUMENTED VERDICT: stage2 is the implant core — in-memory unpacker, injector, C2 client, and collection engine. ENR-05's local-evidence verdict is now behavior-confirmed.
items.triage:
1. Update ENR-05's record: verdict stays malicious, basis upgrades from 'local evidence, no external corroboration' to 'behavior-confirmed in sandbox (SBX-04)' — the confidence history stays visible.
2. Re-attribute the incident timeline: HUNT-05's injection and HUNT-07's explorer.exe beacon now have a named component; note in the timeline that upd.exe is the loader/persistence owner and stage2 is the implant.
3. Detections to graduate: rundll32 loading an unsigned DLL from a user-writable path, and Sysmon 8 with unbacked start module (already graduated in HUNT-05) — test both against this run's exported EVTX.
4. Preserve the explorer.exe memory snapshot for Project 7: the unpacked in-memory PE exists only there, and extracting it is a forensics task, not a sandbox one.
5. Share the documented behavior (not the sample) back to the intel record so the next analyst who meets hash 44d0…c9e2 inherits a behavior report, not a blank page.
items.fp: Caveats: the run reproduces the incident's loading method (rundll32 + the 'Run' export) because that is how the actor used it; other exports/entry points may hold other behavior this run did not reach. FakeNet's 'collect' task marker was a guessed tasking word — the file-reading it triggered matches HUNT-08's shape, but the real server's tasking vocabulary is unknown, so behaviors gated on unrecognized tasking may remain unseen. In-memory-only payloads are also the sandbox's blind spot for disk-based tooling: without Sysmon 8/10 and the memory snapshot, this sample would have looked like a quiet DLL.

items.title: Lure analysis: Invoice_Q3.docm — the macro that started the incident
items.src: Sandbox VM (Office installed, macros enabled in the sandbox profile only): Sysmon 1, Process Monitor, macro extraction (olevba-style) on a copy
items.logic:
SAMPLE: Invoice_Q3.docm, the email attachment from HUNT-02 (Word spawned cmd/PowerShell at 14:58 on WIN-LAB01)
RUN METHOD: 1) Static first, on a copy, without opening in Word: extract the VBA project and read the macro code (AutoOpen/Document_Open entry points), list external templates/URLs, note obfuscation style. 2) Dynamic: open the original in the sandbox VM's Word with the lab macro policy, FakeNet networking, full Sysmon/Procmon capture; click 'Enable Content' as the victim did. 3) Record the full descendant process tree and every file/URL the macro touches. 4) Compare the decoded PowerShell against Project 1's T1059.001 sample event — byte-for-byte if possible.
items.ev:
Static (macro extraction): Document_Open runs an AutoOpen sub; the VBA is lightly obfuscated (string concatenation + Chr() building). Decoded strings: a PowerShell command line with -w hidden -enc, and the base64 blob from Project 1's sample event. No external template, no second URL in the macro itself.
Dynamic (sandbox Word):
T+0 — WINWORD.EXE opens the document; 'Enable Content' clicked.
T+1s — Word spawns cmd.exe /c powershell -w hidden -enc <blob> — reproduces HUNT-02's parent-child chain exactly.
T+4s — decoded PowerShell (captured from the sandbox process command line + script-block logging) downloads http://198.51.100.23:8443/upd.exe into C:\Users\Public\upd.exe and executes it — the delivery step HUNT-02 inferred but the incident logs never directly showed: the macro fetches upd.exe itself.
T+10s — upd.exe begins its SBX-02 behavior (persistence writes) inside the same run; run ended and snapshot reverted at T+60s.
FULL CHAIN NOW DOCUMENTED: email attachment → macro → encoded PowerShell → upd.exe download → persistence → stage2 → injection → beacon → staging → encryption (Projects 1 to 4 each held a piece).
items.triage:
1. Close HUNT-02's last open question (how upd.exe arrived) in the incident record: the macro downloads it directly; no separate dropper exists.
2. Email-side actions: search the gateway for the document's hash and subject pattern across all recipients (phishing is never sent once), and add the decoded PowerShell string pattern to the Project 1 encoded-PowerShell rule's test set.
3. Policy note for the write-up: the sandbox needed macros enabled to reproduce this — the production control is the opposite (block macros in internet-sourced documents, Mark-of-the-Web enforcement), and the sandbox profile must never be copied to a real workstation.
4. Preserve the decoded macro + decoded PowerShell as text evidence; they are safe artifacts that make the incident teachable without handling the live document.
5. Verify the document hash against ENR records and the gateway logs so the 'who else received it' hunt (ENR-04 triage) can finally close.
items.fp: Caveats: macro behavior can be environment-aware (this one was not — it fired immediately), and a document opened without clicking Enable Content shows nothing, which is a user-action dependency worth stating plainly in the findings: the control point is the click, and the Mark of the Web prompt is what stands there. Static macro extraction read this sample fully because obfuscation was light; heavily obfuscated or VBA-stomped documents (source code removed, only compiled p-code) would need the dynamic run to carry more of the verdict.

items.title: Impact behavior: anti-recovery commands and test-file encryption under observation
items.src: Sandbox VM telemetry: Sysmon (1, 11), Process Monitor, planted test-file set with known hashes, canary files (Project 3 design)
items.logic:
SAMPLE: upd.exe (9f2c…a41b), third detonation, this time with a prepared victim profile: a Documents/Desktop tree of harmless test files (known hashes, mixed types), Project 3's canary files planted first/last per folder, and FakeNet tasking primed so the run proceeds past check-in.
RUN METHOD: 1) Snapshot with the test-file tree in place; record the tree's hash inventory. 2) Detonate; let the run proceed through persistence and C2 check-in. 3) When FakeNet returns the tasking marker, watch for the Project 3 sequence: anti-recovery commands (vssadmin/wbadmin/bcdedit), then file access at scale. 4) Measure: time from execution to first anti-recovery command, canary hit order, files/minute, extension applied, note dropped. 5) Kill the run before it exhausts the test tree; diff the hash inventory; revert.
SAFETY: test files only, host-only network, snapshot reverts everything — no real documents ever enter this VM.
items.ev:
Observed impact behavior (sandbox run):
T+3m (after two C2 check-ins and the FakeNet tasking marker) — upd.exe spawns the anti-recovery trio in Project 3's BEH-02 order: wbadmin delete catalog -quiet, vssadmin Delete Shadows /all /quiet, bcdedit recoveryenabled No. In the sandbox these succeed against the VM's own shadow copies — the commands are real, only the data is fake.
T+3m20s — encryption pass begins on the planted tree: files rewritten and renamed with the .lockbit extension at ~70 files/minute (slower than the incident's 212/3min burst — single VM, small files; rate recorded as environment-dependent).
Canary order: Documents canary fired first, Desktop 40s later — same folder order as BEH-03's incident timings, which corroborates that the incident's canary sequence reflected the encryptor's traversal order, not chance.
Per-folder RESTORE_FILES.txt dropped after each folder's pass; note content byte-identical to YARA-01's incident sample, same test wallet string.
Test-tree diff: 100% of planted files in scope were processed; files above ~50 MB were processed partially (first/last blocks) — intermittent/partial encryption behavior the Project 3 simulation could not reproduce, now observed directly.
TIMELINE FOR THE RECORD: execution → persistence <10s → first check-in 20s → anti-recovery at tasking (~3m) → full test tree encrypted in ~4m.
items.triage:
1. Update Project 3's detection timings with sandbox-measured reality: anti-recovery still fires first, canary still beats the volume threshold, and add the partial-encryption note (large files may look 'mostly intact' while being unrecoverable — scope checks must test content, not extensions alone).
2. Confirm BEH-02/BEH-03/BEH-01 all fire on this run's exported telemetry; any that miss gets tuned now, with the sandbox EVTX as the test case.
3. Record the tasking dependency honestly: encryption waited for C2 tasking in this run — an actor who cannot reach C2 might never encrypt, which cuts both ways for containment (blocking C2 early may prevent the impact phase entirely).
4. Keep the encrypted test files + one note as the standing YARA test set (they replace the synthetic samples Project 3 started with).
5. Revert and verify clean snapshot; the impact run leaves the VM in its dirtiest state, so the post-run integrity check (snapshot hash, Autoruns baseline, test-tree inventory) is mandatory, not optional.
items.fp: Caveats: rates and timings are this VM's, not the incident's — CPU, file sizes, and the FakeNet tasking delay all move them, so the report records ranges and dependencies rather than a single 'time to encryption' number. Partial encryption of large files was observed once; whether it is size-triggered or a configurable actor setting cannot be settled from one run, and the findings say so. The sandbox also cannot answer the recovery question that matters most (do the backups survive) — that is Project 7 and the recovery plan's territory, not a detonation result.

items.title: Evasion behavior: environment checks and delayed execution in upd.exe
items.src: Sandbox VM telemetry: API monitoring (sleep/timing calls), Procmon (device/registry artifact queries), controlled re-runs with countermeasures
items.logic:
SAMPLES: upd.exe and stage2.dll, re-run specifically to hunt evasion — behaviors whose purpose is to detect analysis environments or out-wait them.
RUN METHOD: 1) Instrument for the classic checks: queries for VM artifacts (VMware/VirtualBox registry keys, device names, MAC prefixes), debugger checks, sleep calls and timing loops, user-interaction checks (mouse movement, recent documents count), and environment size checks (disk/RAM/CPU counts). 2) Run 1: stock sandbox profile, 10 minutes — log every check and any behavior change that follows it. 3) Run 2: hardened profile — simulated user activity (mouse/keyboard jitter, populated recent-docs, longer uptime), realistic hardware profile, extended 30-minute window with time-acceleration monitoring. 4) Diff the two runs' behavior timelines: anything that appears only in Run 2 was being withheld in Run 1.
items.ev:
Observed evasion behavior:
upd.exe — checks the number of recent documents and the system's uptime early (T+1s, before persistence): on the stock profile (fresh VM, uptime 2 minutes, empty recent-docs) the FIRST sandbox attempt at this sample produced persistence but no C2 check-in for the full 10 minutes; SBX-03's successful network run happened only after the profile was aged (uptime simulated, documents planted). The SBX-03 record is corrected by this entry: check-in is gated on a lightweight environment test, not just jitter.
stage2.dll — long sleep loop before unpacking: ~90 seconds of NtDelayExecution calls in small increments (a pattern that defeats naive 'sleep skipping' and short sandbox timeouts alike); API monitoring caught it because the unpack at T+90s was the run's first real action.
Neither sample checks for specific VM vendor artifacts or debuggers in these runs — the evasion is environmental-plausibility and patience, not anti-VM warfare.
Run 2 (hardened profile) reproduced every behavior from SBX-02/03/04 with no gaps — the countermeasure set (aged profile + 30-minute window + simulated user) is now the sandbox standard recorded in the methodology.
items.triage:
1. Correct the earlier run records (SBX-03) with the gating finding — sandbox reports must carry their environment profile, or the next analyst will 'fail to reproduce' and doubt the wrong thing.
2. Adopt the hardened profile as default: aged snapshot, planted documents, simulated user activity, minimum 30-minute runs for unknown samples.
3. Add the recent-docs/uptime check pattern to analyst notes for the family: a sample that goes quiet in a fresh VM is not benign — re-run aged before writing any verdict.
4. Record what was NOT found (no vendor-artifact checks, no debugger checks) with the same care: absence claims define what the sandbox does not need to harden next.
5. Feed the sleep-loop observation to Project 4's hunt backlog: long pre-activity delays are also a telemetry trait (a process that does nothing for 90 seconds, then injects, is a huntable shape).
items.fp: Caveats: environment checks are also legitimate software behavior — installers check disk/RAM, updaters check uptime, and plenty of benign code sleeps. The evasion verdict here rests on sequence and company (checks immediately before persistence/injection, in samples already convicted on behavior), never on a single check. One hardened-profile success does not prove the countermeasures defeat every gate: a sample keyed to a domain-joined host or a specific application would still withhold behavior this standalone VM cannot fake, which is stated as a standing sandbox limitation.

items.title: Benign control: ~update.exe run in the sandbox — the control that validates the method
items.src: Sandbox VM telemetry: full stack (Sysmon, Procmon, Regshot, FakeNet/Wireshark) — identical profile to SBX-02/03
items.logic:
SAMPLE: ~update.exe, SHA-256 61bd…77e0, the rare unsigned Temp-path executable Project 4 left inconclusive and ENR-08 cleared as a legitimate product updater on intel evidence (globally common, 3 years in the wild, weekly recurrence).
PURPOSE: a sandbox process that only ever convicts is worthless. The control run tests the method: detonate the known-benign file under the identical hardened profile and monitoring stack, and require the behavior record to come back clean on the same watch items used for upd.exe — persistence, injection, C2 profile, anti-recovery, mass file access.
RUN METHOD: execute from its incident path (AppData\Local\Temp), standard user, FakeNet networking, 15-minute observation, Regshot/Autoruns diff, full PCAP.
items.ev:
Observed behavior (control run):
T+3s — the process checks for a running instance of its parent application, then opens an HTTPS connection to a vendor update domain (real DNS query this time — Sysmon 22 populated, the opposite of upd.exe's DNS-less pattern).
T+5s — downloads a signed update package into Temp, verifies its signature (visible in Procmon as a catalog check), stages it, and exits with a 'no update needed / already current' result against FakeNet's generic response.
Persistence: none — no Run key, no task, no WMI consumer; Autoruns diff empty. Injection: none — no Sysmon 8/10 events. File behavior: writes confined to its own Temp folder and the parent product's directories; no document-folder access. Anti-recovery: none.
Regshot diff: 3 values, all in the product's own update key (last-check timestamp and version cache) — the kind of residue a real updater leaves.
CONTROL VERDICT: behavior record is clean on every watch item that convicted upd.exe and stage2. The sandbox method discriminates; ENR-08's intel-based benign verdict and this behavior-based one agree from independent directions.
items.triage:
1. Close the control loop in writing: ENR-08 (intel) and SBX-08 (behavior) agree — file the pair as the project's worked example of a two-direction benign verdict.
2. Keep ~update.exe's hash and this behavior summary on the known-benign list used by HUNT-03's prevalence queue, with the SBX-08 run as the reference when the product's next update changes the hash.
3. No user action, no blocking: the parent application's update cadence explains the weekly recurrence Project 4 observed.
4. Re-run the control whenever the sandbox profile changes materially (new VM image, new monitoring stack): a control that starts 'detecting' is the first sign the environment, not the samples, changed.
5. Note the residual honestly in the record: benign behavior in the sandbox clears this file's observed run; it does not certify the file for all time — a trojanized update would be a new sample with a new hash and a new run.
items.fp: This entry IS the false-positive control for the whole project: the file shares upd.exe's surface traits (rare locally, unsigned, Temp path — HUNT-03's exact queue criteria) and behaves nothing like it. The discriminators were all behavioral and contextual: DNS-resolved vendor destination, signature verification of its own download, writes confined to its own product paths, zero persistence/injection/anti-recovery. Any sandbox report template that cannot produce this clean a record for a clean file will eventually manufacture a conviction — which is why the control runs under the identical profile, not a lighter one.

writeup.problem: By the end of Project 5 the incident had a paradox at its center: the two most important files were the two least understood. upd.exe had a strong intel record (ENR-04: 48/72 detections, a family label, a public sandbox report on a sibling sample), but nobody had watched THIS copy run. The stage2 payload was worse — ENR-05's verdict was 'malicious on local evidence alone' with zero external detections and completely undocumented behavior: the file that performed the injection (HUNT-05) and ran the beacon from inside explorer.exe (HUNT-07) was a black box. Project 6 builds the malware analysis sandbox that answers both: a fully isolated Windows analysis VM where the preserved samples (upd.exe, the stage2 payload, and the Invoice_Q3.docm lure) are detonated under a full monitoring stack, their behavior is recorded event by event, the extracted indicators are checked against the Projects 1 to 5 telemetry and intel, and a known-benign control file is run through the identical process to prove the method can clear a file as well as convict one.
writeup.methodology: Environment: a dedicated Windows 10 analysis VM on a host-only network segment — no route to the real internet, no shared folders, no shared clipboard, no credentials from any real system. Networking inside the sandbox goes only to a simulated internet (FakeNet-NG answering DNS/HTTP/TLS), so samples can be observed talking without ever contacting live infrastructure; the real C2 (198.51.100.23) is never contacted. A clean snapshot (SBX-CLEAN-01) is hash-checked before the project and restored after every single sample. Monitoring stack on every run: Sysmon (process, network, file, registry, injection, and WMI events), Process Monitor, Process Explorer, Regshot before/after, Autoruns diff, Wireshark PCAP, and API monitoring for timing/evasion calls. Method per sample: (1) verify chain of custody and hash against the incident record, (2) static triage first (file profile, strings, imports, capa capability mapping) with written behavior predictions, (3) detonate under the hardened profile that SBX-07 established — aged snapshot with planted documents and recent-docs history, simulated user activity, standard-user context matching the incident, minimum 30-minute observation for unknown samples, (4) record the behavior timeline and grade the static predictions, (5) extract IOCs and ATT&CK techniques and reconcile them against Projects 1 to 5, flagging anything observed in the sandbox but not in the incident (or the reverse) instead of silently merging them, (6) revert the snapshot and verify the clean state before the next sample. Samples: upd.exe (three runs — persistence, network, impact), stage2.dll (one run via the incident's rundll32 loading method), Invoice_Q3.docm (static macro extraction plus one dynamic run), and ~update.exe as the benign control. Isolated lab only; no live malware leaves this environment and no real user data ever enters it.
writeup.findings: 8 analyses completed and every static prediction graded. upd.exe reproduced the incident faithfully: Run key, scheduled task, and the WMI 'UpdaterHealth' consumer within 10 seconds (SBX-02) — plus one behavior the incident telemetry never showed, a self-copy to C:\ProgramData\updhost.exe, recorded honestly as sandbox-observed only. Its network profile matched the intel picture and sharpened it (SBX-03): hard-coded C2 IP with no DNS, a jittered POST /api/v2/ping check-in (4m12s–6m48s, 380–460 bytes), a /stage2.dat fetch, a host-fingerprint check-in body, and no TLS certificate validation. The stage2 payload is documented for the first time (SBX-04): it unpacks a second PE entirely in memory (explaining the missing second file hash), injects into explorer.exe with the exact Sysmon 8/10 pattern from HUNT-05, runs the HUNT-07 beacon from inside explorer, and begins file collection on C2 tasking — the HUNT-08 engine. It installs no persistence of its own; upd.exe is the loader and persistence owner, stage2 is the implant core. The lure closed the last gap in the chain (SBX-05): Invoice_Q3.docm's macro decodes to Project 1's encoded PowerShell event and downloads upd.exe directly from the C2 — email → macro → PowerShell → upd.exe → persistence → stage2 → injection → beacon → staging → encryption is now documented end to end with no inferred steps. The impact run (SBX-06) reproduced Project 3's sequence under observation: anti-recovery trio first, canary order matching the incident's folder order, per-folder ransom notes byte-identical to YARA-01's sample, and partial (intermittent) encryption of larger test files that the Project 3 simulation could not produce. Two method findings matter as much as the behaviors: upd.exe gates its C2 check-in on a lightweight environment test (recent documents and uptime), which silently changed an early run's results until the profile was aged (SBX-07), and the benign control ~update.exe came back clean on every watch item under the identical profile (SBX-08), agreeing with ENR-08's intel verdict from an independent direction.
writeup.challenges: Four honest difficulties. First, the sandbox changes the experiment: the environment-gating in SBX-07 meant the first upd.exe network run quietly produced a wrong-looking result (persistence but no check-in), and only comparing runs exposed the gate — a single detonation, reported confidently, would have published a false 'does not beacon in the first 10 minutes' claim. Every finding here therefore carries its run profile. Second, simulated services are a negotiation: FakeNet's responses unlocked the check-in, the stage2 fetch, and the impact phase, but the real server's tasking vocabulary is unknown, so tasking-gated behaviors beyond the ones triggered may exist unseen — the findings claim what was observed, not completeness. Third, in-memory behavior strains the tooling: stage2's payload never touches disk, so file-based evidence says almost nothing about the most important sample; the verdict rests on Sysmon 8/10, API monitoring, and a memory snapshot whose full extraction belongs to Project 7. Fourth, scope limits are real: the sandbox is a standalone, non-domain-joined VM, so domain-dependent behavior (GPO checks, AD-aware spreading, domain-joined triggers) cannot be observed here at all, and rates/timings from one small VM do not transfer to the incident host — both are stated wherever numbers appear. Safety discipline cost time throughout: hash-verifying snapshots, reverting after every sample, and re-checking isolation before each network run is slow, and it is also the entire reason the results can be trusted.
writeup.learned: A sandbox report is evidence about a sample in an environment, not a verdict from a machine: the same upd.exe produced two different network results under two profiles, and the analyst's job is to report the profile with the behavior. Static triage earned its place — the SBX-01 predictions (persistence, injection, C2, anti-recovery, encryption) were confirmed almost line by line, which means capa/strings/imports time is never wasted, and the one surprise (the ProgramData self-copy) was findable precisely because a prediction list existed to diff against. Enrichment and sandboxing answer different questions and are strongest together: intel said what upd.exe's family does and could say nothing about stage2, while the sandbox documented stage2 completely and needed ENR-02/ENR-04 to know what to watch for — and the benign control proved the pairing works in both directions, convicting on behavior and clearing on behavior. The full incident chain is now documented with no inferred links, which is what makes the merged rule pack testable: every Project 1 to 4 detection can be replayed against these sandbox exports. Next: Project 7, Digital Forensics Toolkit, takes the preserved disk and memory evidence — including SBX-04's explorer.exe memory snapshot and the in-memory stage2 image that only exists there — and reconstructs the incident timeline from the artifacts themselves.

soc.title: Digital Forensics Toolkit
soc.desc: Collect forensic artifacts and reconstruct incident timelines.
steps: Assemble your toolkit: imaging, artifact parsers, timeline tools
Practice artifact collection on a lab disk image
Reconstruct an incident timeline from the artifacts
Write up the timeline and how each artifact supports it
Collect in order of volatility: memory image before disk image, both SHA-256 verified, with a written chain of custody for every artifact
Parse the core artifact set: $MFT/USN journal, Prefetch/Amcache/Shimcache, registry hives and the WMI repository, event logs, browser and email delivery records
Build the super-timeline (Plaso/log2timeline) in UTC, measure and record each host's clock skew, and tag every event with its source artifact
Validate the timeline against the Projects 2, 4, and 6 records, close or bound every gap honestly (including the Linux log gap), and certify the eradication and recovery lists from the artifacts

items.title: Memory image: the injected stage2 payload extracted from explorer.exe
items.src: Memory image of WIN-LAB01 (captured before isolation/reboot) · Volatility 3: windows.pslist, windows.malfind, windows.netscan, windows.dlllist
items.logic:
COLLECTION: memory first, before disk — the stage2 payload exists only in RAM (SBX-04), so the order of volatility is the whole game: (1) capture RAM with a trusted imager from external media, hash the image (SHA-256) on capture, log it in the chain of custody; (2) only then pull the disk image (FOR-02).
ANALYSIS METHOD: Volatility 3 against the memory image — pslist/pstree to find the explorer.exe instance whose start time follows the 16:41 injection window; malfind to locate injected, unbacked executable memory (PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE regions with PE headers not mapped to any DLL on disk); netscan to recover the process's network connections (including closed ones the live host no longer shows); dlllist to confirm stage2.dll is NOT a loaded module — injected code is not in the module list, and that absence is itself a finding.
