EXTRACTION: dump the malfind region for explorer.exe and hash the carved in-memory PE — that file is the only complete copy of stage2's unpacked code.
items.ev:
Memory analysis record (lab capture):
windows.malfind: explorer.exe PID 4212 — 2 injected regions, VadS PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE, MZ header at region start, no file on disk backs either region (matches HUNT-05's unbacked StartModule and SBX-04's in-memory unpack).
Carved PE from the larger region: SHA-256 differs from stage2.dll on disk (44d0…c9e2) as expected — this is the UNPACKED second stage; its strings contain the C2 IP 198.51.100.23, the path /api/v2/ping, and the folder paths Documents/Desktop (the HUNT-08 collection scope).
windows.netscan: explorer.exe -> 198.51.100.23:8443, multiple ESTABLISHED and CLOSED entries spanning 16:41-23:52 — the beacon and the 22:52 exfiltration session, recovered from memory after the host's own connection table had rolled over.
TIMELINE EVENTS PROVEN: injection live by 16:41; beacon ran from inside explorer.exe until host isolation; exfil session at 22:52 corroborated by a second, independent source.
items.triage:
1. Preserve the memory image and the carved PE as primary evidence: two hashes, two custody entries, working copies only for analysis.
2. Feed the carved PE back to Project 6's queue as a new sample (unpacked stage2) — static analysis that was impossible on the packed DLL is now possible.
3. Use netscan's recovered connections to close the network timeline: any destination in memory that firewall logs missed goes to Project 5 as a new indicator.
4. Check the second injected region before attributing everything to stage2: two regions can mean two payloads; here region two is the unpacked code's data section (strings match), recorded as such.
5. Record the capture time and the imager used — memory is only defensible evidence if the collection itself is documented (see FOR-02's custody notes).
items.fp: Caveats: malfind flags legitimate injected code too — accessibility tools, some AV/EDR, and graphics overlays all create unbacked executable regions in explorer.exe on a normal host. The conviction here is the combination: region content (C2 strings, collection paths), the 16:41 timing against Sysmon 8/10, and SBX-04 reproducing the same structure. Memory also smears: a carved PE's timestamps and some strings can be stale remnants of earlier allocations, so every memory-derived claim in the timeline is marked 'memory' as its source and cross-checked against disk or log evidence where one exists.

items.title: Disk image and $MFT/USN journal: the file-system timeline of the whole incident
items.src: Write-blocked forensic disk image of WIN-LAB01 (E01, SHA-256 verified) · $MFT and $UsnJrnl:$J parsed with MFTECmd-style tooling
items.logic:
COLLECTION: disk imaged through a hardware write blocker, E01 format with acquisition hashes; the working analysis uses a verified copy, never the original. Hash on acquisition and hash again before analysis — a mismatch stops the work.
ANALYSIS METHOD: parse the NTFS Master File Table ($MFT) and the Update Sequence Number journal ($UsnJrnl:$J) together. $MFT gives every file's creation/modification times including DELETED files whose records have not been reused; the USN journal gives the ordered sequence of file operations (create, rename, delete, data overwrite) with reasons — together they reconstruct file activity even where the live file system and event logs no longer show it.
TARGET SET: upd.exe and its ProgramData self-copy, stage2.dat and its rename to .dll, Invoice_Q3.docm, docs.7z, the .lockbit-renamed files, and RESTORE_FILES.txt instances.
items.ev:
File-system timeline extracted (all times UTC, $SI timestamps cross-checked against $FN — see caveats):
14:56:12 Invoice_Q3.docm created in Downloads (browser download, FOR-06 confirms the source).
14:58:03 C:\Users\Public\upd.exe created — 5 seconds after the macro's PowerShell started (HUNT-02/SBX-05), the download the incident logs inferred, now proven from disk.
15:22:40 stage2.dat created in Users\Public; 15:23:05 renamed to stage2.dll (USN reason: RENAME_OLD_NAME/NEW_NAME pair).
18:21:5x updhost.exe self-copy created in C:\ProgramData — the SBX-02 sandbox-only observation is RETROACTIVELY CONFIRMED on the real host; the incident telemetry missed it, the disk did not.
22:47:19 docs.7z created (412 MB final size in $MFT); USN shows 1,140 document files read in the preceding minutes (HUNT-08's scope, from disk).
23:41-23:44 212 files renamed with data overwrite + extension change to .lockbit, in the same folder order the canaries fired (BEH-03); RESTORE_FILES.txt created per folder immediately after each folder's pass.
TIMELINE VALUE: every major incident claim from Projects 1 to 4 now has a disk-anchored timestamp independent of the log pipeline.
items.triage:
1. Reconcile this file timeline against the Project 2 SIEM timeline and HUNT-02/06/08: any event whose disk time disagrees with its log time by more than the measured clock skew (FOR-05) gets flagged, not averaged.
2. Promote the ProgramData self-copy finding into the incident record and the retro-hunt list: search the other hosts' images/telemetry for updhost.exe explicitly.
3. Recover the deleted stage2.dat $MFT record's resident data and the pre-encryption copies of two canary files from unallocated space for the evidence set (full deleted-file work is FOR-08).
4. Use the USN rename sequence to certify the encryption scope for recovery: the restore list comes from this journal, not from user recollection.
5. Keep the image mounted read-only for every later query in this project; all parsers run against the verified copy.
items.fp: Caveats — the classic timestamp trap lives here: $MFT carries two timestamp sets, $STANDARD_INFORMATION ($SI, changeable by user-mode tools — timestomping writes here) and $FILE_NAME ($FN, only the kernel updates it). Where they disagree, $FN is trusted and the disagreement itself is reported: in this image upd.exe's $SI creation time was backdated by ~2 days while $FN shows the true 14:58 creation — timestomping (T1070.006) recorded as an additional anti-forensic finding, not silently corrected. USN journals also wrap: this host's journal covered ~9 days, enough for the incident, but on a busier host the journal alone would not reach back — which is why $MFT and USN are always read together.

items.title: Execution artifacts: Prefetch, Amcache, and Shimcache prove what ran, when, and how often
items.src: WIN-LAB01 disk image: C:\Windows\Prefetch\*.pf, Amcache.hve, SYSTEM hive AppCompatCache (Shimcache), UserAssist registry keys
items.logic:
ANALYSIS METHOD: four independent execution witnesses, read together because each covers the others' blind spots.
1) PREFETCH (.pf): per-executable run count, last-run time (and up to 7 earlier runs on Win10), and the files/directories the process touched in its first 10 seconds — proves execution even if the binary is later deleted.
2) AMCACHE: first-seen/install timestamps and SHA-1 of executed binaries — ties a hash to a first execution time.
3) SHIMCACHE (AppCompatCache): file paths + last-modified times for executables the OS has seen; proves presence/execution interest, weaker on exact run time — used as corroboration, never alone.
4) USERASSIST: per-user GUI execution counts and last-run for jsmith — separates what the USER launched from what the SYSTEM ran.
TARGET SET: upd.exe, rundll32.exe (stage2.dll), powershell.exe, certutil.exe, 7z.exe, vssadmin/wbadmin/bcdedit, WINWORD.EXE.
items.ev:
Execution evidence extracted:
UPD.EXE.pf — run count 4, first run 2026-11-20T14:58:11Z, last run 23:38:02Z (the impact run). Prefetch's referenced-files list includes stage2.dat and the Run key's registry path — upd.exe touched both in its first seconds.
RUNDLL32.EXE.pf — run count and times consistent with the stage2 load at 15:23 and a second load at 16:40 (one minute before the HUNT-05 injection) — a loading event the Sysmon record had not isolated.
CERTUTIL.EXE.pf — 1 run, 15:22:41Z, referencing stage2.dat: the HUNT-01 LOLBIN download, confirmed from disk.
7Z.EXE.pf — 1 run, 22:47:19Z, referencing docs.7z and 200+ document paths: HUNT-08's staging, with the read scope visible in the prefetch file list.
Amcache SHA-1 for upd.exe matches the incident hash chain (ENR-04); UserAssist shows jsmith launched WINWORD.EXE and the document, but never upd.exe directly — consistent with the macro delivery (SBX-05), not a user double-clicking the payload.
VSSADMIN/WBADMIN/BCDEDIT prefetch entries all sit at 23:38, matching BEH-02's anti-recovery window.
items.triage:
1. Build the execution table (binary, first run, last run, count, user context) and pin it next to FOR-02's file timeline — disagreements between them are investigation leads, not rounding errors.
2. Treat the 16:40 rundll32 load as a timeline correction: update the incident record so the injection preparation starts at 16:40, with Sysmon's 16:41 thread creation as the effect.
3. Hunt the other hosts for the same prefetch set: a host with CERTUTIL.pf referencing a .dat in Public is in scope even with no alerts.
4. Record run counts in the findings: upd.exe ran 4 times — persistence executions (task + WMI) account for them, which independently corroborates FOR-04's persistence artifacts.
5. Preserve the parsed Amcache/Shimcache exports with the evidence set; they are the fallback execution record if event logs are ever challenged.
items.fp: Caveats: Prefetch proves a binary ran on THIS host — it says nothing about who intended it, and it can be disabled or its files deleted by an admin-level attacker (here they survived, which is itself informative about the actor's cleanup priorities: they edited logs, not execution artifacts). Shimcache timestamps are file last-modified times, not execution times — the single most over-claimed artifact in forensic reports; this project uses Shimcache only as presence corroboration. Prefetch last-run times on Windows 10/11 are reliable, but run counts reset if the .pf is deleted and recreated, so counts are reported as minimums.

items.title: Persistence artifacts: registry hives and the WMI repository, recovered from disk
items.src: WIN-LAB01 disk image: NTUSER.DAT and SOFTWARE/SYSTEM hives, C:\Windows\System32\Tasks, WMI repository (OBJECTS.DATA), services from SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet
items.logic:
ANALYSIS METHOD: parse the offline hives and stores from the disk image — disk-resident persistence survives process death, log clearing, and (for WMI) the removal of the live subscription.
1) RUN KEY: jsmith's NTUSER.DAT — Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, value 'UpdateCheck'; the hive's key last-write time timestamps the persistence install.
2) SCHEDULED TASK: the task FILE on disk (System32\Tasks\UpdateCheck) plus the TaskCache registry keys — file creation time and the XML agree or the disagreement is a finding.
3) WMI REPOSITORY: parse OBJECTS.DATA (the WMI repository database) for __EventFilter, CommandLineEventConsumer, and __FilterToConsumerBinding instances in root\subscription — this recovers the 'UpdaterHealth' consumer even though HUNT-04 found it live; on disk it can be recovered even if later deleted from the live repository.
4) SERVICES: enumerate services from the SYSTEM hive and diff against the host role baseline (the PsExec service from Project 1's T1021.002 rule should appear or its absence explained).
items.ev:
Persistence artifacts recovered from the image:
Run key 'UpdateCheck' = C:\Users\Public\upd.exe — NTUSER.DAT key last-write 2026-11-20T18:21:09Z, matching Sysmon 13 to the second (Project 1's T1547.001 event, now disk-anchored).
Task file C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\UpdateCheck — created 18:21:07Z, XML identical to the Project 1 sample (logon + hourly triggers, upd.exe action).
WMI repository: __EventFilter 'UpdaterHealthFilter' (daily 03:00 Win32_LocalTime query), CommandLineEventConsumer 'UpdaterHealth' (upd.exe -silent), and their binding — all present in OBJECTS.DATA. The repository copy proves the subscription existed independent of the live WMI service state, and its presence closes HUNT-04's last question: the consumer fired at 03:00 during the Project 2 window (the off-hours svc activity), not just in theory.
Services diff: PSEXESVC service entry present with a demand-start config (Project 1's lateral-movement event); no other non-baseline services.
COMPLETE PERSISTENCE SET FROM DISK: Run key + scheduled task + WMI subscription + one remote-exec service — three self-starting mechanisms plus the lateral entry, all recoverable after the host is dead.
items.triage:
1. Certify eradication against this list, not against the live host: remediation must remove all four entries and the check is done on a post-clean image or the hives directly.
2. Export the WMI repository instances as evidence before any cleanup — deleting the consumer destroys the live copy, and the repository parse is the durable record.
3. Cross-date the persistence installs against FOR-03's execution counts: upd.exe's 4 runs map to initial + task + WMI firings — any unmapped run would be a new lead (here all 4 map).
4. Push the disk-recovery method into the IR playbook: for the next incident, WMI repository parsing is a standard step, since live enumeration failed to be anyone's first move in Projects 1 to 4.
5. Record the 03:00 WMI firing as a confirmed timeline event (it explains the Project 2 off-hours activity on WIN-LAB01) and update INV-06's record.
items.fp: Caveats: registry key last-write times stamp the KEY, not the individual value — a Run value added to an existing Run key updates the key time, but so does any other value change in that key, so the 18:21:09 time is corroborated by Sysmon 13 rather than trusted alone. Legitimate software writes the same locations constantly (FOR-03's FP lesson applies to artifacts too): what convicts this set is the target path (Users\Public), the unsigned binary, and three mechanisms installed within 4 minutes by one process. WMI repository parsing is also version-sensitive — a corrupt or upgraded repository can under-report instances, so a clean repository parse lowers confidence, it does not clear a host by itself.

items.title: Super-timeline: every artifact on one clock (Plaso) and the clock-skew problem solved
items.src: Plaso (log2timeline) super-timeline over: WIN-LAB01 disk image + memory-derived events, Windows EVTX/Sysmon, LINUX-LAB01 artifacts (FOR-07), firewall logs — all normalized to UTC
items.logic:
METHOD: build one super-timeline instead of five partial ones.
1) INGEST: Plaso parsers over the disk image (MFT, registry, prefetch, EVTX, browser), the Linux artifacts, and the firewall CSV, each event keeping its SOURCE tag — an event without a named source does not enter the timeline.
2) NORMALIZE: everything to UTC. The lab's sources disagreed on timezone in Project 2 (Linux local vs firewall UTC); the disk image's registry TimeZoneInformation and the Linux /etc/localtime settle each host's offset from evidence, not assumption.
3) MEASURE SKEW: anchor events that two sources recorded independently (the 01:58 firewall scan vs the Linux sshd first failure; the 14:58 macro event in both Sysmon and $MFT) and compute each source's offset: WIN-LAB01 +0s (NTP-disciplined), LINUX-LAB01 +74s fast, FW-EDGE -3s. Apply the corrections and RECORD them — a corrected timeline that hides its corrections is not evidence.
4) QUERY: filter the super-timeline per actor value (IPs, accounts, hashes, process names) to produce the incident narrative in FOR-05's sample and the findings.
items.ev:
Super-timeline, key events (UTC, skew-corrected, source in brackets):
01:58:02 scan of 38 ports [firewall] → 02:03-02:07 SSH brute force + deploy logon [Linux auth.log/journald] → 02:09 sudoers edit + support2 created [Linux, FOR-07] → 02:11-02:14 RDP brute force + jsmith logon [Windows EVTX] → 02:12-02:47 Linux auth.log GAP [absence — bounded by FOR-07] → 03:00 WMI UpdaterHealth firing + first beacon [WMI repo + firewall]
14:56:12 Invoice_Q3.docm downloaded [browser + $MFT] → 14:58:03 macro → PowerShell → upd.exe created [Sysmon + $MFT + prefetch] → 15:05 discovery burst [Sysmon] → 15:22 certutil stage2 download [Sysmon + prefetch] → 16:40 rundll32 loads stage2 [prefetch] → 16:41 injection into explorer.exe [Sysmon 8/10 + memory] → 18:21 persistence trio installed [registry + task file + WMI repo] → 22:47 docs.7z staging, 1,140 files read [USN + prefetch] → 22:52 exfil session [firewall + memory netscan] → 23:38 anti-recovery trio [Sysmon + prefetch] → 23:40 canary order Documents→Desktop [$MFT/FIM] → 23:41-23:44 encryption pass, 212 files [USN journal]
Every line carries at least one disk/memory source: the timeline no longer depends on the log pipeline the attacker edited.
items.triage:
1. Publish the timeline as the incident's single narrative: Projects 2 and 4's timelines are superseded by this one, and the corrections (16:40 rundll32 load, ProgramData self-copy at 18:21, 03:00 WMI firing) are listed as explicit deltas.
2. Mark confidence per event in the stored copy: proven (two+ sources), supported (one disk/log source), inferred (gap-bounded, FOR-07) — readers must be able to see which is which.
3. Hand the corrected per-host clock offsets to the SIEM team: LINUX-LAB01's +74s skew is a configuration defect to fix, not just a forensic footnote.
4. Use the timeline to certify dwell time and scope for the incident report: first malicious event 01:58, first compromise 02:07, data staged 22:47, impact 23:41 — all artifact-backed.
5. Archive the Plaso storage file with the evidence set so any event in the narrative can be re-queried to its raw artifact.
items.fp: Caveats: a super-timeline is only as honest as its gaps — Plaso cannot ingest what was never recorded, so the 02:12-02:47 Linux gap appears in the output as an explicit absence, not a smooth narrative bridge. Timestamp precision varies by artifact (USN and EVTX to the second or better; Shimcache only file-times; memory-derived times inherit the capture context), and the stored timeline keeps each event's native precision instead of pretending uniform accuracy. Skew corrections are measurements with error bars (±2s here), so events within a few seconds across hosts are reported as 'same window', never as a false-precision sequence.

items.title: Delivery artifacts: browser history, Zone.Identifier, and the email trail of Invoice_Q3.docm
items.src: WIN-LAB01 disk image: browser history (Edge/Chrome SQLite), Zone.Identifier alternate data streams, Outlook/OWA cache remnants, Downloads folder artifacts
items.logic:
ANALYSIS METHOD: prove the lure's arrival from the endpoint side, because the email gateway's retention had already rolled over.
1) BROWSER HISTORY: parse the browser's History SQLite (urls + downloads tables) for Invoice_Q3.docm: source URL, referrer chain, download start/complete times, and the tab's session history before it.
2) ZONE.IDENTIFIER ADS: read the file's ZoneId=3 alternate data stream — the Mark of the Web — which records that the file came from the internet zone and (for browser downloads) the exact source and referrer URLs.
3) MAIL TRAIL: search the image for the attachment's other copies — Outlook's attachment cache / OST remnants and the mail client's local store — to establish whether it arrived by mail, browser download, or both.
4) CORRELATE: the arrival time must sit immediately before FOR-02's 14:56:12 $MFT creation and HUNT-02's 14:58 Word launch; the three sources must tell one story.
items.ev:
Delivery evidence extracted:
Browser downloads table: Invoice_Q3.docm, downloaded 2026-11-20T14:56:09-14:56:12Z from a webmail attachment URL (the user's Outlook on the web session) — so the 'email attachment' of HUNT-02/SBX-05 reached the disk as a browser download from webmail, which is why no Outlook desktop cache copy exists.
Zone.Identifier on the file: ZoneId=3, HostUrl = the webmail attachment service URL, ReferrerUrl = the webmail inbox — Mark of the Web present and intact: the file was internet-sourced, and Office's protected-view/MOTW controls were the control point the user's Enable Content click bypassed (SBX-05).
Session history: the inbox tab shows the message opened at 14:55, attachment downloaded at 14:56, and no other attachments downloaded that day — scoping the lure hunt to this one message.
$MFT creation 14:56:12 = download completion time exactly: three independent artifacts (browser DB, ADS, $MFT) agree to the second.
TIMELINE EVENTS PROVEN: initial access vector = phishing email opened in webmail, attachment downloaded 14:56, executed 14:58. The gateway-side hunt from ENR-04 can now be scoped by sender/message from the webmail record instead of by hash alone.
items.triage:
1. Extract the sender and message identifiers from the webmail record and hand them to the mail team for the tenant-wide search ENR-04 started — endpoint evidence just made that search precise.
2. Record the MOTW finding in the incident report: the control existed and was bypassed by a user click, which directs remediation at training + macro policy (block internet-sourced macros), not at a missing tool.
3. Check the browser history for the actor's other touches: no C2 or payload URLs appear in the browser (the downloads were LOLBIN/sample-driven, HUNT-01/SBX-03) — recorded as a negative finding.
4. Preserve the History SQLite and the file's ADS in the evidence export; ADS streams are lost if the file is copied carelessly, so the lure is stored as a forensic container copy, not a plain file copy.
5. Close the delivery question in the incident record: vector proven from three endpoint artifacts after gateway logs expired — the standing lesson is to image endpoints before retention windows close.
items.fp: Caveats: browser history is user-context evidence — it shows what this browser profile did, and a shared or synced profile can blur who clicked; here the host is single-user and UserAssist (FOR-03) ties the Word launch to the same account and minute. Zone.Identifier can be stripped by some download paths and archivers, so its ABSENCE would prove nothing — its presence, with URLs, is the strong direction. Webmail-in-browser also means 'email artifact' and 'browser artifact' are the same evidence on modern endpoints; reports should say webmail explicitly rather than implying a desktop mail client.

items.title: Linux forensics: LINUX-LAB01 artifacts bound the 02:12-02:47 log gap instead of guessing it
items.src: LINUX-LAB01 disk image: journald (persistent), wtmp/btmp, /home/deploy/.bash_history, /etc/passwd + /etc/sudoers with backups, auth.log remnants, file mtimes
items.logic:
ANALYSIS METHOD: the auth.log was truncated during the incident (INV-08) — so reconstruct the Linux side from the artifacts the attacker did not clean.
1) JOURNALD: the persistent journal keeps its own binary log with monotonic + realtime timestamps; entries the rsyslog/auth.log path lost can survive here, and journal integrity (sealed/rotated segments) is checked first.
2) SESSION RECORDS: wtmp (logins) and btmp (failed logins) are binary databases most cleanup scripts forget — parse with last/utmpdump for the deploy session's true span.
3) SHELL HISTORY: deploy's .bash_history (and root's) — written at shell exit, often surviving a live cleanup; timestamps are absent by default, so sequence is evidence, exact times are not.
4. ACCOUNT ARTIFACTS: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/sudoers and their '-' backups (passwd-, sudoers-) — diffing current vs backup recovers WHAT changed even when the log of the change is gone.
5) FILE MTIMES: sudoers/passwd mtimes bound WHEN the change landed, cross-checked against journald.
items.ev:
Linux reconstruction results:
journald: intact and persistent — it holds sshd and sudo entries for the full night, including 41 events inside the auth.log gap window (02:12-02:47). The gap was an auth.log truncation, not a logging outage: INV-08's tampering assessment is confirmed and its unknown window SHRINKS from 35 minutes to the events journald also lacks (none found — journald coverage is complete for this host).
Gap-window events recovered: deploy's sudo session continues (a crontab -e for deploy at 02:19 — a Linux persistence mechanism Projects 2 never saw), support2's first SSH key added to authorized_keys at 02:26, and the auth.log truncation command itself at 02:31 (journald recorded the shell's systemctl/rsyslog interaction and the file write).
wtmp: deploy session 02:07-03:12 from 203.0.113.87 (matches INV-02, extends the session end 25 minutes past the last auth.log entry); btmp confirms the 47 failures' exact span.
.bash_history (deploy): the INV-03 sequence in order — visudo, useradd support2, passwd support2 — plus crontab -e, the authorized_keys edit, 'history -c', and the truncation: the actor's own cleanup list, preserved by the shell they forgot to scrub.
sudoers vs sudoers- diff: exactly one added line (support2 ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL); passwd mtime 02:10 matches INV-03's sudo timestamps.
TIMELINE EVENTS PROVEN: full Linux night reconstructed — compromise 02:07, persistence (sudoers + account + cron + SSH key) 02:09-02:26, log tampering 02:31, session end 03:12.
items.triage:
1. Update INV-08's record: the 'unknown' window is closed by journald — revise the incident report's Linux section from bounded-unknown to artifact-proven, and credit the correction explicitly.
2. Add the two newly found persistence mechanisms (deploy crontab, support2 authorized_keys) to the eradication checklist for LINUX-LAB01; the Project 2 cleanup missed both because it worked from the truncated log.
3. Fleet lesson into the playbook: forward logs off-host AND verify journald persistence — this host was saved by a default nobody remembered enabling.
4. Preserve the journal files and wtmp/btmp in the evidence set with their hashes; binary logs need their native parsers documented for reproducibility.
5. Re-run the Project 2 Linux patterns (INV-02/03) against the journald export so the SIEM record is complete for the merged timeline (FOR-05 already ingested these events).
items.fp: Caveats: .bash_history is the most over-trusted artifact on Linux — it is written at shell exit (a killed shell loses it), it can be edited by the account owner, and it carries no timestamps; here it is used for SEQUENCE and corroborated line-by-line against journald and file mtimes before any line is believed. Journald itself is not tamper-proof against root — a thorough attacker can delete journal files — so the honest claim is narrower: on THIS host the journal survived and is internally consistent with wtmp, mtimes, and the firewall record. The truncation at 02:31 also means auth.log-based detections (Project 2) have a permanent blind spot that only off-host forwarding truly fixes.

items.title: Deleted-artifact recovery: carved log records, the original stage2.dat, and shadow-copy diffing
items.src: WIN-LAB01 disk image: unallocated space, $LogFile, Volume Shadow Copies, $Recycle.Bin, carved EVTX fragments
items.logic:
ANALYSIS METHOD: recover what deletion was supposed to remove, from the four places deleted data actually goes.
1) UNALLOCATED + $MFT RESIDUE: deleted files whose MFT records survive (FOR-02) plus carving unallocated clusters by header/footer for the stage2.dat content and the pre-rename originals of encrypted documents.
2) $LOGFILE: NTFS's own transaction journal — a short, dense record of recent file operations that can corroborate rename/delete order for the encryption window.
3) VOLUME SHADOW COPIES: the image's surviving VSS snapshots (the attacker deleted the LIVE host's shadows at 23:38 — BEH-02 — but the disk image was taken from the FILE-LAB01-hosted VM storage whose snapshot chain predates the deletion; what survives is stated precisely in the sample) — diff a pre-incident snapshot's file set against the live set for a ground-truth change list.
4) CARVED EVTX FRAGMENTS: scan unallocated for event-log record signatures to recover fragments of any cleared log channel.
items.ev:
Recovery results:
stage2.dat original content: carved from unallocated (the file was renamed, not deleted — its $MFT record and data survived intact); carved copy's hash = 44d0…c9e2, matching the incident record exactly. The sandbox (SBX-04) and the disk now agree on the sample byte-for-byte.
Pre-encryption originals: 196 of the 212 .lockbit files have recoverable original content in unallocated/VSS diff — recovery scope for the restore plan is now a list, not an estimate. The remaining 16 were overwritten in place; recorded as unrecoverable from this image, backups are their only path.
$LogFile: corroborates the 23:41-23:44 rename order from FOR-02's USN sequence (two NTFS journals agreeing) and shows the RESTORE_FILES.txt creations interleaved per folder, matching BEH-04.
EVTX carving: 63 event-record fragments recovered from unallocated, all duplicates of records already in the forwarded SIEM copies — a negative result that matters: no additional hidden channel of activity was found in the carved set, and the report says so instead of implying one.
VSS note (precision): the live host's shadow copies were deleted at 23:38 as Project 3 recorded; the recoveries above come from unallocated space and the VM storage snapshot taken at acquisition — the report does not claim the attacker's deletion failed.
items.triage:
1. Hand the 196-file recovery list to the restore team with hashes: restore from carved/VSS copies only after hash verification, and keep the 16 unrecoverable files as the explicit backup-restore list.
2. Close the sample chain of custody: carved stage2.dat hash = preserved sample hash = ENR-05 record — three-way agreement filed.
3. Record the negative EVTX result in the findings: 'no additional activity found in carved records' is a scope statement the incident report needs, with its limit (carving is fragmentary) attached.
4. Add $LogFile corroboration to the timeline evidence for the encryption window (FOR-05 updated: encryption events now carry three sources).
5. Define the retention action: keep the disk image and VSS chain until the incident is formally closed — every recovery claim in this entry depends on them surviving.
items.fp: Caveats: carved data has no reliable timestamps of its own — a carved file's times come from its surviving $MFT record or not at all, and carved fragments can be partial or overwritten mid-file; every recovery here was hash-verified or content-checked before being counted, and the 196/212 figure excludes anything that failed verification. VSS and snapshot availability is environment luck, not a control: on a bare-metal host with shadows deleted at 23:38 this entry would recover far less, and the findings must not let a good outcome here read as a guarantee for the next incident.

writeup.problem: Every earlier project worked from copies: the SIEM's forwarded logs (Project 2), endpoint telemetry (Project 4), intel records (Project 5), and sandbox re-runs (Project 6). Copies can be edited, expire, or disagree — and in this incident all three happened: the Linux auth.log was truncated mid-incident, the email gateway's retention rolled over, and the three log sources disagreed on time. Project 7 builds the digital forensics toolkit that goes back to the originals: forensic images of WIN-LAB01 (memory and disk) and LINUX-LAB01, collected in order of volatility with hashes and chain of custody, parsed for the artifacts that survive cleanup — $MFT and USN journal, Prefetch/Amcache, registry hives and the WMI repository, journald and wtmp, browser and Mark-of-the-Web records — and merged into one super-timeline where every event names the artifact that proves it. The goal is a timeline that can be defended line by line, an eradication list certified against the disk rather than the live host, and an honest statement of what cannot be proven.
writeup.methodology: Collection: WIN-LAB01's memory was captured before isolation completed (the stage2 payload lives only in RAM — SBX-04), then its disk was imaged through a write blocker to E01 with SHA-256 acquisition hashes; LINUX-LAB01 was imaged the same way. Every artifact carries a chain-of-custody entry (what, from which host, when, by whom, hash), and all analysis ran on verified working copies. Order of volatility governed everything: memory, then disk, then the already-forwarded logs. Parsing toolkit: Volatility 3 for memory (pslist, malfind, netscan, dlllist); MFTECmd-style parsing for $MFT and $UsnJrnl:$J; Prefetch, Amcache, and Shimcache parsers plus UserAssist for execution evidence; offline registry hive parsing and a WMI repository (OBJECTS.DATA) parser for persistence; browser History SQLite and Zone.Identifier ADS for delivery; journald, wtmp/btmp, shell history, and account-file diffing on Linux; Plaso (log2timeline) to merge everything into one UTC super-timeline. Two discipline rules ran throughout: (1) every timestamp is cross-checked against a second artifact before it enters the timeline, and the $SI/$FN timestamp pair is compared on every key file so timestomping shows up as a finding instead of silently corrupting times; (2) clock skew is measured from anchor events two sources share, corrected, and the corrections recorded (WIN-LAB01 +0s, LINUX-LAB01 +74s fast, FW-EDGE -3s). Isolated lab evidence only; originals are never modified.
writeup.findings: 8 artifact analyses completed, and the incident timeline is now artifact-proven end to end. Memory (FOR-01): the injected stage2 code was carved out of explorer.exe as an unpacked PE — C2 strings, /api/v2/ping, and the Documents/Desktop collection scope inside it — and netscan recovered the beacon and the 22:52 exfiltration session from RAM after the live connection table had rolled over. File system (FOR-02): $MFT/USN gave disk-anchored times for every major event and two corrections to the record — upd.exe's $SI creation time was timestomped back ~2 days while $FN kept the true 14:58 creation, and the C:\ProgramData\updhost.exe self-copy that SBX-02 saw only in the sandbox is confirmed on the real host at 18:21. Execution artifacts (FOR-03) independently prove the full tool chain (upd.exe ran 4 times; certutil once at 15:22; 7z once at 22:47; the anti-recovery trio at 23:38) and add a 16:40 rundll32 stage2 load one minute before the injection. Persistence (FOR-04) was recovered entirely from disk: Run key, task file, the WMI 'UpdaterHealth' subscription from the repository database, and the PsExec service — including proof the WMI consumer actually fired at 03:00 in the Project 2 window. Delivery (FOR-06) is proven three ways (browser downloads table, Zone.Identifier with webmail URLs, $MFT creation to the second): phishing via webmail, downloaded 14:56, executed 14:58, Mark of the Web present and bypassed by the Enable Content click. Linux (FOR-07) is the project's biggest correction: persistent journald survived intact, so the 02:12-02:47 'gap' was an auth.log truncation, not missing history — the window is fully reconstructed, including two persistence mechanisms Project 2's cleanup missed (a deploy crontab and an SSH key for support2) and the truncation command itself at 02:31. Recovery (FOR-08): 196 of 212 encrypted files have hash-verified recoverable originals in unallocated/VSS-diff; 16 are unrecoverable from the image and are the explicit backup list. The super-timeline (FOR-05) runs 01:58 scan → 02:07 first compromise → 03:00 WMI firing/beacon → 14:56 lure → 14:58 execution → 16:41 injection → 18:21 persistence → 22:47 staging → 22:52 exfiltration → 23:38 anti-recovery → 23:41 encryption, every line sourced.
writeup.challenges: Four honest difficulties. First, artifacts disagree by design and by attack: $SI timestamps are user-changeable (the upd.exe timestomp), Shimcache times are file times rather than run times, shell history has no times at all, and each source needed its own trust rule — the timeline is a weighed argument, not a merge. Second, the clock-skew work was unavoidable and humbling: LINUX-LAB01 ran 74 seconds fast, which at incident tempo is the difference between 'before' and 'after'; the corrections are recorded with ±2s error bars, and cross-host events inside that window are reported as simultaneous, not sequenced. Third, survival was luck in two places — journald persistence and the VM snapshot chain were defaults nobody deliberately configured for forensics, and on a bare-metal host with shadows deleted and journald volatile, FOR-07 and FOR-08 would recover far less; the report credits the luck instead of dressing it up as process. Fourth, scope limits remain: memory was captured after isolation began, so early volatile state (the first beacon's process context) is gone; carved data is fragmentary and only hash-verified recoveries are counted; and nothing on either image can prove what happened on hosts that were never imaged — the timeline's scope is these two hosts plus the firewall record, stated as such.
writeup.learned: Forensics is where the incident becomes provable. Projects 1 to 6 produced a strong working story; this project is the one that can say, line by line, which artifact proves each claim — and that discipline changed the story in five places (the timestomp, the ProgramData self-copy, the 16:40 load, the 03:00 WMI firing, and the closed Linux gap), which is the best argument for doing it even when the logs look complete. The practical lessons are concrete: collect memory first or lose the in-memory payload forever; parse the WMI repository and journald even when the 'main' logs look fine, because cleanup targets the famous artifacts and forgets the structural ones; treat every timestamp as a claim needing a second witness; and record negative results and luck honestly, because the next incident's plan will be built from this report. The toolkit's outputs feed everything downstream: the certified persistence list drives eradication, the 196/16 recovery split drives restoration, the corrected timeline is the incident record, and the carved unpacked stage2 goes back to Project 6's queue as a newly analyzable sample. Next: Project 8, Cloud Security Dashboard, takes the same evidence-first approach to cloud misconfigurations.

soc.title: Cloud Security Dashboard
soc.desc: Identify cloud misconfigurations and security risks.
steps: Pick a cloud account or lab tenant you are authorized to assess
List the misconfigurations you will check for
Build the dashboard: findings grouped by risk
Document the top risks and the fix for each
Run the automated sweep (Prowler / ScoutSuite) for breadth, then hand-verify every critical and high finding with CLI configuration evidence before recording it
Prove exposure safely where the check allows it: anonymous access tests against storage, and flow-log review for network exposure, from an authorized assessment position only
Record for each check the misconfigured configuration, the risk it creates, the fix, and the legitimate exceptions, mapped to ATT&CK
Remediate in the lab tenant, re-scan to close each finding, and add Config rules so the same misconfigurations alarm on drift instead of waiting for the next assessment

items.title: Public S3 bucket: the forensic evidence bucket allows anonymous List and Get
items.src: AWS S3 bucket policy + ACL + Block Public Access settings · Prowler (s3 bucket checks) · anonymous access test from outside the account
items.logic:
CHECK: for every bucket in the account — (1) get-bucket-acl: any grant to the AllUsers or AuthenticatedUsers groups? (2) get-bucket-policy: any statement with Principal "*" allowing s3:GetObject or s3:ListBucket without a restrictive Condition? (3) get-public-access-block, per bucket and at account level: all four settings true?
FAIL = an anonymous read or list succeeds from an unauthenticated vantage point (aws s3 ls s3://<bucket> --no-sign-request, run from outside the account).
RISK: anyone on the internet can enumerate and download the bucket's contents — in this tenant, that is the Project 7 forensic images and the SIEM archive exports.
FIX: enable Block Public Access at account and bucket level, delete public policy statements, and share genuinely public content through signed URLs or a CDN origin-access setup instead.
items.ev:
Bucket: lab-soc-evidence-01 (holds the Project 7 WIN-LAB01 / LINUX-LAB01 disk and memory images plus SIEM archive exports)
Bucket-level Block Public Access: BlockPublicPolicy=false, RestrictPublicBuckets=false — relaxed during image-upload troubleshooting and never reverted.
Bucket policy statement: {"Sid":"PublicRead","Effect":"Allow","Principal":"*","Action": ["s3:GetObject","s3:ListBucket"],"Resource":["arn:aws:s3:::lab-soc-evidence-01/*","arn:aws:s3:::lab-soc-evidence-01"]}
Anonymous test from outside the account: aws s3 ls s3://lab-soc-evidence-01 --no-sign-request → success, 214 objects listed, including win-lab01-memory.raw and win-lab01-disk.e01; a test Get of the acquisition hash file also succeeded.
VERDICT: FAIL — critical. The incident's primary evidence was internet-readable. Chain of custody stays defensible only because Project 7 recorded the acquisition hashes separately from the bucket.
items.triage:
1. Remediate first, investigate second: enable Block Public Access (account + bucket) and delete the public policy statement — the exposure is live until this is done.
2. Check access reality, not just configuration: review the bucket's server access logs and CloudTrail data events for anonymous or external GetObject calls, and record what the evidence shows (and the window it cannot cover — see CLD-05).
3. Re-verify the evidence itself: re-hash the stored images against Project 7's acquisition hashes. Matching hashes = exposed but intact; any mismatch is a new incident.
4. Find the change: CloudTrail management events show who attached the policy and when (here: the upload-troubleshooting session run by the over-privileged user in CLD-03).
5. Re-run the anonymous test after the fix and file the before/after outputs as this check's evidence pair.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions exist: a bucket hosting a public website or a public dataset is public on purpose. The bar is documentation and content: the exception is recorded per bucket, the bucket holds only content meant to be public, and Block Public Access stays on for everything else. The classic misread is the AuthenticatedUsers ACL group — it means any AWS account on earth, not 'our accounts'. Tune: any bucket named or tagged internal, evidence, backup, or logs fails this check regardless of stated intent.

items.title: Root account and console users without MFA; a live root access key exists
items.src: IAM credential report (generate-credential-report) · CloudTrail sign-in and root-activity review
items.logic:
CHECK: from the IAM credential report — (1) root user: mfa_active must be true AND both root access keys inactive; (2) every console user (password_enabled=true): mfa_active must be true; (3) any enabled password that has never been used is flagged for review.
FAIL = root without MFA, any active root access key, or any console user without MFA.
RISK: one phished or brute-forced password owns the whole tenant. Project 2's incident began with exactly this shape — password-only logons against RDP and SSH; a cloud console password without MFA is the same door with every resource behind it.
FIX: MFA on root, delete root access keys entirely, and enforce MFA with a policy that denies everything except MFA self-enrollment until a device is registered.
items.ev:
Credential report excerpt (lab tenant, report generated at assessment time):
root — password_enabled=true, mfa_active=FALSE, access_key_1_active=TRUE (created at tenant setup, last used 41 days ago), access_key_2_active=false
analyst-jsmith — password_enabled=true, mfa_active=true, one access key, age 132 days (see CLD-07)
lab-deployer — password_enabled=true, mfa_active=FALSE, AdministratorAccess attached (CLD-03); this is the account that ran the Project 7 image-upload session (CLD-01)
svc-siem-ingest — password_enabled=false, keys only: the correct service pattern, recorded as such
VERDICT: FAIL — critical. Two independent account-takeover paths (a root API key and a password-only admin user) guard the entire tenant.
items.triage:
1. Enroll root MFA and delete the root access keys; verify with a freshly generated credential report, not the console banner.
2. Force lab-deployer's MFA enrollment before its next sign-in via the deny-without-MFA policy, and review its CloudTrail history for the whole unprotected window.
3. Explain the root key's 'last used 41 days ago': here it maps to the tenant setup session in CloudTrail. Unexplained root key use is an incident, not a finding.
4. Add the account-wide guardrail (an SCP / identity policy requiring MFA for console access) so the next user created cannot repeat this.
5. File the post-fix credential report with this check; it closes on report evidence only.
items.fp: Few legitimate exceptions. Break-glass accounts exist to bypass normal controls, but they are documented, vaulted, alarmed on any use, and MFA-protected wherever the platform allows. A service identity with password_enabled=false is not a finding — key-only is the correct pattern. Tune: the credential report can lag reality by a few hours, so the dashboard timestamps the report it read and never clears this check from a console screenshot.

items.title: Over-privileged IAM: AdministratorAccess on a daily-use user and a wildcard ingest policy
items.src: IAM policy documents (attached policies + policy versions) · Access Analyzer findings · CloudTrail granted-vs-used comparison (90 days)
items.logic:
CHECK: (1) list every user and role holding AdministratorAccess or an equivalent (Action:* on Resource:*) — each needs a documented, non-daily-use justification; (2) scan every customer-managed policy for wildcard actions or resources broader than its stated job; (3) compare each principal's granted permissions against the actions it actually used in CloudTrail over 90 days.
FAIL = standing admin on a daily-use identity, or wildcards that exceed the job.
RISK: the most-used identity is the most-phished one. Admin rights convert a single compromise into tenant-wide control: create users, silence logging (CLD-05), rewrite bucket policies (CLD-01).
FIX: least privilege per job, with replacement policies generated from actual usage (Access Analyzer), and admin moved to a separate just-in-time role requiring MFA.
items.ev:
Findings (lab tenant):
lab-deployer (daily-use console user, no MFA — CLD-02): AdministratorAccess attached directly to the user. Its CloudTrail usage over 90 days: 23 distinct actions (s3:PutObject, a slice of ec2:*, iam:PassRole once). Admin was granted 'to be safe' for one upload project and never revisited.
Role siem-ingest-role: customer policy 'IngestAll' = {"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:*"],"Resource":"*"} — for a job that writes to ONE prefix, siem-archive/incoming/. As written it can also read every bucket in the account and delete the evidence bucket.
Access Analyzer: 2 external-access findings, both generated from the same wildcard policy.
VERDICT: FAIL — high. Neither principal needs what it holds; both grants are convenience, not requirements.
items.triage:
1. Generate replacement policies from 90 days of CloudTrail usage and attach them BEFORE detaching admin or wildcards — least privilege without breaking the ingest job or the deployer workflow.
2. Move admin into a separate role: assumable only by named users, only with MFA, one-hour sessions. The daily user keeps read access plus its scoped writes.
3. Rescope siem-ingest-role to its single bucket prefix with write-only actions (PutObject, no GetObject, no Delete) — the role that delivers logs must never be able to read or erase them.
4. Review CloudTrail for any past use of the excess rights (PassRole and policy changes first) and record the result either way.
5. Re-run Access Analyzer after the change; zero unexplained findings is the closure bar.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: a small lab tenant will always have SOME admin path — the finding is standing admin on a daily identity, not the existence of an admin role. Time-boxed elevation during a migration is normal when it is ticketed and expires. Tune: granted-vs-used needs a full business cycle (90 days here) or seasonal jobs (quarterly restores, year-end reports) look unused and get cut, breaking them. Flag unused permissions for human review; auto-remove nothing.

items.title: Security groups expose SSH and RDP to the entire internet (0.0.0.0/0)
items.src: EC2 security group rules (describe-security-groups) · VPC Flow Logs for accepted vs rejected connection evidence
items.logic:
CHECK: every security group, every inbound rule. FAIL = any rule with CidrIp 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 on an administrative port (22, 3389). REVIEW = 0.0.0.0/0 on any non-web port (databases, dashboards, proxies). Public 80/443 passes only on a group attached to an actual public web tier.
RISK: this is Project 2's INV-01 / INV-02 written as a configuration — the lab was brute-forced through internet-facing RDP and SSH for hours. An open 22/3389 in the cloud restarts that clock on day one.
FIX: no direct admin ports at all: administer through the provider's session service (SSM Session Manager) or a VPN; where a jump host must exist, restrict its group to named office/VPN ranges.
items.ev:
describe-security-groups excerpt:
sg-lab-jump (attached to the EC2 jump host): tcp/22 from 0.0.0.0/0 and tcp/3389 from 0.0.0.0/0. Rule description: 'temp - remove after setup'. Setup finished five weeks before this assessment.
sg-lab-web: tcp/80 and tcp/443 from 0.0.0.0/0, attached to the dashboard web instance — a legitimate public tier (see FP notes).
sg-lab-data: tcp/5432 from sg-lab-web only — the correct pattern, kept as the in-account example.
VPC Flow Logs, last 7 days, jump host: 11,204 rejected inbound attempts to ports 22/3389 from 300+ distinct external IPs — the internet found it immediately. Zero accepted external admin sessions: every real admin connection came through the VPN range that was also allowed.
VERDICT: FAIL — high. The exposure is proven live by flow logs, and the legitimate path already exists, so closing the ports costs nothing.
items.triage:
1. Prove zero legitimate dependence first (flow logs: no accepted external admin sessions in 7 days; the VPN range covers all real use), then remove both 0.0.0.0/0 rules the same day.
2. Move administration to SSM Session Manager — no inbound ports, and every session is logged to the CLD-05 trail. Disable SSH password authentication on the jump host.
3. Hunt backwards: search flow logs and host auth logs since the group was created for any ACCEPTED external 22/3389 session. None found here; a single hit converts this finding into an incident run with Project 2's playbook.
4. Add the preventive control: Config rules (restricted-ssh, restricted-common-ports) so the next 'temporary' opening alarms immediately.
5. Sweep the whole account, not just this group — sibling groups created in the same setup session were checked together.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: 80/443 open to the world on a genuine public web tier is the internet working as intended (sg-lab-web passes). A short-lived open rule during a vendor support session does happen — it needs a ticket, an expiry, and the Config-rule alarm, or it becomes this finding in five weeks. Tune: alert on the port-plus-source combination (admin ports from anywhere), not on 'public security group' generally, or every web tier becomes noise and the real exposure gets ignored.

items.title: Audit logging gaps: single-region CloudTrail, validation off, GuardDuty in 1 of 3 regions
items.src: CloudTrail trail configuration (describe-trails) · GuardDuty detector list per region · log bucket policy and retention review
items.logic:
CHECK: (1) a trail exists with IsMultiRegionTrail=true logging management events in every region the account uses; (2) LogFileValidationEnabled=true; (3) the log bucket is private (the CLD-01 standard), versioned, and not deletable by the roles it audits (the CLD-03 standard); (4) GuardDuty (or equivalent detection) has an enabled detector in every active region; (5) data events are logged for the evidence and log buckets (object-level reads and writes).
FAIL = any active region unlogged, validation off, or a detection service absent where resources run.
RISK: Project 2's lesson in cloud form — the attacker truncated auth.log and only a second log source saved the timeline. A single-region trail without validation is logs that live on the box they describe.
FIX: one multi-region trail with validation, delivering to a locked, versioned log bucket; GuardDuty on in every active region; data events on for evidence and log buckets.
items.ev:
Trail and detector review (regions in use: us-east-1, us-west-2, ca-central-1):
Trail 'lab-main': IsMultiRegionTrail=FALSE (us-east-1 only), LogFileValidationEnabled=FALSE, delivering to bucket lab-soc-logs (private — passes the CLD-01 standard; see CLD-08).
Proven consequence during the assessment: the CLD-01 policy change was made in us-east-1 and IS in the trail. Two test resource changes made in ca-central-1 as part of this assessment appear NOWHERE — the region hosting the dashboard's RDS instance (CLD-06) had no audit record at all.
GuardDuty: detector enabled in us-east-1 only; us-west-2 and ca-central-1 have no detector.
Data events: not enabled on any trail — object-level access to the evidence bucket (CLD-01's central question) is recorded only by the bucket's own access logs, not by CloudTrail.
VERDICT: FAIL — high. Logging exists and looks reassuring on the console home page, while an entire region and all object-level access sit outside it.
items.triage:
1. Convert the trail to multi-region with log file validation, then prove delivery: make a test change in ca-central-1 and find it in the trail within 15 minutes. Configuration claims are not evidence.
2. Enable GuardDuty in all active regions and route its findings into the queue the SOC already works (the Project 1 rule pack gains the cloud findings feed).
3. Turn on data-event logging for the evidence and log buckets specifically — account-wide data events are a cost decision; evidence buckets are not optional.
4. Lock the log bucket: versioning plus Object Lock retention, and a bucket policy denying deletes to every role except a break-glass security role (pairs with the CLD-03 fix).
5. State the gap honestly in the assessment: activity in us-west-2 and ca-central-1 before this fix is unauditable from CloudTrail, and that limitation stays on the record.
items.fp: Cost is the real pressure here, and the honest tuning is scoping, not disabling: management events everywhere are cheap and non-negotiable; data events are enabled selectively (evidence, logs, sensitive buckets) because account-wide object logging is genuinely expensive at scale. A region with zero resources and an SCP denying its use does not need a detector — but 'we don't use that region' must be proven by the SCP, not asserted. Log file validation has no cost excuse: it is free, and it is what makes a log file evidence (Project 7's FOR-05 standard).

items.title: Publicly accessible, unencrypted RDS instance with a snapshot shared to all accounts
items.src: RDS configuration (describe-db-instances, describe-db-snapshots) · attached security group review · CloudTrail snapshot-share events
items.logic:
CHECK, per database instance: (1) PubliclyAccessible must be false; (2) StorageEncrypted must be true; (3) no snapshot shared with 'all' (public) or with external accounts without a ticket; (4) the database port is reachable only from application security groups, never 0.0.0.0/0 (pairs with CLD-04); (5) automated backups and deletion protection on for anything holding real data.
FAIL = a public endpoint, a public snapshot, or unencrypted storage on a data-holding instance.
RISK: a public snapshot is the quietest breach in cloud security — restoring a copy needs no exploit and no password, and leaves almost no trace on the source account. A public endpoint with a weak master password repeats Project 2's brute force against the database itself.
FIX: private subnets only; encryption via snapshot-copy into an encrypted instance and a swap; unshare the snapshot; rotate the master credentials into a secrets manager.
items.ev:
describe-db-instances excerpt:
Instance lab-tickets-db (PostgreSQL; holds the lab's ticketing and asset records): PubliclyAccessible=TRUE, StorageEncrypted=FALSE, DeletionProtection=false. Its security group allows 5432 only from the jump group — the one part of this entry done right.
Snapshots: manual snapshot 'tickets-pre-migration' is shared with ALL accounts (public). Any AWS account can restore a full copy of the ticketing database. The share was set during a migration rehearsal and never revoked.
Master username is the engine default, and its password follows the tenant-setup password pattern (the CLD-02 hygiene problem, reaching the database).
VERDICT: FAIL — critical on the snapshot alone: the database has effectively already been published. The endpoint and encryption findings compound it.
items.triage:
1. Unshare the snapshot immediately and record the exact window it was public. Check CloudTrail for restore-from-snapshot events by external accounts in that window — none found, recorded as checked, not assumed.
2. Rotate the master credentials into a secrets manager. A published snapshot plus a known-pattern password means the data is treated as exposed even with no restore event found.
3. Rebuild privately: snapshot, encrypted copy, new instance in private data subnets, swap the application endpoint, then delete the unencrypted original and its snapshots.
4. Enable deletion protection and automated backups on the replacement, and add Config rules (rds-instance-public-access-check, rds-snapshots-public-prohibited, rds-storage-encrypted) so this class cannot recur silently.
5. Brief the data owner with the precise exposure statement: what data, public from when to when, what access evidence exists, and what remains unknowable — the Project 7 standard for gap statements.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: a genuinely public dataset can justify a public snapshot under the same bar as CLD-01's public bucket — content intended for publication, owner sign-off, an expiry date. A development instance with synthetic data still fails if it shares a network path to real systems. Tune: 'publicly accessible' behind a restrictive security group is defense-in-depth debt, not safety — the check fails it anyway, because groups change (CLD-04 is the proof) and the endpoint flag is the control that survives a group edit.

items.title: IMDSv1 still allowed on EC2, and stale or never-used access keys
items.src: EC2 instance metadata options (describe-instances) · IAM credential report (key age and last-used columns)
items.logic:
CHECK A (instance metadata): every EC2 instance must have MetadataOptions.HttpTokens='required' (IMDSv2 only). With IMDSv1 allowed, any SSRF flaw or local process can GET http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ and steal the instance role's temporary credentials.
CHECK B (access keys): from the credential report, flag keys older than 90 days without rotation, keys not used in 90+ days (unused means delete), and keys held by users who also have console passwords (one human, two doors).
FAIL = any instance permitting IMDSv1, or any key past the age/no-use bar without a documented exception.
RISK: stolen cloud credentials are the pivot in most cloud breaches this dashboard is modeled on; stale keys and IMDSv1 are the two cheapest sources of them.
FIX: enforce IMDSv2 as the account default, scope instance roles to their job (CLD-03), rotate or delete every flagged key, and prefer short-lived role credentials over user keys.
items.ev:
Metadata and key evidence (lab tenant):
Jump host: HttpTokens=optional (IMDSv1 allowed). Its instance role is the wildcard siem-ingest-role from CLD-03 — the worst pairing in the tenant: one SSRF or one curious local process on the jump host yields s3:* credentials.
Dashboard web instance: HttpTokens=required — passes, set correctly by a newer launch template. The fleet is inconsistent, and the inconsistency is the finding's shape.
Credential report, access keys: analyst-jsmith's key is 132 days old, last used 2 days ago (active but unrotated). lab-deployer has a second key, age 210 days, last used NEVER — a live, forgotten key on the admin user; deleted during the assessment. svc-siem-ingest's key is 88 days old and used daily (passes, with a rotation note).
VERDICT: FAIL — high. The never-used admin key is the single most dangerous object in this entry: valid, forgotten, and all-powerful.
items.triage:
1. Delete the never-used deployer key on the spot — deleting an unused key breaks nothing by definition — and confirm the deletion in the next credential report.
2. Set HttpTokens=required on the jump host and re-test its workloads (session manager, ingest agent); then set IMDSv2 as the account-level default for new launches so the fleet stops drifting.
3. Rotate analyst-jsmith's key with the standard two-key overlap procedure, and put the 90-day rotation on a recurring task instead of relying on memory.
4. Shrink what a theft would buy: replace the jump host's wildcard role with the scoped ingest policy from CLD-03's fix, so even a successful metadata theft is contained.
5. Search CloudTrail for the flagged keys' historical use from unusual source IPs — a stale key that was quietly used is an incident (Project 2's method), not a hygiene item.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: some older agents and third-party appliances genuinely cannot perform the IMDSv2 token flow — they get a documented exception, a tightly scoped role, and network rules around the metadata address where the platform allows. A true service account's long-lived key is sometimes unavoidable (the ingest key here); it passes with rotation evidence and usage monitoring rather than deletion. Tune: age alone never fails a key in this dashboard — age plus no use, or age plus a human user, is the failing combination. That keeps the finding list short enough to actually act on.

items.title: Control check (passes): the log archive bucket is private, versioned, and encrypted; EBS encryption by default is on
items.src: S3 bucket configuration for lab-soc-logs (policy, versioning, encryption) · account-level EBS encryption setting · same test method as CLD-01
items.logic:
CONTROL PURPOSE: a dashboard that only fails things is as untrustworthy as a sandbox that only convicts (SBX-08). This entry re-runs CLD-01's exact standard against the tenant's log archive bucket, plus the account's storage-encryption defaults, and requires the evidence to come back clean.
CHECKS: (1) lab-soc-logs: no public policy statement or ACL grant, bucket-level Block Public Access fully on, anonymous list/get test denied; (2) versioning enabled with MFA-delete / Object Lock retention on the log prefix; (3) default server-side encryption on every bucket; (4) EBS encryption by default enabled at account level.
PASS = all four, evidenced the same way a FAIL would be.
items.ev:
Control evidence (lab tenant):
lab-soc-logs: bucket policy contains no public statement (only the CloudTrail delivery principal and the security role); Block Public Access: all four settings true; anonymous test: aws s3 ls s3://lab-soc-logs --no-sign-request → AccessDenied.
Versioning: enabled; the log prefix carries an Object Lock retention period, so delivered log files cannot be altered or deleted inside retention (the CLD-05 fix's target state, already true here).
Default encryption: SSE enabled on all buckets in the account inventory; EBS 'encryption by default' = enabled for the account.
VERDICT: PASS. The team demonstrably knew how to configure a bucket correctly — which sharpens CLD-01's lesson: the evidence bucket's exposure was configuration drift during troubleshooting, not a knowledge gap. Drift is fought with continuous checks (Config rules), not with training alone.
items.triage:
1. Keep the control in the dashboard permanently: it is re-run on every scan, and the day it flips to FAIL is the day the drift problem is proven to be back.
2. Point the Config rules (bucket-level Block Public Access, versioning, encryption checks) at this bucket as the known-good reference when tuning them for the rest of the account.
3. Use this bucket's configuration as the template for remediating CLD-01: same policy shape, same access-block settings, copied deliberately rather than improvised.
4. Record the pass with its date and evidence, exactly like a failure — an undated 'we checked once' is how controls quietly die.
5. No remediation, no user action: a pass that generates tickets teaches people to ignore the dashboard.
items.fp: A pass is a point-in-time claim with the same honesty rules as Project 7's negative results: it says these four settings held, evidenced this way, on this date — nothing more. It does not certify the bucket's contents, its access history (that is CLD-05's logging question), or next month's configuration. The control would stop passing if any one of the four settings changed, which is precisely why it is checked by the same automated path as the failures instead of by someone's memory of having set it up correctly.

writeup.problem: Projects 1 to 7 secured and then investigated an on-premise lab. The merged SOC platform those projects built now also lives in a cloud tenant: S3 buckets holding the Project 7 forensic images and the SIEM archives, an EC2 jump host for administration, and an RDS database for ticketing. Cloud breaches rarely start with an exploit; they start with a configuration — a public bucket, a password-only admin, a 'temporary' open port, logging that was never really on. This tenant was stood up quickly, under time pressure, during Projects 6 and 7, and it shows. Project 8 builds the cloud security dashboard: a repeatable set of misconfiguration checks where every finding carries the actual configuration as evidence, the risk it creates, the fix, and the legitimate exceptions, held to the same standard as the rest of the board.
writeup.methodology: Scope: one AWS lab tenant the project is authorized to assess (account alias lab-soc), three regions in use (us-east-1, us-west-2, ca-central-1), covering IAM users and roles, S3 buckets (evidence, logs, SIEM archive), EC2 instances and security groups, RDS, CloudTrail, and GuardDuty. Tooling: Prowler and ScoutSuite for the automated sweep (breadth), the AWS CLI for hand-pulled configuration evidence, the IAM credential report and Access Analyzer for identity findings, and VPC Flow Logs plus CloudTrail when a finding needed proof of actual exposure rather than theoretical exposure. Method per check: (1) let the scanner flag broadly, (2) hand-verify every critical and high finding against the live configuration before recording it — scanner output alone never becomes a finding, (3) where safe and authorized, prove the exposure (an anonymous --no-sign-request access test against storage; flow-log review for network rules), (4) record the misconfigured configuration, the risk, the remediation, and the false-positive / legitimate-exception notes, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, (5) remediate inside the lab tenant, (6) re-scan to close, and add AWS Config rules so the same classes alarm on drift. The assessment ran with read-only credentials; all changes were made deliberately, as fixes, after findings were recorded.
writeup.findings: 8 checks recorded: 3 critical, 4 high, and 1 passing control, spanning 7 ATT&CK tactics. Critical: CLD-01, the Project 7 forensic evidence bucket was publicly listable and readable (anonymous test listed 214 objects, including the disk and memory images) after a troubleshooting change was never reverted — its integrity was re-verified against the separately recorded acquisition hashes. CLD-02, the root account had no MFA and a live root access key, and the daily admin user had no MFA either. CLD-06, the ticketing database was publicly accessible and unencrypted, with a manual snapshot shared to all accounts — effectively already published. High: CLD-03, standing AdministratorAccess on the daily user (23 actions actually used in 90 days) and a wildcard s3:* ingest role that could read or delete the evidence it feeds; CLD-04, SSH and RDP open to 0.0.0.0/0 on the jump host for five weeks past their 'temporary' purpose, with flow logs showing 11,204 rejected attempts in 7 days and zero legitimate external use; CLD-05, a single-region CloudTrail with validation off and GuardDuty in only 1 of 3 regions, proven by two assessment test changes in ca-central-1 leaving no audit record at all; CLD-07, IMDSv1 allowed on the jump host (paired with that wildcard role) and a never-used 210-day-old access key on the admin user. The control, CLD-08, passed cleanly: the log archive bucket is private, versioned, locked, and encrypted, and EBS encryption by default is on. Remediation inside the lab tenant: the bucket was locked down and evidence hashes verified, MFA enforced and the root and stale keys deleted, the open admin ports closed, the snapshot unshared and credentials rotated, the trail converted to multi-region with validation, and GuardDuty enabled everywhere; the RDS encrypted rebuild is the one fix staged as a follow-up change rather than done on the spot. The pattern across findings is the real result: this tenant repeated the on-premise incident's root causes — password-only access, internet-facing admin ports, and logs the attacker could reach — in cloud form.
writeup.challenges: Four honest difficulties. First, scanner noise: the automated sweep returned dozens of findings, most informational or inapplicable to a lab tenant, and the discipline of hand-verifying every critical and high against live configuration is what turned a scanner dump into eight findings worth acting on — it is also most of the work. Second, configuration versus reality kept diverging: the jump host's rules were described as temporary, the trail looked enabled from the console home page, and only flow logs, an anonymous access test, and a deliberate test change in an unlogged region separated 'looks configured' from 'actually works'. Third, remediation has blast radius: tightening the ingest role or the deployer's permissions can break the pipeline the SOC runs on, so replacements were generated from 90 days of actual usage and attached before anything was detached. Fourth, the limits are real: this is one tenant on one provider — the check logic is AWS-shaped and would need rework for Azure or GCP; it is a point-in-time assessment in a system that drifts weekly, which is why Config rules, not this document, are the durable control; and some exposure questions are only boundable, not answerable — object-level logging was off for part of the public bucket's life, so 'no downloads found' covers the logged window and is recorded with that limit attached, the same honesty rule as Project 7's gaps.
writeup.learned: Cloud misconfigurations are process failures with configuration symptoms. Every serious finding here was a reasonable action that never got revisited: a troubleshooting relaxation, a 'temporary' firewall rule, admin granted 'to be safe', a snapshot shared for one rehearsal. Nobody chose an insecure tenant; the tenant drifted into one, and the control check (CLD-08) proves the knowledge to do it right was present all along. Evidence-first works in the cloud exactly as it did in forensics: the findings that changed behavior were the ones proven — an anonymous listing of the evidence bucket, flow logs counting eleven thousand knocks on an open port, a test change that left no trace in the logs. Identity is the perimeter in practice, not in slogan: MFA plus least privilege would have blunted five of the seven failures before any other control mattered, which sets up Project 9's Active Directory work as the same fight on-premise. And logging must be designed before it is needed: multi-region, validated, and locked away from the roles it audits — the cloud version of forwarding logs off the host. The dashboard's durable output is the check set plus the Config rules behind it, so the next drift alarms in hours instead of surfacing at the next assessment. Next: Project 9, Active Directory Security Lab.

soc.title: Active Directory Security Lab
soc.desc: Practice identity protection, access controls, and system hardening.
steps: Build a small lab domain: one DC, one workstation, test accounts
Audit password policy, privileged groups, and stale accounts
Apply hardening changes one at a time and re-test
Document before/after: what changed and why it matters
Collect the domain baseline with BloodHound/SharpHound and PingCastle plus Get-AD* exports (groups, SPNs, ACLs, delegation, password policies) and record the before state for every check

Verify each critical path safely inside the lab domain only: request an SPN ticket, test the helpdesk ACL path with a throwaway account, and run a time-boxed Responder capture to prove the LLMNR exposure
Remediate one change at a time (group membership, SPN/gMSA migration, ACL removal, delegation, hardening GPO) and re-test the affected service after each change
Re-collect and file the after state: zero SPNs on non-gMSA accounts, no unconstrained delegation, no non-Tier-0 rights over Tier-0 objects, and the control check still passing

items.title: Privileged group sprawl: Domain Admins holds daily-use, service, and leftover incident accounts
items.src: Get-ADGroupMember for Domain Admins / Enterprise Admins / Schema Admins / Backup Operators · BloodHound group membership export · Security 4728/4732 membership-change events
items.logic:
CHECK: export the effective (recursive) membership of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins, and Backup Operators. FAIL = any daily-use workstation account, any service account, or any account that also reads email / browses the web holding Tier-0 membership; Schema Admins and Enterprise Admins should be empty outside a change window.
RISK: Project 2's incident is the worked example — jsmith was phished and brute-forced as an ordinary user; if that same account is also a Domain Admin, the first foothold is the whole domain. Every extra member is another password whose theft equals domain compromise, and Backup Operators can read the DC's volume shadow copies (ntds.dit) without ever being called an admin.
FIX: Tier-0 membership limited to a small set of dedicated admin accounts that never log on to workstations, administered from a privileged access workstation; everyone else gets scoped, just-in-time elevation.
items.ev:
Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins' (LAB.LOCAL, recursive):
- LAB\administrator (built-in, expected, vaulted)
- LAB\adm-rpatel (dedicated admin account, expected)
- LAB\jsmith (DAILY-USE account — the Project 2 phish/brute-force victim; reads mail and browses from WIN-LAB01)
-LAB\svc_backup2 (service account created DURING the Project 1 intrusion, EventID 4732 — never removed, see AD-04)
Enterprise Admins: LAB\jsmith (again). Schema Admins: LAB\adm-rpatel, standing membership with no schema change in 14 months.
Backup Operators: LAB\svc-siem-ingest — a log-shipping service account that can also restore files over the DC's own volumes.
VERDICT: FAIL — critical. 6 effective Tier-0 principals where the design calls for 2, and one of them is an attacker-created account.
items.triage:
1. Remove svc_backup2 from Domain Admins immediately and disable the account — it is incident residue (AD-04), not an admin decision; review Security 4728/4732 and 4662 on DC-LAB01 for everything it did with the rights.
2. Move jsmith to a separate dedicated admin account (adm-jsmith) in the AD-08 pattern: daily account keeps no admin rights, admin account never touches WIN-LAB01's browser or mail.
3. Empty Schema Admins and Enterprise Admins outside change windows; document the add/remove procedure instead of standing membership.
4. Replace svc-siem-ingest's Backup Operators membership with a scoped backup role on the file servers only — the log shipper must never be able to restore over a DC.
5. Re-export group membership and file the before/after lists; then alert on 4732 (member added to Domain Admins) as a standing Project 1 rule so the group cannot silently regrow.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: a documented break-glass account and a small named admin team are supposed to be here — the finding is daily-use, service, and forgotten accounts, not the existence of Domain Admins. Temporary elevation for a migration is normal when it is ticketed, time-boxed, and removed on the ticket's close date. Tune: review membership on evidence (logon types per account — a Domain Admin with interactive workstation logons is the red flag), not on headcount alone; a two-person shop will legitimately have proportionally more admins than an enterprise.

items.title: Kerberoastable service accounts: SPNs on user accounts with RC4 and 6-year-old passwords
items.src: Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -like '*'} with password-age and encryption-type attributes · BloodHound kerberoastable flag · Security 4769 (TGS request) events with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4)
items.logic:
CHECK: list every account carrying a ServicePrincipalName. FAIL = an SPN on a regular user account (not a group Managed Service Account), a password older than 12 months, RC4 (0x17) tickets being issued for it, or membership in a privileged group. Any authenticated user can request a TGS ticket for an SPN and crack the RC4-encrypted ticket offline — no lockout, no alert by default.
RISK: this is credential theft that never touches LSASS and never fails a logon: one low-privilege account (or the Project 2 foothold) requests tickets, cracks at leisure, and returns as the service account.
FIX: migrate services to group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA, automatic 30-day rotation, uncrackable-length passwords), require AES (msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes), and reset any legacy SPN account's password to 25+ random characters today.
items.ev:
Kerberoastable accounts in LAB.LOCAL:
- LAB\svc-sql — SPN MSSQLSvc/db-lab01.lab.local:1433, password last set 6.2 YEARS ago, member of Domain Admins until AD-01's cleanup, TicketEncryptionType RC4. A 4769 review on DC-LAB01 shows 14 RC4 TGS requests for this SPN in one hour from WIN-LAB01 during the Project 4 hunt window — requested by jsmith's session, never investigated because 4769/RC4 was not being collected as a detection.
- LAB\svc-report — SPN HTTP/report.lab.local, password age 3.8 years, RC4 allowed.
- LAB\svc-siem-ingest — SPN on a user account, but password age 40 days and AES-only: the near-miss that shows the pattern done almost right (still a user account, still crackable in principle).
VERDICT: FAIL — critical. svc-sql combines every risk factor at once: SPN, ancient password, RC4, and (until AD-01) Domain Admin rights.
items.triage:
1. Reset svc-sql and svc-report passwords immediately to long random values and set AES-only encryption — assume the tickets already requested in the 4769 window were cracked offline; rotation is the only remediation that matters.
2. Hunt the 4769s: list every account that requested RC4 tickets for these SPNs in the last 90 days and treat unexpected requesters as investigation leads (Project 4 method), not noise.
3. Migrate both services to gMSAs in the lab and delete the SPNs from the user accounts; verify the services start under the gMSA before removing anything.
