4. Add the standing detection: alert on 4769 with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 for SPN accounts, and on any single user requesting tickets for many distinct SPNs in minutes (roasting is a burst, not one ticket).
5. Re-run the SPN export and file it: the closure bar is zero SPNs on non-gMSA accounts, or a dated exception per remaining one.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: some legacy applications genuinely require an SPN on a named account and cannot use a gMSA — they get a 25+ character managed password, AES enforced, no privileged group membership, and the 4769/RC4 alert pointed at them specifically. Requesting a TGS ticket is also normal Kerberos operation; the FP trap is alerting on 4769 volume alone. Tune on the combination: RC4 encryption type, SPN account sensitivity, and requester-to-SPN rarity — a user's first-ever ticket request for the SQL SPN is the signal, the file server's daily tickets are not.

items.title: Weak identity policy: 7-character domain passwords, no lockout, one pre-auth-disabled and one reversible-encryption account
items.src: Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy + Get-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy · account flags: Get-ADUser for DONT_REQ_PREAUTH and ENCRYPTED_TEXT_PWD_ALLOWED · Security 4625 lockout review (4740)
items.logic:
CHECK: (1) Default Domain Policy — minimum length, complexity, history, maximum age; (2) lockout threshold and duration (threshold 0 = lockout disabled = unlimited online guessing); (3) every account flag that weakens authentication: Kerberos pre-authentication not required (AS-REP roastable — anyone can request an AS-REP for the account and crack it offline, no credentials needed at all) and 'store passwords using reversible encryption' (effectively plaintext in the directory).
RISK: Projects 1 and 2 watched 12 RDP failures and 47 SSH failures succeed because nothing slowed the guessing down. This policy is why: 7 characters, no lockout, and two accounts whose hashes can be taken offline without a single failed logon to alert on.
FIX: 14+ character minimum (passphrases), lockout threshold 10 with a 15-minute duration, fine-grained policies for admins and service accounts (AD-08 shows the admin one done), pre-auth required on every account, reversible encryption nowhere.
items.ev:
Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy (LAB.LOCAL): MinPasswordLength=7, ComplexityEnabled=True, PasswordHistoryCount=5, MaxPasswordAge=180 days, LockoutThreshold=0 (DISABLED), ReversibleEncryptionEnabled=False at policy level.
Account-flag sweep:
- LAB\svc-legacy — DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set (added for an old scanner appliance, appliance retired last year). AS-REP roastable by any unauthenticated requester.
- LAB\kiosk-reports — ENCRYPTED_TEXT_PWD_ALLOWED set, so its password is recoverable in cleartext from the directory by anyone who compromises the DC — and its password is shared with two other kiosk accounts (see AD-07's reuse theme).
- Fine-grained policies: one exists (the AD-08 admin policy) and applies to admins only; service accounts fall back to the weak default.
VERDICT: FAIL — high. The domain's baseline still permits exactly the attacks Projects 1 and 2 recorded.
items.triage:
1. Clear the two account flags today: enable pre-auth on svc-legacy and remove reversible encryption from kiosk-reports, then reset both passwords — a flag change does not un-expose a hash or a cleartext password already recoverable.
2. Raise the default policy in stages (length 14, lockout 10/15 min) with comms to the lab users first; a surprise length change plus no lockout history is how you lock out a whole office on day one.
3. Add fine-grained policies for service accounts (25+ characters, no interactive logon) so AD-02's rotation fix is enforced by policy, not by memory.
4. Verify with evidence: pull a 4740 (lockout) test event by deliberately failing a lab account's logon 10 times, and re-run the flag sweep to zero.
5. Pair the policy with the Project 1 detections (T1110.001/T1110.003): lockout blunts online guessing, the rules catch what still gets tried, and password spraying (low-and-slow, under the lockout threshold) is exactly why both layers exist.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions are narrow: pre-auth disabled is sometimes demanded by genuinely old devices — the bar is a named device, a compensating long password, network restriction to that device's traffic, and an expiry date on the exception; 'an appliance we retired' is not an exception, it is this finding. Lockout tuning is a real trade-off: too aggressive and an attacker (or a forgetful user) denial-of-services every account; 10 attempts / 15 minutes is the lab's balance, and helpdesk unlock volume is the metric to watch after the change, not a reason to leave lockout off.

items.title: Stale and leftover accounts: incident-created accounts still enabled, 11 accounts dormant over 180 days
items.src: Get-ADUser with LastLogonDate / PasswordLastSet / Enabled · Security 4720 (account created) and 4725/4726 (disabled/deleted) review · BloodHound dormant-account view
items.logic:
CHECK: every enabled account against three tests — (1) no logon in 180+ days, (2) password never expires on a non-service account, (3) created during a known incident window or by a compromised creator. FAIL = an enabled account nobody can name an owner and a purpose for.
RISK: dormant accounts are pre-positioned access: their passwords are old (pre-dating AD-03's fixes), nobody notices their logon (there is no normal pattern to deviate from), and attacker-created accounts like support2 and svc_backup2 ARE persistence — leaving them enabled leaves the incident's doors installed.
FIX: disable first, delete after a 30-day hold with the owner's sign-off; every account gets a named owner and a review date; incident-created accounts are removed as part of incident closure, not discovered by the next assessment.
items.ev:
Dormancy sweep, LAB.LOCAL (142 enabled user accounts):
- LAB\support2 — created 2026-11-20 02:10 during the Project 2 Linux/Windows incident window (the Linux-side persistence account's domain twin), ENABLED, last logon: never. Nobody in the lab can say why it exists — because an attacker made it.
- LAB\svc_backup2 — created 3 minutes before its Domain Admins addition in Project 1 (EventID 4720 then 4732), still enabled (AD-01 removed its group rights; this check removes the account).
- 11 further enabled accounts with LastLogonDate older than 180 days, including 2 former contractors and a 'temp-reception' shared account; 3 of the 11 have PasswordNeverExpires set.
- 4 enabled accounts have never logged on at all and are not tied to any onboarding record.
VERDICT: FAIL — high. Two of these are not hygiene, they are unclosed incident actions.
items.triage:
1. Disable support2 and svc_backup2 immediately (do not delete yet — preserve the SIDs and group history for the incident record), then sweep 4768/4624 for any use of either account across the whole retention window before deletion at 30 days.
2. Disable the 11 dormant accounts in one change with notice to their listed managers; a disable that nobody complains about in 30 days becomes a delete — the complaint-driven test is the safest ownership check a small lab has.
3. Clear PasswordNeverExpires from every non-service account; service accounts move under AD-02's gMSA/rotation regime instead.
4. Assign every remaining account a named owner and review date in its description attribute, and add a monthly dormant-account report to the dashboard so staleness is a trend line, not an annual surprise.
5. Close the loop in the incident record: Projects 1 and 2 listed these accounts as IOCs — this check is where their removal is evidenced, closing that containment item formally.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: seasonal and parental-leave accounts, break-glass accounts (dormant BY DESIGN — they are identified, vaulted, and alarmed on any logon, which is the opposite of forgotten), and service accounts whose 'logon' is a batch type that LastLogonDate can under-report on some DC configurations — verify against all DCs (LastLogon is not replicated; use LastLogonDate / the -Properties sweep across DCs) before disabling anything that runs a job. Tune: disable-then-hold means a false positive costs a phone call, not an outage; never auto-delete on dormancy alone.

items.title: Dangerous ACLs and GPO rights: Helpdesk can edit a GPO linked to the Domain Controllers OU and holds GenericAll over the Domain Admins group
items.src: BloodHound ACL edges (GenericAll, WriteDacl, WriteOwner, ForceChangePassword) · Get-GPPermission / GPMC delegation review · Security 4662 (directory service access) on group and GPO objects
items.logic:
CHECK: enumerate who can modify the objects that control the domain — (1) ACLs on the Domain Admins group and other Tier-0 groups (GenericAll / WriteDacl / AddMember), (2) edit rights on every GPO linked to the Domain Controllers OU or the domain root, (3) ForceChangePassword rights over privileged accounts, (4) OU delegation that includes GPO-link or account-operator powers beyond its stated job. FAIL = any non-Tier-0 principal holding a path that ends in Tier-0 control.
RISK: ACL paths are quiet privilege escalation: no exploit, no malware — a helpdesk credential (the most phished credential class there is) edits one GPO, and at next policy refresh every domain controller runs the attacker's setting or script. BloodHound exists because humans cannot see these paths in the ACL editor.
FIX: strip Tier-0-object rights back to Tier-0 admins, delegate helpdesk work at the workstation-OU level only (password resets for standard users, workstation GPOs), and alert on 4662 writes to Tier-0 objects.
items.ev:
BloodHound shortest-path review, LAB.LOCAL (SharpHound collection, lab-authorized):
-LAB\Helpdesk (group, 5 members) — GenericAll on the Domain Admins group object: any member can add any account to Domain Admins directly. Granted during a staffing crunch 'temporarily', 11 months ago.
-LAB\Helpdesk — Edit rights on GPO 'DC Baseline' linked to the Domain Controllers OU: the GPO that also carries the DC audit policy from AD-08. One logon-script or scheduled-task preference in this GPO executes as SYSTEM on DC-LAB01 at refresh.
- LAB\svc-report — ForceChangePassword over LAB\adm-rpatel (a delegation experiment, never reverted): a service account can reset a Tier-0 admin's password without knowing the old one.
- Workstation-OU delegation for the same Helpdesk group (reset standard-user passwords, join computers) — correct and scoped; kept as the model for the fix.
VERDICT: FAIL — critical. Two independent one-step paths from a helpdesk or service credential to full domain control, neither of which fires any Project 1 rule until the moment it is used.
items.triage:
1. Remove the GenericAll ACE on Domain Admins and the DC-GPO edit right today; verify with a fresh SharpHound collection that both paths are gone — ACL fixes are proven by re-collection, not by the editor's OK button.
2. Remove svc-report's ForceChangePassword right over adm-rpatel and review 4662 events for any historical write by these principals to Tier-0 objects (none found; recorded as checked, with the retention limit stated).
3. Rebuild the helpdesk delegation deliberately at the workstation OU (the scoped pattern already present), and document each delegated right with its business reason.
4. Add the detection pair: alert on 4662 with AccessMask indicating write/DACL changes on the Domain Admins group, the AdminSDHolder object, and DC-OU GPOs, plus a Project 1-style rule on GPO modification events (5136/5141) for DC-linked GPOs.
5. Schedule the BloodHound collection quarterly: ACL drift is this project's CLD-style lesson — every 'temporary' grant in this entry was reasonable on the day it was made.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: Account Operators and delegated OU admins are real roles — the line is scope. Resetting a standard user's password in the workstation OU is the job; any right whose object is Tier-0 (Domain Admins group, DC OU GPOs, AdminSDHolder, a Tier-0 account's password) is not delegable, full stop. BloodHound also flags theoretical paths that group policy or AdminSDHolder's hourly ACL reset would actually stomp — verify each critical path by reading the live ACL (and, in the lab, by testing it with a throwaway account) before reporting it as exploitable; a path that SDProp resets within the hour is still a finding, but its window belongs in the notes.

items.title: Delegation abuse: unconstrained delegation on a member server and a service that can delegate to the DC
items.src: Get-ADComputer / Get-ADUser delegation attributes (TrustedForDelegation, TrustedToAuthForDelegation, msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo) · BloodHound delegation edges · Security 4624 logon-type review on the delegating host
items.logic:
CHECK: (1) every computer and account with TrustedForDelegation=true (UNCONSTRAINED delegation — the host receives a copy of every authenticating user's TGT, including Domain Admins); (2) every constrained-delegation entry (msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo) and whether its target list reaches a Tier-0 service; (3) resource-based delegation set by non-admins. FAIL = unconstrained delegation anywhere except a domain controller, or constrained delegation that can reach DC services (CIFS/LDAP on a DC).
RISK: compromise the unconstrained host and you harvest the TGT of the next admin who connects — then you ARE that admin everywhere (the printer-bug/coercion family of attacks forces exactly that connection). It converts one member-server compromise into domain compromise without cracking anything.
FIX: remove unconstrained delegation entirely; where an application truly needs delegation, use constrained delegation to its own backend service only, mark Tier-0 accounts 'sensitive and cannot be delegated', and prefer resource-based delegation owned by the resource's Tier-0 admins.
items.ev:
Delegation sweep, LAB.LOCAL:
- FILE-LAB01 (member file server, the Project 3 share-encryption victim) — TrustedForDelegation=TRUE (unconstrained), set when a legacy file-audit tool was trialled. Every user who maps a share hands this host their TGT; the host was already proven reachable by an attacker in Project 3 (BEH-06).
- LAB\svc-report — msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo includes cifs/DC-LAB01.lab.local: this service can impersonate ANY user (except delegation-protected ones) to the DC's file service — a standing path from a service-account compromise to DC file access, beside its AD-05 password-reset right. This account appears in three findings; that repetition is itself the lesson.
-WIN-LAB02 — constrained delegation to its own app backend only (HOST/app-lab02), the correct shape; recorded as the in-domain example.
- Tier-0 accounts: 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated' set on the built-in Administrator only — adm-rpatel and adm-jsmith (post-AD-01) were NOT flagged until this check.
VERDICT: FAIL — high. One unconstrained member server plus one over-scoped constrained entry, both invisible to log-based detection until used.
items.triage:
1. Clear TrustedForDelegation on FILE-LAB01 and reboot/verify the file services still run (the legacy tool is gone; nothing current needs the TGTs). Then treat historical exposure honestly: any Tier-0 logon to FILE-LAB01 while unconstrained was a potential TGT handover — check 4624s for admin connections to it and rotate accordingly if found.
2. Remove cifs/DC-LAB01 from svc-report's AllowedToDelegateTo; if the report job needs DC files, give it a read-only share permission as itself instead of impersonation rights.
3. Set 'sensitive and cannot be delegated' on every Tier-0 admin account (this also blunts AD-02-style ticket abuse against those accounts).
4. Re-collect with BloodHound and confirm zero unconstrained hosts and no delegation edge terminating on a DC.
5. Add delegation attributes to the quarterly ACL review from AD-05 — delegation is an ACL-class risk and drifts the same way.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: domain controllers are unconstrained by design (that IS Kerberos) and are excluded from the check; a small number of legacy web applications genuinely need constrained delegation to their own database — the bar is target scope (their backend, never a DC), protocol transition off unless required, and the delegation-protected flag on every privileged account so the blast radius is standard users only. 'The vendor said to enable delegation' without a target list is how FILE-LAB01 got here; the vendor conversation is about which SPN, not whether.

items.title: System hardening gaps: no LAPS, one shared local admin password, LSASS protection off, SMB/LDAP signing not enforced, LLMNR and NTLMv1 still on
items.src: GPO review (workstation and DC baselines) · LAPS / Windows LAPS deployment state (ms-Mcs-AdmPwd / msLAPS attributes) · registry evidence: RunAsPPL, RequireSecuritySignature (SMB), LDAPServerIntegrity, LmCompatibilityLevel, LLMNR policy · Responder-style lab test for LLMNR poisoning
items.logic:
CHECK, five hardening controls as one workstation/DC baseline: (1) LAPS deployed — every workstation's local Administrator password unique and directory-managed; FAIL = one shared local admin password (pass-the-hash makes it a skeleton key to every workstation). (2) LSASS protection — Credential Guard / RunAsPPL on; FAIL = LSASS readable the way Project 1's T1003.001 rule watched happen. (3) SMB signing REQUIRED on DCs and servers, LDAP signing + channel binding enforced on DCs; FAIL = relay attacks stay open. (4) NTLMv1 refused (LmCompatibilityLevel 5, NTLMv2 only). (5) LLMNR and NetBIOS name resolution disabled; FAIL = a lab Responder run answers name queries and harvests NTLMv2 hashes from typos.
RISK: these are the controls that decide whether one workstation compromise stays one workstation. Without them, Projects 1 to 4's entire chain — phish, LSASS dump, lateral movement, hash relay — works with commodity tooling and no exploits.
FIX: one hardening GPO baseline applied in stages (audit mode for signing first, then enforce), Windows LAPS to the workstation OU, RunAsPPL via GPO, LLMNR off, NTLMv1 refused — re-testing lab services after each single change.
items.ev:
Baseline review, LAB.LOCAL (GPO 'Workstation Baseline' + DC GPO + spot registry checks):
- LAPS: NOT deployed. The local Administrator password on WIN-LAB01 and WIN-LAB02 is the SAME password (verified by a controlled logon test in the lab) — set at imaging. One hash from Project 1's LSASS scenario unlocks every workstation.
- LSASS: RunAsPPL not configured on WIN-LAB01/WIN-LAB02 (registry Lsa\RunAsPPL absent); Credential Guard not enabled. Project 1 detected LSASS access; nothing prevents it succeeding.
- Signing: SMB signing enabled but NOT required on FILE-LAB01; DC LDAP signing = 'none required' (Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements), channel binding not enforced — NTLM relay to LDAP/SMB remains viable.
- Protocols: LmCompatibilityLevel=3 (NTLMv1 responses still sent); LLMNR enabled by default. A 20-minute authorized Responder run on the lab segment captured 4 NTLMv2 hashes from mistyped share names — including one from a service context.
VERDICT: FAIL — high (the shared local admin password alone is high; the set together is the finding).
items.triage:
1. Deploy Windows LAPS to the workstation OU first: unique, auto-rotating local admin passwords end the skeleton-key problem without changing how admins work day to day; verify retrieval permissions are Tier-1/Tier-0 only (a LAPS read right is itself an AD-05-class ACL).
2. Enable RunAsPPL on workstations via GPO in audit mode for a week, review the LSA warnings, then enforce — and keep Project 1's LSASS rule as the detection pair, since RunAsPPL raises the bar rather than making dumping impossible.
3. Stage the signing changes: SMB signing required on servers, then LDAP signing + channel binding on DCs in audit mode (watch for the unsigned-bind sources the audit events name — usually one old app), then enforce. Announce each stage; signing breaks the thing you forgot, once, in the lab instead of in production.
4. Set LmCompatibilityLevel=5 and disable LLMNR/NetBIOS via GPO; re-run the Responder test — the closure evidence is a silent 20 minutes, not a policy screenshot.
5. File the before/after GPO exports with this check; the baseline GPO becomes the template Project 10's reviewers will recognize as the on-premise twin of a CIS benchmark.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions are per-device and dated: an old NAS or multifunction printer that cannot do SMB signing gets its own restricted VLAN/OU and an exception entry, not a domain-wide 'signing optional'. RunAsPPL can clash with a few legacy credential providers and some EDR/SSO plug-ins — audit mode exists precisely to find them before enforcement. LLMNR has one honest use (tiny workgroups without DNS); a domain with working DNS is not it. Tune: every exception names the device, the control it cannot meet, the compensating network restriction, and an expiry — an undated exception list is just the finding, reformatted.

items.title: Control check (passes): Protected Users, a 20-character fine-grained admin policy, Recycle Bin, and DC auditing forwarded to the SIEM all hold
items.src: Protected Users group membership + authentication policies · Get-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy (Tier-0 PSO) · Get-ADOptionalFeature (Recycle Bin) · Advanced Audit Policy on DC-LAB01 + SIEM ingestion check for 4728/4732/4662/4769
items.logic:
CONTROL PURPOSE: a hardening assessment that only fails things is as untrustworthy as Project 8's dashboard would be without CLD-08. This entry re-runs the standard against the parts of LAB.LOCAL that were deliberately built right, and requires the same evidence quality as a failure.
CHECKS: (1) Tier-0 admin accounts are members of Protected Users (no NTLM, no DES/RC4, no delegation, 4-hour TGT lifetime) and log on without the failures that would prove it is not really applied; (2) a fine-grained password policy (PSO) for Tier-0: 20+ characters, history 24, lockout on; (3) AD Recycle Bin enabled (deleted objects recoverable without authoritative restore); (4) Advanced Audit Policy on the DCs covers account/group management and directory changes, and the events actually arrive in the SIEM (4728/4732 powered Project 1's rule; 4662 and 4769-RC4 power AD-05 and AD-02's new detections).
PASS = all four, evidenced the same way a FAIL would be.
items.ev:
Control evidence, LAB.LOCAL:
- Protected Users: contains LAB\adm-rpatel (and LAB\adm-jsmith was added as part of AD-01's fix, verified by a test logon — Kerberos-only, delegation refused as designed). Authentication Silo policy present and applied.
- Tier-0 PSO 'PSO-Tier0-Admins': MinPasswordLength=20, PasswordHistoryCount=24, LockoutThreshold=5, applied to the Tier-0 group — the one fine-grained policy AD-03 found, and the template for its service-account fix.
- Recycle Bin: Get-ADOptionalFeature shows 'Recycle Bin Feature' enabled for the forest; a lab test object was deleted and restored with attributes intact during this assessment.
- Auditing: DC Advanced Audit Policy — Account Management and DS Access subcategories on Success+Failure; a test 4732 (add/remove a throwaway account to a test group) appeared in the SIEM within 2 minutes, joining the Project 1 rule that watches it.
VERDICT: PASS. The domain's Tier-0 core was built correctly — which sharpens every other finding: the failures in AD-01 to AD-07 are drift and scope creep around a sound core, not a domain that was never designed.
items.triage:
1. Keep this control in the dashboard and re-run it with every assessment: the day Protected Users is quietly emptied or the audit forwarding breaks, this entry flips to FAIL and that flip is the alert.
2. Extend the passing patterns instead of re-inventing them: AD-03's service-account PSO copies PSO-Tier0-Admins, and AD-01's new admin accounts join Protected Users at creation — the control is the template.
3. Protect the control itself: membership of Protected Users and edits to the DC audit GPO are Tier-0 changes under AD-05's rules (and the GPO edit right removed there was, until this project, the control's biggest threat).
4. Record the pass with its date and evidence exactly like a failure — an undated 'auditing is on' is how forwarding silently dies for a quarter.
5. No remediation, no tickets: a pass that generates work teaches people to stop checking.
items.fp: A pass is a point-in-time claim with the same honesty rules as Project 7's negative results: these four controls held, evidenced this way, on this date. It does not certify the rest of the domain (AD-01 to AD-07 are the proof), and Protected Users has real operational edges — it breaks legacy NTLM-dependent admin workflows and cannot include the built-in Administrator or any account that must delegate, which is why membership is Tier-0-only and every addition is tested with a logon. The control would stop passing if any one of the four checks changed, which is why it is re-run by the same collection path as the failures instead of trusted from setup notes.

writeup.problem: Every project so far treated identity as evidence: Projects 1 and 2 logged the brute force that worked, Project 4 hunted the accounts the actor created, Project 8 found the same failures wearing cloud clothes (password-only admins, standing privilege, logs nobody could trust). Project 9 turns to the source: the Active Directory domain itself, LAB.LOCAL, where those accounts, groups, and policies actually live. The questions are configuration questions. Who really holds Domain Admins? Which service accounts can be cracked offline by anyone with a normal logon? What could a phished helpdesk account actually do? Which hardening controls that would have broken the Projects 1 to 4 attack chain — LAPS, LSASS protection, signing, tiering — are actually on? A domain answers all of these honestly if you collect it properly, and the answers decide whether the next phish is a ticket or a domain compromise.
writeup.methodology: Scope: the lab domain LAB.LOCAL only — DC-LAB01, WIN-LAB01, WIN-LAB02, FILE-LAB01 — assessed with read-only collection first and changes made deliberately afterward, in an isolated lab the project is authorized to test. Tooling: BloodHound with SharpHound for group membership, ACL paths, and delegation edges (the graph view no ACL editor gives you); PingCastle for a second, independent health-check opinion; Active Directory PowerShell (Get-ADGroupMember, Get-ADUser/Get-ADComputer attribute sweeps, Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy, fine-grained policy and optional-feature queries) for hand-pulled evidence; Group Policy review for the hardening baseline; and the DC Security log (4720/4728/4732, 4662, 4769) joined back to the Project 1 SIEM so configuration claims could be checked against event reality. Method per check: (1) collect the configuration as evidence, never from memory or the console's summary view, (2) where safe inside the lab, prove the path — request the SPN ticket, walk the helpdesk ACL with a throwaway account, run a 20-minute Responder capture, test the shared local admin password by logging on, (3) record the misconfiguration, the risk in terms of the earlier projects' attack chain, the remediation, and the legitimate exceptions, mapped to ATT&CK, (4) remediate one change at a time and re-test the affected service, (5) re-collect and file the after state. All verification attacks ran against lab accounts created or designated for the purpose.
writeup.findings: 8 checks recorded: 3 critical, 4 high, and 1 passing control, spanning identity protection, access control, and hardening. Critical: AD-01, Domain Admins held 6 effective principals including a daily-use account (jsmith — the Project 2 victim), a service account, and svc_backup2, the attacker-created account from Project 1, still privileged; AD-02, two Kerberoastable service accounts with RC4 tickets and passwords 6.2 and 3.8 years old, with DC logs showing 14 RC4 TGS requests for the SQL service SPN during the incident window that nobody had a detection for; AD-05, the Helpdesk group held GenericAll over the Domain Admins group and edit rights on a GPO linked to the Domain Controllers OU — two one-step paths from the most phishable credentials in the building to full domain control. High: AD-03, a 7-character default password policy with lockout disabled, one AS-REP-roastable account (pre-auth off for a retired appliance), and one account storing its password with reversible encryption; AD-04, 11 enabled accounts dormant over 180 days plus the incident's two created accounts (support2, svc_backup2) still enabled — unclosed containment items from Projects 1 and 2; AD-06, unconstrained delegation on FILE-LAB01 (the Project 3 share-encryption host, harvesting the TGT of everyone who connects) and a reporting service that could delegate to CIFS on the DC; AD-07, no LAPS (one local admin password verified identical across workstations), LSASS protection off, SMB/LDAP signing not enforced, NTLMv1 still answered, and a lab Responder run that captured 4 NTLMv2 hashes in 20 minutes. The control, AD-08, passed on evidence: Tier-0 admins sit in Protected Users under a 20-character fine-grained policy, the Recycle Bin is enabled and was test-restored, and DC auditing forwards 4728/4732/4662/4769 into the SIEM. Remediation in the lab: incident accounts disabled, Tier-0 membership cut to the dedicated admin accounts, SPN passwords rotated and gMSA migration started, the helpdesk ACLs and delegation removed, LAPS deployed, and the signing/LLMNR/NTLM changes staged through audit mode. The through-line matches Project 8 exactly: a sound Tier-0 core, surrounded by reasonable one-day decisions that were never revisited.
writeup.challenges: Four honest difficulties. First, proof versus safety: an ACL path in BloodHound is a claim until it is walked, but walking it means adding an account to Domain Admins, even a throwaway one in a lab — every verification here used designated test accounts, was removed in the same session, and is recorded; in a production assessment several of these paths would stay 'graph-proven, ACL-verified, not exercised' and the report would say so. Second, remediation breaks things in characterful ways: Protected Users refuses delegation and NTLM, so one legacy admin workflow failed on contact; signing in audit mode named one old application binding LDAP unsigned, which had to be fixed before enforcement; gMSA migration needs the service to actually restart under the new identity. Each fix was staged one change at a time for exactly this reason. Third, the telemetry has edges: LastLogon is not replicated between DCs, 4769 was only useful once someone looked at the encryption-type field, and AdminSDHolder's hourly reset means an ACL reading can be true at collection time and stomped an hour later — findings carry their collection method and time for that reason. Fourth, scope limits: this is one small single-domain forest assessed with lab freedom; a multi-domain enterprise adds trust paths, forest-level ACLs, and change-control timelines this project did not have to survive, and some exposures are only boundable — FILE-LAB01's unconstrained window can be checked for admin logons, but 'no TGT was ever abused' is a statement about logs, recorded with that limit attached.
writeup.learned: Identity is the perimeter stopped being a slogan in this project and became a list: Domain Admins membership, SPN passwords, two ACLs, one delegation flag. Every critical finding was a standing configuration, not an exploit — the domain was not hacked past its defenses, it was configured so that ordinary credentials were worth far more than they should be. The graph view is the skill: nobody in the lab believed the helpdesk could own the domain until BloodHound drew the one-step path, because ACL editors show rights object by object and attacks chain them. Configuration and detection are one system, not two: AD-02 only became a detection (4769 with RC4) after the assessment explained which field mattered, AD-05's fix ships with a 4662 alert, and AD-08's passing audit pipeline is what makes the other checks provable at all — the same loop Project 8 closed with Config rules. Drift is the enemy in both worlds: cloud or on-premise, every serious finding began as a reasonable, temporary, ticketed decision. And the incident bookkeeping matters: Projects 1 and 2 named svc_backup2 and support2 as IOCs two projects ago, and only this assessment actually removed them — containment is not finished when the firewall rule lands, it is finished when the directory is clean. Next: Project 10, Kubernetes Security Assessment, takes the same configuration-first method to cluster RBAC and workload settings.

soc.title: Kubernetes Security Assessment
soc.desc: Review cluster configurations, permissions, and RBAC.
steps: Stand up a throwaway local cluster to assess
Review RBAC: who can do what, flag over-privileged roles
Check workload configs: privileged pods, secrets, network policies
Write the assessment: findings ranked by risk with fixes
Collect the before state: kube-bench output, full RBAC exports (clusterrolebindings, rolebindings, can-i reviews per identity), NetworkPolicy list, and the workload manifests for every namespace

Prove the critical paths safely inside the throwaway cluster only: read a namespace Secret with the default SA token from inside a pod, test pod-to-pod reachability the missing NetworkPolicies allow, and submit a privileged pod spec where Pod Security should refuse it

Remediate one change at a time (cluster-admin bindings, per-workload service accounts, collector pod spec, secrets rotation and etcd encryption, network policies, control-plane flags, hardened pod template) and re-test the affected workload after each change

Re-run kube-bench and the RBAC export and file the after state: no standing cluster-admin beyond the named admin group, restricted Pod Security enforced, default-deny networking in every namespace, API audit events landing in the SIEM, and the control namespace still passing

items.title: Cluster-admin sprawl: cluster-admin is bound to a leftover intern account and a standing CI service account
items.src: kubectl get clusterrolebindings (subjects review) · kubectl auth can-i --list per subject · CIS Kubernetes Benchmark 5.1.1 (cluster-admin role use)
items.logic:
CHECK: export every ClusterRoleBinding whose roleRef is cluster-admin and review each subject. PASS = only a small named admin group. FAIL = any individual user outside that group, any service account with standing cluster-admin, or any binding nobody can explain. Then verify with kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<subject> that the grant is real, not just listed.
RISK: cluster-admin is Domain Admins for a cluster (Project 9's AD-01 in YAML): it can read every Secret in every namespace, create privileged pods (K8S-03), and rewrite RBAC itself. Every extra subject is another credential whose theft is total cluster compromise, and a CI token is exactly the kind of long-lived, widely-stored credential that leaks.
FIX: cluster-admin only for the named admin group; humans get namespace-scoped Roles; automation gets a scoped Role/ClusterRole for its one job, with short-lived tokens where the platform supports them.
items.ev:
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide | grep cluster-admin (lab-k8s):
- cluster-admin -> Group lab-cluster-admins (2 named admins — expected, the control pattern)
- temp-cluster-admin -> User intern-dev — created 4 months ago for a weekend storage migration, never removed. kubectl auth can-i --list --as=intern-dev confirms full cluster-admin, including get/list secrets in all namespaces.
- ci-deployer-admin -> ServiceAccount ci/ci-deployer — the CI pipeline's standing identity, cluster-admin 'so pipelines never fail on permissions'. Its token is stored as a CI secret on the build runner, outside the cluster's own controls.
CIS 5.1.1 verdict for this cluster: FAIL.
VERDICT: FAIL — critical. 3 effective cluster-admin paths where the design calls for 1 group, and one of them is a pipeline token that lives on a build server.
items.triage:
1. Delete the temp-cluster-admin binding today and review the API audit trail (once K8S-06's logging exists) plus the intern account's token use; an unexplained standing grant is treated as suspect until its history is read.
2. Replace ci-deployer with a scoped identity: a ClusterRole limited to the namespaces and verbs the pipeline actually uses (get/list/watch + create/update/patch on deployments and services in soc-apps and soc-prod), generated from the pipeline's real API calls, attached before the admin binding is removed so deploys do not break.
3. Rotate the CI token when the binding changes — the old token's power came from the binding, but rotation closes the stored-copy question for good.
4. Give intern-dev (and every human) namespace-scoped Roles per namespace instead: edit in their working namespace, view elsewhere.
5. Re-export the bindings and file the before/after lists; add a standing review (this export, monthly) because bindings drift exactly the way AD group membership did in AD-01.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: break-glass cluster-admin for the platform team is supposed to exist — as a group, named, and reviewed, which the lab-cluster-admins binding already models. A bootstrap binding created by the cluster installer (system:masters equivalents) is platform plumbing, not a finding. Tune: judge bindings by subject type and storage, not headcount — a service account token copied onto a build runner is riskier than three named humans in the admin group, because its use is unattended and its storage is outside the cluster.

items.title: Default service account abuse: workloads run as the namespace default SA, token automounted, holding edit rights and secret access
items.src: kubectl get rolebindings,roles -n soc-apps · pod spec review (serviceAccountName, automountServiceAccountToken) · CIS 5.1.5 / 5.1.6 (default service account use)
items.logic:
CHECK, per namespace: (1) does any RoleBinding grant rights to the namespace's default ServiceAccount? (2) do workload pods omit serviceAccountName (so they run as that default SA)? (3) is automountServiceAccountToken unset/true on pods that never call the Kubernetes API? FAIL = the default SA holds any permission beyond nothing, or API tokens are mounted into pods that do not need them.
RISK: a pod's SA token is its identity. Any single pod compromise in soc-apps (the dashboard, the ingest worker) inherits the default SA's rights: here that includes get/list Secrets and create/patch Deployments in the namespace — read the SIEM's database credentials, then redeploy a workload with your own image. The token is the pivot, mounted by default into every container.
FIX: one dedicated ServiceAccount per workload with a least-privilege Role; automountServiceAccountToken: false on every workload that does not call the API; the default SA bound to nothing, everywhere.
items.ev:
Namespace soc-apps review:
RoleBinding soc-apps/deployer-binding: Role 'deployer' (verbs: get,list,watch on secrets; create,update,patch on deployments; get,list on pods) bound to ServiceAccount soc-apps/default.
Workloads: deployments siem-web, siem-ingest, intel-dashboard — none sets serviceAccountName, so all three run as default; none sets automountServiceAccountToken: false, so every container carries the token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token.
Proof (lab, from inside the siem-web pod): kubectl --token=<mounted token> get secrets -n soc-apps returned all 6 namespace Secrets, including the SIEM database password — from the web tier's identity.
VERDICT: FAIL — high. The most exposed workload in the namespace holds the keys to the whole namespace.
items.triage:
1. Create dedicated ServiceAccounts (sa-siem-web with no API permissions, sa-siem-ingest with only its configmap/secret reads) and point each Deployment at its own; set automountServiceAccountToken: false wherever the app never calls the API.
2. Delete the deployer RoleBinding to default and reduce the deployer Role itself to the CI identity from K8S-01 — secret access moves out of the namespace's ambient identity entirely.
3. Roll the pods and re-run the in-pod proof: the web pod's environment should now contain no usable token, and a hand-carried token test against the API should return Forbidden for secrets.
4. Sweep every namespace for the same shape (the default namespace had the same binding pattern on a test Role — removed in the same change).
5. Record the pattern as a manifest-review rule for the merged platform: a Deployment with no serviceAccountName is a review failure, not a style nit.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: some platform agents (metrics collectors, ingress controllers) genuinely need API access — they get their own named ServiceAccount and a Role written for their exact calls, which is the opposite of this finding. A short-lived debug pod with a token is normal when it is deleted in the same session; a standing token in a production web tier is not. Tune: the check fails on the combination (default SA + any binding + automounted token), not on tokens alone — a dedicated SA with a scoped Role and a workload that calls the API is the correct pattern and passes.

items.title: Privileged pods: the log-collector DaemonSet runs privileged with hostPID, hostNetwork, and the host root filesystem mounted
items.src: DaemonSet / Pod spec review (securityContext, volumes) across all namespaces · CIS 5.2.2 / 5.2.3 / 5.2.5 (privileged containers, hostPID, hostNetwork) · kubeaudit privileged check
items.logic:
CHECK: list every Pod/DaemonSet/Deployment with securityContext.privileged=true, hostPID or hostNetwork=true, hostPath volumes (especially / or /var/run/docker.sock / container runtime socket), or added capabilities SYS_ADMIN / NET_ADMIN without a documented need. FAIL = any of these on a workload whose job does not strictly require that exact access.
RISK: a privileged container with the host root filesystem mounted is not a container anymore: write to /host/etc, drop an SSH key or a cron entry, and the attacker owns the NODE — then every pod on it, every Secret they hold (K8S-02), and a launch point inside the cluster network (K8S-05). This is the cluster's escape-to-host path, pre-installed.
FIX: collectors read logs through a read-only hostPath on /var/log (or the runtime's log path) with privileged=false, hostPID=false; nothing mounts / ; runtime sockets are never mounted into general workloads.
items.ev:
DaemonSet kube-system/node-log-collector (ships node and pod logs to the Project 1/2 SIEM — the containerized forwarder):
securityContext: privileged: true, hostPID: true, hostNetwork: true
volumes: hostPath path: / mounted at /host (read-write), plus hostPath /var/log at /var/log
Actual need, established by testing the replacement: read /var/log and the container log directory, report its own metrics. Nothing in the job needs privilege, the host PID namespace, or a writable host root.
Also found: pod default/netshoot-debug, left running for 19 days after a network debugging session: NET_ADMIN + SYS_ADMIN added, hostNetwork: true — a standing debug shell on the host network namespace.
VERDICT: FAIL — critical. The escape path is a DaemonSet, which means it runs on every node, by design, all the time.
items.triage:
1. Rewrite the collector's spec: privileged: false, hostPID: false, hostNetwork: false, the / hostPath mount deleted, /var/log mounted readOnly: true, runAsNonRoot where the image allows, drop ALL capabilities. Roll it node by node and confirm log flow into the SIEM never gaps (the collector is production telemetry — the fix must not blind the SOC it feeds).
2. Delete the netshoot debug pod and record the rule: debug pods are created per incident and deleted in the same session; a 19-day-old debug pod is a finding, not a tool.
3. Verify the escape is closed: from the new collector pod, attempts to write outside its mounts and to see host processes fail; file the before/after pod specs and the test output.
4. Enforce it going forward with Pod Security Standards (K8S-07): the restricted/baseline profile would have refused this DaemonSet at admission.
5. Sweep all namespaces for hostPath and privileged — the sweep that found netshoot is the sweep that has to become the standing check.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions are real but narrow: node-level agents from the platform itself (the CNI, the CSI driver, the kube proxy) genuinely need host access — they are named, vendor-supplied, pinned by digest, and reviewed per component. A log collector is the classic gray case: it needs host LOG FILES, and vendors ship privileged defaults because they work everywhere; the assessment's job is to prove the narrower spec works (done here) rather than accept the default. Tune: flag the capability, then judge by the mount table and the test — privileged with a read-only /var/log is a conversation; privileged with / writable is a critical, full stop.

items.title: Secrets hygiene: etcd encryption at rest is off, credentials sit as literal env values in Git manifests, and the developer Role can list namespace Secrets
items.src: API server flags (--encryption-provider-config) · manifest repository review (env values in Deployment specs) · RBAC review: who can get/list secrets per namespace (kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n <ns> --as=<subject>)
items.logic:
CHECK, three layers: (1) STORAGE — is the API server started with --encryption-provider-config so Secrets are encrypted in etcd, or are they base64-only (base64 is an encoding, not encryption — anyone with the etcd data or a backup reads every Secret)? (2) DELIVERY — do manifests in Git carry literal secret values in env or config files instead of referencing Secret objects? A committed credential is a published credential: rotate it, do not just delete the line. (3) ACCESS — which human and workload identities can get/list Secrets in each namespace, verified with can-i, not assumed from Role names?
RISK: three independent read paths to the same credentials — the etcd backup, the Git history, and an over-broad Role — and any one of them hands over the SIEM database password and the ingest API token that Projects 5 and 8 treated as crown jewels.
FIX: encryption provider configured on the API server (and existing Secrets rewritten to be stored encrypted); credentials only in Secret objects (or an external secrets store), never literal in Git; secret read access limited to the specific workloads that consume them.
items.ev:
Layer evidence, lab-k8s:
(1) API server pod spec (kube-system/kube-apiserver): no --encryption-provider-config flag. A direct etcd read in the lab returned the soc-apps database Secret as base64 JSON — decoded in one step to the live password.
(2) Git manifest apps/siem-ingest/deployment.yaml: env SIEM_API_TOKEN and DB_PASSWORD set as literal values, committed 3 months ago, still valid today (tested against the ingest endpoint). Git history holds them even if the file is fixed.
(3) kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n soc-apps --as=dev-reader (the standard developer identity): yes — the developer Role includes get/list/watch on secrets 'for debugging'.
VERDICT: FAIL — high. The credentials protecting the merged platform's data are recoverable from a backup, a repo clone, or a normal developer token.
items.triage:
1. Rotate first: the SIEM API token and database password are treated as compromised (Git history + broad read access) — issue new values, deploy them as proper Secret objects, and confirm the old values fail before anything else proceeds.
2. Enable encryption at rest: add --encryption-provider-config (aescbc with a key held outside the cluster, or the cloud KMS where available), restart the API server in the lab's maintenance pattern, then rewrite existing Secrets (kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace) so stored copies are actually encrypted, and verify with a second etcd read showing ciphertext.
3. Purge the literals from the manifests and rewrite the deployment to envFrom/secretRef; note honestly in the finding that Git history still contains the old (now rotated, therefore dead) values — rotation is what makes the history harmless.
4. Strip secrets verbs from the developer Role; debugging uses kubectl logs and describe, and the one legitimate secret reader (the ingest workload's SA from K8S-02) keeps get on its named Secret only.
5. Re-run all three layer checks and file the evidence: etcd ciphertext sample, manifest diff, and can-i output showing 'no' for the developer identity.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: a throwaway lab Secret for a disposable test service is still handled the same way — the habit is the control, and 'it is only the lab' is how literal credentials reached a real ingest token here. External-secrets tooling changes where the value lives, not the RBAC question: the sync identity becomes the sensitive one and is reviewed instead. Tune: base64 in a manifest for NON-secret config (a configmap value) is not a finding; the check keys on credential-shaped values and on the three layers together — any single layer failing is a finding, because each is an independent path to the same secret.

items.title: No NetworkPolicies outside the control namespace: any pod can reach any pod, the cloud metadata address, and the API server
items.src: kubectl get networkpolicies -A · in-cluster reachability tests from a test pod (database port, API server, 169.254.169.254) · CIS 5.3.2 (network policies in place)
items.logic:
CHECK: every namespace should carry at least a default-deny NetworkPolicy plus explicit allows for the traffic the application actually needs. FAIL = a namespace with zero policies (Kubernetes' default is allow-all: every pod can open a connection to every other pod and to any egress destination). Verify by test, not by listing alone: from a pod in the namespace, attempt the database port of another app, the API server, and the link-local metadata address 169.254.169.254 (Project 8's CLD-07 lesson — in a cloud-hosted cluster that address hands out node credentials).
RISK: network policy is the cluster's internal firewall. Without it, the web tier's compromise (K8S-02's starting point) reaches the SIEM database and the threat-intel store directly, and egress to anywhere makes command-and-control and exfiltration a networking non-event — Project 2's beaconing pattern with no firewall in the way.
FIX: default-deny ingress and egress per namespace, then allow lists built from the application's real flows (observed first, enforced second).
items.ev:
kubectl get networkpolicies -A: policies exist ONLY in soc-prod (the K8S-08 control namespace). soc-apps, ci, and default have none.
Reachability proof (lab, from a throwaway pod in soc-apps, deleted after the test):
- soc-apps -> siem-db Service port 5432: CONNECTED (the web tier can open the database directly, bypassing the app)
- soc-apps -> kubernetes API server (10.96.0.1:443): CONNECTED (expected for API clients; here the caller is a web pod whose only defense is its SA's RBAC — see K8S-02)
- soc-apps -> 169.254.169.254: CONNECTED in this kind cluster there is no metadata service, recorded honestly — on the cloud-hosted version of this cluster the same test is the CLD-07 credential path, which is why egress policy includes the metadata address explicitly
VERDICT: FAIL — high. Segmentation exists only in the one namespace that was built as the control.
items.triage:
1. Observe before enforcing: run the CNI's flow logging (or a week of conntrack/service logs) to list the flows soc-apps actually uses — web->app, app->db, ingest->SIEM, everything->DNS — so the allow list is the application's real shape, not a guess that breaks it.
2. Apply default-deny (ingress and egress) to soc-apps, ci, and default, then the allow policies per flow, one namespace at a time, testing the application after each.
3. Always allow DNS egress explicitly (the classic self-inflicted outage: default-deny without DNS makes every name lookup fail and looks like an application bug).
4. Re-run the reachability proof from the same test pod: database direct = refused, metadata address = refused, the application's own flows = working. File both runs.
5. Make 'no NetworkPolicy in namespace' a standing dashboard check — a new namespace is born allow-all, so the policy set has to be part of the namespace template, not a follow-up ticket.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: none for default-deny itself — every real application has a describable flow set, and 'we do not know our flows yet' is a reason to observe first (step 1), not to skip policy. Some CNIs and service meshes implement policy differently (or add their own layer); the check is about effective reachability, proven by the test pod, so a mesh-enforced deny passes on evidence even with no NetworkPolicy objects. Tune: do not copy policies between namespaces blindly — the CI namespace legitimately reaches the API server to deploy, the web namespace never does; per-namespace flows are the point.

items.title: Control plane gaps (kube-bench): anonymous authentication left on, no API audit logging, kubelet authentication/authorization weak on the workers
items.src: kube-bench run against CIS Kubernetes Benchmark (master + node targets) · API server and kubelet configuration review · audit policy / log path check
items.logic:
CHECK: run kube-bench for breadth, then hand-verify the failures that matter: (1) API server --anonymous-auth must be false (anonymous requests otherwise reach the API unauthenticated, limited only by RBAC mistakes — and K8S-01/K8S-02 are exactly those mistakes); (2) an audit policy must be configured with a log path or backend (--audit-policy-file, --audit-log-path) so API actions are recorded — without it the cluster has no answer to 'who read that Secret' (Project 2's INV-08 gap, in cluster form); (3) kubelet: anonymous auth disabled and authorization mode Webhook on every node, or the node's kubelet API (10250) serves pod logs and exec to unauthenticated callers who can reach it (and K8S-05 says pod-network callers can).
RISK: anonymous access paths plus no audit trail is the worst pairing in this project: access that should not exist, and no record if it is used.
FIX: the kube-bench remediations for the three items, applied as control-plane changes in the lab's maintenance pattern, with the audit log shipped to the SIEM like every other source in Projects 1 and 2.
items.ev:
kube-bench (lab-k8s, master + 2 node targets): 11 FAIL lines total; the three that matter, hand-verified:
[FAIL] 1.2.1 Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false — actual: the API server runs with anonymous auth enabled (left on while debugging an ingress problem; system:anonymous maps to system:unauthenticated, and combined with one over-broad binding found during K8S-02's sweep it could list pods in a namespace).
[FAIL] 3.2.1 / 3.2.2 Ensure that a minimal audit policy is created and the audit log path is set — actual: neither flag present. Proven consequence: the Secret reads performed as K8S-04 evidence left NO API audit record anywhere; the cluster cannot reconstruct who accessed what.
[FAIL] 4.2.1 / 4.2.2 kubelet anonymous auth and authorization — actual on both workers: --anonymous-auth=true, --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow. From the test pod (K8S-05), the kubelet API answered a /pods request unauthenticated.
Passing, recorded: the read-only kubelet port (10255) is disabled, etcd serves over TLS between peers, and the API server's --authorization-mode is Node,RBAC (not AlwaysAllow).
VERDICT: FAIL — high. The failures are individually simple flags; together they are unauthenticated reach plus total blindness.
items.triage:
1. Set --anonymous-auth=false on the API server and restart it in the maintenance pattern; verify health checks and the admin group's access still work (system:masters / the admin group authenticate by certificate, unaffected by the flag).
2. Write a minimal audit policy (log Metadata for reads, RequestResponse for Secret and RBAC changes — the events Projects 1 and 2 taught this board to value), set the log path, and ship the audit log to the SIEM as a named source; prove it by reading a Secret and finding the event.
3. Fix the kubelets: --anonymous-auth=false, --authorization-mode=Webhook on both workers, rolling restart, and re-test the /pods request — it must return 401/403.
4. Close the specific exposure the anonymous window allowed: review bindings for system:unauthenticated and any anonymous-granted rights found in the K8S-02 sweep, and remove them (the flag fix stops new anonymous use; the binding review closes what it could reach).
5. Add kube-bench to the standing checks on a schedule, with the full output filed — benchmark drift is the same drift story as Projects 8 and 9, and the schedule is the control.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: health-check and monitoring endpoints sometimes justify narrowly-scoped anonymous access to /healthz-style paths — that is an API server flag design point, not a reason to leave full anonymous authentication on. kube-bench also flags items that do not apply to a kind cluster's packaging (file ownership on paths the installer manages differently); each such line is recorded as not-applicable WITH the reason, never silently dropped — a benchmark report with unexplained skips is how real failures get waved through next time. Tune: hand-verify every FAIL before it becomes a finding (the scanner-breadth-then-verify method from Project 8), and treat audit logging as the non-negotiable: its absence converts every other finding's history into 'unknown'.

items.title: Workload hardening gaps: containers run as root, privilege escalation allowed, :latest images, and no resource limits outside the control namespace
items.src: Manifest review for soc-apps and default (securityContext, image tags, resources) · Pod Security Standards namespace labels (pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce) · kubeaudit / kubesec manifest scans
items.logic:
CHECK, per workload, the Pod Security 'restricted'-leaning basics: (1) runAsNonRoot true and no runAsUser 0; (2) allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and capabilities drop ALL (add back only named needs); (3) seccompProfile set; (4) images pinned by tag or digest — never :latest, which makes 'what is running' unanswerable and rollbacks fictional; (5) resource requests AND limits set, so one runaway or hostile pod cannot starve the node (the noisy-neighbor denial of service that needs no exploit); (6) namespaces labelled for Pod Security Standards enforcement so admission refuses the next bad spec instead of the next assessment finding it.
RISK: individually these are medium; stacked on the web tier they are the difference between 'a container was compromised' and 'a root container with no limits redeployed itself' — they decide the blast radius of K8S-02 and K8S-03's starting points.
FIX: a hardened pod template applied per workload (test-booted first), images pinned by digest in the manifests, and PSA enforce=baseline (then restricted where the app allows) on every namespace.
items.ev:
Manifest sweep, soc-apps + default (kube-system platform agents excluded — K8S-03 covers them):
- siem-web: runs as root (no runAsNonRoot, image default user), allowPrivilegeEscalation unset (= true), capabilities not dropped, image soc/siem-web:latest, NO resource requests or limits. This is the internet-facing tier, carrying K8S-02's token.
- siem-ingest: runAsUser 1000 set (partial credit, the pattern exists in-repo), but image still :latest and limits absent.
- intel-dashboard: image pinned by digest and limits set — it was rebuilt during Project 5 and quietly done right; kept as the in-repo example.
- Namespaces: soc-apps and default carry NO pod-security.kubernetes.io labels, so admission enforces nothing; soc-prod carries enforce=restricted (K8S-08).
- One test deployment in default requests 90% of a node's memory with no limit — a config error today, a denial of service the day it is real.
VERDICT: FAIL — medium. No single line here owns the cluster; together they guarantee a compromise lands as root, unpinned, and unbounded.
items.triage:
1. Build the hardened template from the intel-dashboard example (it already passes): non-root user, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, drop ALL, seccomp RuntimeDefault, digest-pinned image, requests+limits sized from the app's observed use.
2. Apply per workload with a test boot each time — non-root breaks apps that write to their own install directory; fix with an emptyDir at the write path or an image change, never by quietly reverting to root.
3. Pin every image by digest in the manifests and record the digest in the finding evidence, so 'what ran on the day' is answerable later (Project 7's standard).
4. Label soc-apps enforce=baseline first (admission starts refusing the worst specs without breaking the current fleet's restarts), fix the refusals, then move to restricted; default gets baseline plus the resource quota that caps the 90%-memory class of error.
5. Re-run the manifest sweep and file it: the closure bar is zero root / :latest / unlimited workloads outside named platform exceptions.
items.fp: Legitimate exceptions: a small set of images genuinely ship root-only (older vendor images, some databases' entrypoints) — they get a dated exception, a namespace of their own where practical, and every OTHER control on this list applied harder. Init containers and migration jobs sometimes need a capability the steady-state app does not; scope it to the init container, not the pod. Tune: severity stays medium on purpose — these are blast-radius controls, and inflating them to critical would bury K8S-01 and K8S-03, which are the actual open doors. The dashboard ranks open doors first, hardening debt second, and says so.

items.title: Control check (passes): the soc-prod namespace enforces restricted Pod Security, scoped service accounts, default-deny networking, and digest-pinned workloads
items.src: Namespace labels + admission test · Role/RoleBinding export for soc-prod · NetworkPolicy list and reachability test · manifest review — the same methods as K8S-01 to K8S-07, pointed at the control
items.logic:
CONTROL PURPOSE: an assessment that only fails things is as untrustworthy as Project 8's dashboard without CLD-08 or Project 9's without AD-08. This entry re-runs the project's own standards against soc-prod, the namespace where the merged platform's production copies run, and requires the evidence to come back clean on every axis the other checks failed: (1) RBAC — no cluster-admin, no default-SA bindings, per-workload SAs with scoped Roles; (2) POD SECURITY — namespace labels enforce the restricted Pod Security profile, proven by an admission test, not by reading the label; (3) NETWORK — default-deny plus explicit allows, proven by the K8S-05 reachability test; (4) WORKLOADS — non-root, escalation off, digest-pinned images, requests and limits set; (5) SECRETS — consumed from the external store as mounted files, with no human identity able to list Secrets in the namespace.
PASS = all five, evidenced the same way a FAIL would be.
items.ev:
Control evidence, lab-k8s / soc-prod:
(1) RBAC: bindings export shows 3 Roles (prod-web, prod-ingest, prod-dashboard), each namespaced, each bound to its own ServiceAccount; the default SA has zero bindings; kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n soc-prod --as=dev-reader returns no.
(2) Pod Security: labels pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted present; admission test — submitting a privileged test pod spec returned: Forbidden, violates PodSecurity restricted:latest (missing runAsNonRoot, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, drop ALL). The control refuses the K8S-03 shape at the door.
(3) Network: default-deny-all plus 4 allow policies; the K8S-05 test pod in soc-prod could NOT reach the database port directly or the metadata address, and the application's own flows worked.
(4) Workloads: all 4 deployments non-root, escalation false, images pinned by digest, requests and limits set; a ResourceQuota caps the namespace.
(5) Secrets: values arrive as mounted files from the external secrets store; no Secret objects readable by any human Role in the namespace.
VERDICT: PASS. The target state for the whole cluster already exists inside it — K8S-01 to K8S-07 are not knowledge gaps, they are the namespaces that were never brought up to this namespace's standard.
items.triage:
1. Keep this namespace as the template: K8S-02, K8S-05, and K8S-07's fixes copy soc-prod's Role shapes, policy set, and pod template deliberately rather than improvising per namespace.
2. Re-run this control with every assessment, admission test included — a label quietly removed or a binding quietly added flips it to FAIL, and that flip is the drift alarm for the whole cluster.
3. Protect the control itself: edits to soc-prod's bindings and labels are cluster-admin actions under K8S-01's rules, and the API audit log from K8S-06's fix is what records them.
4. Record the pass with its date and evidence exactly like a failure — an undated 'prod is hardened' is how controls quietly die (the AD-08 / CLD-08 rule).
5. No remediation, no tickets: a pass that generates work teaches people to stop checking.
items.fp: A pass is a point-in-time claim with the same honesty rules as Project 7's negative results: these five axes held, evidenced this way, on this date. It does not certify the cluster (K8S-01 to K8S-07 are the proof), the nodes' host OS, or the supply chain behind the pinned digests — pinning says WHICH image ran, not that the image is good; that is Project 11's vulnerability question. The control would stop passing if any one axis changed, which is why it is re-run by the same collection path as the failures instead of trusted from setup notes.

writeup.problem: The merged SOC platform built across Projects 1 to 9 now also runs as containers: the SIEM, the ingest pipeline, and the dashboards were containerized into a small Kubernetes cluster (lab-k8s) so the stack can be rebuilt and moved as one unit. Kubernetes concentrates every earlier project's lesson into one API: identity is RBAC, hardening is a pod spec, network segmentation is a policy object, and logging is a control-plane flag — and the defaults are permissive on all four. A cluster stood up quickly, by copying working manifests and granting whatever made things run, ends up exactly like the cloud tenant in Project 8 and the domain in Project 9: reasonable decisions, never revisited, adding up to standing privilege everywhere. Project 10 is the assessment: review the cluster's configurations, permissions, and RBAC against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark, prove the dangerous paths inside the throwaway cluster, and record findings with the configuration as evidence, the risk, the fix, and the legitimate exceptions.
writeup.methodology: Scope: one throwaway local cluster the project is authorized to assess — lab-k8s, a 3-node kind cluster (1 control plane, 2 workers) running the containerized SOC platform across five namespaces: kube-system (platform agents), soc-apps (SIEM web, ingest, threat-intel dashboard), ci (pipeline), default (leftover test workloads), and soc-prod (the hardened production namespace, assessed as the control). Tooling: kube-bench for the CIS benchmark sweep (breadth), kubectl for hand-pulled evidence (RBAC exports, can-i authorization reviews per identity, manifest and pod-spec review), kubeaudit/kubesec-style manifest checks, and in-cluster test pods for reachability and token proofs. Method per check, the same as Projects 8 and 9: (1) let the scanner flag broadly, (2) hand-verify every critical and high finding against the live configuration before recording it, (3) where safe inside the throwaway cluster, prove the path — use the web pod's mounted token against the API, run the reachability tests, submit the privileged spec the control namespace should refuse, (4) record the misconfiguration, the risk in terms of the earlier projects' attack chains, the remediation, and the false-positive / legitimate-exception notes, mapped to ATT&CK, (5) remediate one change at a time and re-test the workload, (6) re-run and file the after state. All proof actions ran against lab identities and test pods created for the purpose and deleted in the same session.
writeup.findings: 8 checks recorded: 2 critical, 4 high, 1 medium, and 1 passing control, spanning RBAC, workload configuration, secrets, networking, and the control plane. Critical: K8S-01, cluster-admin was bound beyond the named admin group to a leftover intern account (grant 4 months old, from a finished migration) and to the CI pipeline's service account, whose token lives on the build runner; K8S-03, the log-collector DaemonSet ran privileged with hostPID, hostNetwork, and the host root filesystem mounted read-write on every node — a pre-installed escape to the host — beside a 19-day-old debug pod with host networking. High: K8S-02, all soc-apps workloads ran as the namespace default service account with its token automounted, and that account held secret reads and deployment writes — proven from inside the web pod by listing the namespace's Secrets, including the SIEM database password; K8S-04, secrets were exposed three ways at once: etcd encryption at rest off (a lab etcd read returned the database Secret as plain base64), live credentials committed as literal env values in the Git manifests, and a developer Role that could list namespace Secrets; K8S-05, no NetworkPolicies existed outside the control namespace, and reachability tests showed the web tier connecting directly to the database port and the API server; K8S-06, kube-bench's hand-verified failures — anonymous authentication left on at the API server, no API audit policy or log path at all (the K8S-04 evidence reads left no record anywhere), and kubelets answering unauthenticated requests on both workers. Medium: K8S-07, workloads ran as root with privilege escalation allowed, :latest images, and no resource limits outside the control namespace. The control, K8S-08, passed on all five axes: soc-prod enforces restricted Pod Security (proven by an admission refusal), uses scoped per-workload service accounts, default-deny networking, digest-pinned non-root workloads, and externally-stored secrets no human Role can list. Remediation inside the lab cluster: the stray cluster-admin bindings deleted and the CI identity rescoped, per-workload service accounts created and the default account unbound, the collector rewritten unprivileged with log flow verified, credentials rotated and etcd encryption enabled with existing Secrets rewritten, default-deny policies applied per namespace from observed flows, anonymous auth disabled and API audit logging shipped to the SIEM, and the hardened pod template rolled out from the control namespace's example.
writeup.challenges: Four honest difficulties. First, proof versus disruption: the collector being fixed is the thing shipping logs to the SIEM, and the CI identity being rescoped is the thing deploying the fixes — every critical remediation had to keep the platform's own plumbing alive, so replacements were built and verified before the old grant was removed, one change at a time. Second, Kubernetes' defaults argue with you: tokens automount unless told not to, namespaces are born allow-all, and manifests copied from vendor quick-starts arrive privileged because that is what makes a demo work on the first try — most findings here were defaults nobody chose, which is precisely why admission enforcement (Pod Security) matters more than manifest review alone. Third, the telemetry has a hole by design until you close it: with no API audit policy there is no history to review for the anonymous-auth window or the standing grants, so several exposure questions are only boundable ('these bindings existed; their use before audit logging is unknowable from the API') and are recorded with that limit attached, the same honesty rule as Project 2's log gap and Project 7's negative results. Fourth, scope limits: this is one small, self-managed kind cluster — a managed cloud cluster (EKS/GKE/AKS) hides parts of the control plane behind the provider (kube-bench's master checks change shape), adds IAM-to-RBAC mapping this project did not have to assess, and the CNI choice changes how network policy is enforced and observed. The check logic transfers; the flag locations and some evidence paths would need rework, and the write-up says so rather than pretending one cluster stands for all clusters.
writeup.learned: Kubernetes is Projects 8 and 9 wearing one API: cluster-admin is Domain Admins (K8S-01 is AD-01), a service account token is a password that mounts itself into every workload (K8S-02), a privileged pod is unconstrained delegation you can schedule (K8S-03 is AD-06 with a YAML accent), and an unaudited API server is the single-region CloudTrail (K8S-06 is CLD-05). The transferable skill is the method, not the flags: collect the configuration as evidence, prove the path safely, fix one change at a time, and re-collect. Defaults are the real adversary — nobody on this project chose an insecure cluster; the cluster shipped insecure and drifted less than the cloud tenant did, because soc-prod proves someone built one namespace to the standard. That control namespace is the project's most useful output: assessments usually end with a list of what is wrong, but K8S-08 hands the remediation phase a working template in the same cluster, on the same versions, already tested against the same applications. Enforcement beats review: the restricted Pod Security profile refusing a bad spec at admission is worth more than any quarterly manifest audit, the same way Project 8's Config rules outlast its report. And identity remains the perimeter: five of the seven failures shrink or vanish when RBAC is scoped, tokens are not ambient, and the API records who did what. Next: Project 11, Vulnerability Management Lab, takes the pinned digests and configurations recorded here and asks the next question — what is actually vulnerable in what is running.

soc.title: Vulnerability Management Lab
soc.desc: Scan authorized systems, prioritize findings, and create reports.
steps: Define scope: only systems you own or are authorized to scan
Run a first scan against your lab targets
Prioritize findings: severity plus exploitability plus exposure
Create the report a manager could act on
Define the authorized scope in writing before scanning: the lab hosts, the domain controller, the file server, and the lab-k8s images only, with scan windows and a named owner for every asset
Run discovery plus credentialed vulnerability scans (Nessus/OpenVAS) over the scope and Trivy over every pinned container image, and save the raw scanner output as evidence

Prioritize every finding with CVSS plus CISA KEV plus exploitability plus exposure plus asset criticality, validate the scanner's false positives against patch and backport evidence, and consolidate duplicates into single findings

Produce the three reports (executive summary, technical findings, remediation tracker with owners and SLAs), remediate in priority order, and rescan every fixed asset so each finding closes on rescan evidence

items.title: Patch first: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) in the threat-intel dashboard's Java logging library
items.src: Credentialed Nessus scan of lab hosts + Trivy scan of the lab-k8s images pinned in Project 10 · CISA KEV catalog and EPSS for prioritization · manual inventory of log4j-core jars on the dashboard workload
items.logic:
SCAN: credentialed (authenticated) vulnerability scan of the authorized lab scope, plus a Trivy scan of every container image digest recorded in Project 10 — an unauthenticated scan alone misses local patch state and library-level findings like this one.
PRIORITY: CVSS 10.0 is only the start of the ranking. This finding is KEV-listed (actively exploited in the wild), has public exploit code everywhere, sits in a workload reachable from the lab network, and the vulnerable code path (logging attacker-controlled strings) is the dashboard's normal operation — a lookup string in a searched indicator is exactly the trigger. Priority 1 of this cycle, 7-day remediation SLA, ahead of findings with equal CVSS but no exposure.
FIX: upgrade log4j-core to a fixed 2.17+ release (or remove the JndiLookup class as the emergency stopgap), rebuild and redeploy the image with a new pinned digest, then rescan — the finding closes on rescan evidence, not on the change ticket.
items.ev:
Scanner output (credentialed scan, lab scope, 2026-11-20):
Plugin: Apache Log4j RCE (CVE-2021-44228) — CRITICAL, CVSS 10.0, KEV: yes
Asset: intel-dashboard workload (Project 5's dashboard), soc-apps namespace, service port 8080/tcp reachable from the lab LAN
Evidence: log4j-core-2.14.1.jar present in the image layer and on the running container's classpath (verified by file inventory inside the lab image, not banner alone); the application logs the indicator strings users submit for enrichment — the exact input class Log4Shell triggers on.
Cross-check: Trivy on the pinned digest reports the same CVE against the same jar — two scanners, one finding, counted once.
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — critical, Priority 1. No exploit was run against the dashboard; the version, the reachability, and the input path are the proof standard for this CVE.
items.triage:
1. Stopgap today if the upgrade cannot ship immediately: remove JndiLookup from the classpath (or set log4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true where the version honors it) and restrict the dashboard's network reachability using Project 10's NetworkPolicies — then treat the upgrade as still due, a stopgap is not a fix.
2. Check for prior exploitation before patching erases the trail: search the dashboard and SIEM logs (Projects 1 and 2) for JNDI lookup patterns (${jndi:ldap / ${jndi:rmi) in submitted indicators and outbound LDAP/RMI connections from the workload — none found in the retained window, recorded as checked with that window stated.
3. Upgrade the library, rebuild the image, pin the new digest in the manifest (Project 10's standard), redeploy, and confirm the old digest is no longer running anywhere in the cluster.
4. Rescan the asset and file the clean plugin output with this finding; update the remediation tracker: owner, fix date, rescan date.
5. Sweep the whole estate for the same library — Log4j hides inside vendor tools and plugins; the jar inventory (not just the scanner) is the sweep of record, and it found one further copy inside an unused test tool, removed with its host tool.
items.fp: Scanner FPs are common on this CVE: several products bundle a log4j jar that is present but never loaded, and version banners alone have flagged patched builds that backported the fix. The validation used here is classpath plus reachability plus input path — a jar that is not on the running classpath is recorded as a validated non-finding with the evidence, not silently deleted and not counted in the report's totals. The reverse error matters more: an unauthenticated scan of this estate did NOT flag Log4Shell at all (no banner to read), which is the standing argument for credentialed scanning in this lab's method.

items.title: Domain controller missing its Netlogon patch: Zerologon exposure (CVE-2020-1472) on DC-LAB01
items.src: Credentialed Nessus scan of DC-LAB01 (patch audit via authenticated registry and file-version checks) · patch inventory against the Microsoft update catalog · scanner's safe (non-exploiting) Zerologon check
items.logic:
