SCAN: the credentialed scan audits the DC's installed-patch state directly; the scanner's Zerologon check used is the safe variant that inspects patch level and Netlogon configuration — no exploit attempt is made against a domain controller, even a lab one, because the real exploit can disrupt authentication and proves nothing the patch audit does not.
PRIORITY: CVSS 10.0, KEV-listed, and the asset is the Tier-0 domain controller Project 9 hardened — asset criticality is the multiplier: this patch gap hands an unauthenticated network attacker a path to Domain Admin on the one machine every other control trusts. Priority 1 alongside VULN-01; the pair are this cycle's entire critical queue.
FIX: apply the current cumulative update chain to DC-LAB01 (the missing Netlogon fix is long superseded — the real finding is a patch process that let a DC fall multiple cycles behind), confirm Netlogon enforcement mode, reboot in the lab's maintenance pattern, and rescan.
items.ev:
Scanner output (credentialed scan, 2026-11-20):
Plugin: Netlogon Elevation of Privilege (CVE-2020-1472) — CRITICAL, CVSS 10.0, KEV: yes
Asset: DC-LAB01 (LAB.LOCAL domain controller, Project 9's Tier-0 host)
Evidence: patch audit shows the DC three cumulative-update cycles behind the lab's other Windows hosts; the Netlogon security update is absent from the installed list and the relevant file versions predate the fix. Domain Controller Enforcement Mode registry value not set.
Context from Project 9: AD-01 already removed the leftover admin accounts on this DC — this finding is the other half of the same lesson: the accounts are clean and the platform underneath them is unpatched.
VERDICT: CONFIRMED by patch audit — critical, Priority 1. Exposure is internal-network (Netlogon is not internet-facing here), which is why it ranks level with VULN-01 rather than above it: reachability is part of the score, not a footnote.
items.triage:
1. Snapshot/backup the lab DC before patching (a DC patch failure is an authentication outage for the whole lab), then apply the full cumulative chain, not just the single CVE's update — the chain is what the rescan will verify.
2. Set Domain Controller Enforcement Mode for Netlogon secure channel enforcement and watch the DC's event log for non-compliant device accounts before and after — in this lab, one legacy test device needed its trust repaired, found by the log review rather than by an outage.
3. Reboot in the maintenance window and verify authentication end to end: workstation logon, Kerberos ticket issue (Project 9's 4769s), and the SIEM's log forwarding from the DC all confirmed working.
4. Rescan DC-LAB01 credentialed and file the patch-audit output: the closure bar is zero missing security updates on the Tier-0 host.
5. Fix the process, not just the patch: the DC joins the same monthly patch ring as every other host with a named owner — a Tier-0 asset three cycles behind is a cadence failure (see VULN-06), and the tracker records it that way.
items.fp: The common FP here is a scanner reading the wrong signal on a DC — an unauthenticated check can flag the Netlogon service's behavior on a fully patched controller, which is why this finding rests on the authenticated patch and file-version audit instead. The opposite trap is 'we applied that update in 2020': superseded and re-released updates mean the installed-list evidence, not memory, decides. No exploitation proof was attempted or needed; for DC vulnerabilities the safe-check-plus-patch-audit standard is deliberate and is stated in the report so a reader does not mistake restraint for uncertainty.

items.title: SMBv1 still enabled and MS17-010 unpatched on the file server (CVE-2017-0144, EternalBlue class)
items.src: Credentialed Nessus scan of FILE-LAB01 + Nmap SMB scripts (smb-protocols, smb-vuln-ms17-010) from an authorized scan position · SMB configuration audit (Get-SmbServerConfiguration) on the host
items.logic:
SCAN: two independent methods — the credentialed scanner's patch audit and a network-side SMB protocol enumeration — because this finding has two halves (an obsolete protocol enabled AND its patch missing) and each method proves one half.
PRIORITY: the CVE family is old, KEV-listed, and wormable — the ransomware pattern Projects 1 and 3 were built around — but the asset is internal-only and the lab's other hosts are patched, which bounds spread. High, 30-day SLA, ranked below the two criticals and above everything local-only: exploitability and self-propagation outweigh its age.
FIX: apply the patch chain, then disable SMBv1 server-side (it has no remaining client in this lab — proven before disabling, see triage), keep SMB signing required (pairs with Project 9's AD-07), and rescan with both methods.
items.ev:
Scanner and enumeration output (2026-11-20):
Nmap smb-protocols against FILE-LAB01: dialects NT LM 0.12 (SMBv1), 2.0.2, 2.1, 3.0 — SMBv1 offered by the server.
smb-vuln-ms17-010: VULNERABLE (safe check) — and the credentialed patch audit agrees: the MS17-010 rollup is absent, FILE-LAB01 is two cycles behind (kept back with DC-LAB01 in the same skipped ring, VULN-06).
Host configuration: EnableSMB1Protocol = True; SMB signing enabled but not required (Project 9's AD-07 noted the domain-wide half of this).
Shares on the host: lab evidence copies and the SIEM archive drop — the Project 3 ransomware scenario's exact target set.
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — high. A 2017 vulnerability persisting in 2026 is not a scanner curiosity; it is the patch process failing on the oldest, best-understood item in the catalog.
items.triage:
1. Prove SMBv1 has no real clients before touching it: review the host's SMB session logs for two weeks of connections — every lab client negotiated SMB 3; the one SMBv1 speaker was the scanner itself. Disabling a protocol on a guess is how file servers fall over.
2. Patch first, then disable SMBv1 (Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature / Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false), then set SMB signing to required on the server in step with Project 9's domain change.
3. Verify the shares still serve: the SIEM archive drop and the evidence-copy share tested from WIN-LAB01 and LINUX-LAB01 (SMB3 sessions) after the change.
4. Rescan both ways: Nmap no longer offers SMBv1, the credentialed audit shows the rollup installed. File both outputs.
5. Hunt backwards with Project 1's rules: SMB admin-share and lateral-movement detections reviewed for FILE-LAB01 over the exposure window — no anomalous sessions found, recorded with the window stated.
items.fp: MS17-010 checks have a known FP history: early unauthenticated checks flagged patched hosts, which is why this finding requires the credentialed patch audit to agree with the network check before it is reported. The reverse also occurs — a host can be patched yet still offer SMBv1, and scanners that report only the CVE half understate it; the protocol stays a finding on its own because SMBv1's other flaws and its downgrade value to an attacker do not depend on one CVE. Tune: 'SMBv1 detected' from a banner-only tool is a lead, never a reported finding, in this lab's standard.

items.title: Linux privilege escalation: sudo vulnerable to Baron Samedit (CVE-2021-3156) on LINUX-LAB01
items.src: Credentialed Nessus scan of LINUX-LAB01 (authenticated package audit over SSH) · package inventory (dpkg) and sudo version check on the host · Project 2's auth.log context for who holds local accounts
items.logic:
SCAN: authenticated package audit — the scanner logs in over SSH and compares installed package versions against the distribution's fixed versions, which is the only reliable way to scan Linux patch state (banner checks misread backports, see the FP notes).
PRIORITY: CVSS 7.8 understates this one in this estate's specific history: it is a LOCAL privilege escalation, and Project 2 proved a local account on this exact host (deploy) can be taken over from the internet — a low-privilege foothold here is one sudoedit away from root, and root on this host is what edited sudoers and wiped auth.log in INV-03 and INV-08. Exploitability plus this host's incident history rank it high, 30-day SLA, above the container findings whose vulnerable code is not reachable.
FIX: upgrade the sudo package to the distribution's fixed version, verify, and rescan; no configuration workaround is accepted as closure.
items.ev:
Scanner output (credentialed scan, 2026-11-20):
Plugin: sudo heap-based buffer overflow (CVE-2021-3156, 'Baron Samedit') — HIGH, CVSS 7.8, KEV: yes
Asset: LINUX-LAB01 (the SSH/sudo host from Project 2's investigation)
Evidence: authenticated audit reports sudo 1.8.31 installed; the distribution's fixed version is 1.9.5p2-3ubuntu5.13 (backport-inclusive version string checked against the Ubuntu security notice, not a raw upstream comparison — see FP notes). sudo -V on the host confirms 1.8.31, and sudoedit is present, the affected code path.
Accounts that gain root if this fires: every local account, including deploy (reset after Project 2, still a valid low-privilege logon) — the finding's blast radius is 'any foothold becomes root'.
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — high. Version evidence from two sources (package audit and the host itself) with the distribution's fix version as the comparison.
items.triage:
1. Patch sudo from the distribution repository and confirm the new version on the host (sudo -V) before rescanning — the rescan verifies the package database, the version check verifies reality.
2. Review who could have used it: sudo and auth logs for the exposure window, with Project 2's INV-08 caveat attached — the 02:12-02:47 gap in that incident means 'no evidence of use' is bounded to the surviving logs, and the report says exactly that.
3. Check for the persistence a root attacker would leave (Project 2's INV-03 list: sudoers diff against the known-good snapshot, new accounts, authorized_keys) — sudoers matches the post-incident rebuilt version, no new accounts found.
4. Rescan credentialed: plugin clears only when the fixed package version is present.
5. Add LINUX-LAB01 to the same monthly patch ring as the Windows hosts (VULN-06's fix) — this host fell behind for the same reason the DC did: it was nobody's named patching job.
items.fp: Linux version scanning's classic FP is the backport: distributions fix vulnerabilities without changing the upstream version number, so a scanner (or an analyst) comparing '1.8.31 < 1.9.5' naively will both miss real fixes and invent false ones. This project validates every Linux finding against the distribution's own security notice and the package's full version string including the Ubuntu revision suffix. The same scan produced one such FP on this host (an OpenSSH banner hit) — it is documented in VULN-07's validation work and excluded from the totals, which is what makes the totals trustworthy.

items.title: Container image debt: 87 Trivy findings in the siem-ingest image, 4 critical — fixed by rebuilding the base, not by chasing CVEs
items.src: Trivy image scans of every digest pinned in Project 10's manifests · image layer and package inventory (OS packages + language libraries) · reachability review: which flagged packages the workload actually executes
items.logic:
SCAN: Trivy against the exact digests Project 10 pinned — scanning a tag would audit an image that may not be the one running. Every CVE is then triaged in three buckets: (a) in a package the workload executes AND reachable — real findings; (b) in the image but in code the workload never runs — remediation by rebuild, lower urgency; (c) no fix available upstream — recorded with a review date, never silently dropped.
PRIORITY: the headline critical is curl's SOCKS5 heap overflow (CVE-2023-38545, CVSS 9.8) — but the ingest workload never uses a SOCKS5 proxy, so its real-world rank drops below VULN-01 to VULN-04, whose vulnerable code paths are live. The OpenSSL denial-of-service (CVE-2022-0778) in the same image IS in a linked library the service loads. Net: high as a single 'rebuild the image' finding, 30-day SLA — one rebuild clears 80+ rows, which is the correct unit of work.
FIX: rebuild siem-ingest on the current maintained base image, re-pin the digest, redeploy, rescan; add image scanning to the rebuild path so the next base-image drift alarms at build time.
items.ev:
Trivy summary (image: soc/siem-ingest@sha256:<digest pinned in Project 10>, base image 14 months old):
Total: 87 vulnerabilities (4 critical, 23 high, 41 medium, 19 low) across OS packages and one language library set.
Critical detail: CVE-2023-38545 curl (9.8) — package present, SOCKS5 code path NOT used by the workload (no proxy configuration anywhere in its environment or code); CVE-2022-0778 OpenSSL (7.5, listed high) — library loaded by the ingest service at runtime, reachable parsing path.
Composition check: 71 of the 87 findings trace to the stale OS base layer alone; the application layer contributes 16. The intel-dashboard image (rebuilt during Project 5) scans at 9 total by comparison, and soc-prod's images (VULN-08) at zero critical/high.
VERDICT: CONFIRMED as one rebuild finding — high. Reported as a single prioritized item with the full CVE list attached, not as 87 separate findings inflating the report.
items.triage:
1. Rebuild on the current base image first and rescan the result before redeploying: the rebuild cleared 79 of 87 in the lab build, including both named CVEs; the remaining 8 are medium/low with fixes queued in the next base refresh.
2. Redeploy with the new pinned digest (Project 10's manifest standard), verify the ingest pipeline end to end — logs flowing into the SIEM is the acceptance test, the scanner output alone is not.
3. Record the bucket-(c) items honestly: 2 findings with no upstream fix at scan time get named entries in the tracker with a 30-day re-check date instead of disappearing.
4. Wire Trivy into the image build path with a fail threshold (critical with a fix available blocks promotion to soc-apps), so image debt is caught when it is created.
5. Set the standing cadence: base images refreshed monthly alongside host patching (VULN-06) — container patching is patching, and it joins the same ring and the same report.
items.fp: Container scanners over-report by design: they match package inventories, not running code, so a vulnerable library in an unused layer or a binary the workload never invokes still prints red. The discipline here is reachability triage with the evidence written down (the curl/SOCKS5 reasoning is recorded in the finding, so a reviewer can disagree with facts, not vibes). The opposite error is dismissing image findings wholesale — the OpenSSL item in this same image is genuinely loaded at runtime. Tune: report image debt as rebuild findings with reachable items named individually; a raw 87-line CVE dump is scanner output, not a vulnerability report.

items.title: The root cause: patch cadence failure — WIN-LAB01 and WIN-LAB02 three cycles behind, PrintNightmare exposed (CVE-2021-34527)
items.src: Credentialed Nessus patch audits across all Windows hosts (missing-patch rollup per host) · service configuration review (Print Spooler state per host) · patch history from Windows Update records
items.logic:
SCAN: beyond single CVEs, the scan's missing-patch rollup is read as a pattern per host: how many cumulative cycles behind, which KEV entries are inside the gap, and which risky services run without a compensating reason.
PRIORITY: the named item is PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527, CVSS 8.8, KEV) — remote code execution / privilege escalation through the Print Spooler, a service running on WIN-LAB01 and WIN-LAB02 although neither host prints. But the finding's real subject is the cadence: DC-LAB01 (VULN-02), FILE-LAB01 (VULN-03), and these workstations all fell behind in the same skipped rings. Fixing CVEs one at a time without fixing the ring guarantees next quarter's report reads the same. High, 30-day SLA for the rollup; the spooler mitigation applies today.
FIX: disable the Print Spooler on hosts that do not print (today, no patch window needed), bring both hosts fully current, and put every lab host on one named monthly patch ring with the scan as its verification.
items.ev:
Patch rollup (credentialed scan, 2026-11-20):
WIN-LAB01: 47 missing security updates across 3 cumulative cycles; KEV entries inside the gap include CVE-2021-34527 (PrintNightmare). Print Spooler service: Running, Automatic. The host has no printers installed and no print jobs in its history — pure exposure, no function.
WIN-LAB02: 39 missing updates, same cycles, spooler also running (this host was the Project 10 assessment's second workstation).
Contrast inside the same estate: the rebuilt WIN-LAB02 image used for VULN-08's control and the soc-prod hosts are current — the ring works where it is actually run.
Patch history shows the gap is not a failed update: no install attempts in the skipped cycles. The ring simply was not run for these hosts while Projects 5 to 10 consumed the lab time.
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — high as a cadence finding with one KEV item named. Reported once, at the pattern level, with per-host patch lists attached.
items.triage:
1. Mitigate PrintNightmare today without waiting for the patch window: stop and disable the Print Spooler on WIN-LAB01 and WIN-LAB02 (neither prints; the one lab printer hangs off a different host), and verify the service state in the rescan.
2. Patch both hosts fully current in one maintenance pass each, reboot, and re-run the credentialed audit: closure is zero missing security updates, not 'the named CVE is gone'.
3. Stand up the single monthly patch ring: every lab host (Windows, Linux, DC, file server) plus container base images (VULN-05), a named owner, a fixed week, and this scan re-run as the ring's report card.
4. Add the drift alarm: a host more than one cycle behind appears on the board as an open item automatically — the next cadence failure should surface in 30 days, not at the next annual-style assessment.
5. Record the honest cause in the tracker: the ring was skipped under project time pressure, three times. Naming the process failure is what keeps the fix procedural instead of personal.
items.fp: Missing-patch counts need analyst judgment: scanners count superseded updates and optional previews alongside real security gaps, so the 47 and 39 here are the scanner's security-relevant rollup after superseded items were collapsed — the raw count was higher and would have been the less honest number to report. A host mid-patch-window can also show gaps that are already scheduled; the check is cycles behind (three) and KEV content, not any nonzero count. Tune: report cadence (cycles behind, KEV in gap) as the headline and keep the full patch list as an attachment — managers act on the pattern, analysts work from the list.

items.title: Weak transport security on the SIEM web dashboard: TLS 1.0/1.1 enabled, SWEET32 cipher, expired internal certificate
items.src: Nessus web/TLS plugins + testssl.sh enumeration against the dashboard service · configuration review of the dashboard's TLS termination · certificate inventory (issuer, expiry, SANs)
items.logic:
SCAN: scanner TLS plugins give breadth; testssl.sh gives the authoritative protocol and cipher enumeration; the certificate is inspected directly. All three are read together — TLS findings are the most over- and under-reported class in scanner output.
PRIORITY: medium, and the reasoning is written down because mediums are where prioritization earns its keep: TLS 1.0/1.1 and the 3DES cipher (SWEET32, CVE-2016-2183) are real weaknesses, but exploiting them needs a network position and large traffic volumes, the dashboard is internal-only, and the credentials it carries are the lab SIEM's. It ranks below every KEV and reachable-RCE item and above informational noise, on a 90-day SLA — and the expired certificate is bundled in because it trains users to click through warnings, which is a phishing gift (Project 13's topic).
FIX: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only, 3DES and other legacy ciphers removed, and a valid certificate from the lab's internal CA with the dashboard's real name in the SAN list.
items.ev:
Enumeration evidence (2026-11-20):
testssl.sh against the SIEM dashboard (WIN-LAB01, 443/tcp): protocols offered — TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2 (TLS 1.3 absent); cipher suites include TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA (SWEET32-affected, 64-bit block cipher).
Certificate: self-signed at lab setup, expired 74 days before the scan, CN does not match the dashboard's current hostname — every analyst's browser warns on every visit, and the team has learned to proceed anyway.
Scanner agreement: Nessus flags TLS 1.0, the sweet32 plugin, and the expired/untrusted certificate as three separate mediums; this report consolidates them into one transport-security finding with one fix, the same anti-inflation rule as VULN-05.
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — medium. All three sub-items verified by direct enumeration and certificate inspection, not by plugin output alone.
items.triage:
1. Issue the replacement certificate from the lab internal CA with the correct SANs and install it first — it is the sub-item with daily human impact (warning fatigue) even though it is cryptographically the least severe.
2. Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1 and remove 3DES at the dashboard's TLS termination, then confirm every lab client still connects: the SIEM's own agents and the analysts' browsers all negotiate TLS 1.2, verified per client, not assumed.
3. Enable TLS 1.3 where the stack supports it and record the final protocol/cipher list as the estate's baseline for any future web service.
4. Rescan with testssl.sh and file the before/after enumerations; the closure bar is the enumeration, not the scanner's plugin clearing.
5. Put certificate expiry on the board as a dated check (30-day warning) — an expired cert found by a scanner means the calendar control was missing, and that control is the fix's durable half.
items.fp: TLS scanning is FP-prone in both directions: scanners flag 'TLS 1.0 detected' from a single handshake probe that some stacks answer for compatibility even when the protocol cannot actually negotiate a session — here the enumeration completed real TLS 1.0 and 1.1 sessions, which is the confirmation standard used. Scanners also flag self-signed certificates on purely internal test services that never carry credentials; those are recorded as informational with the reasoning, not padded into the medium count. Tune: a TLS finding is reported when the weak protocol or cipher demonstrably negotiates AND the service carries credentials or data worth protecting — both halves, evidenced.

items.title: Control check (passes): the rebuilt workstation image and soc-prod containers scan clean — zero critical, zero high, zero KEV
items.src: Same credentialed Nessus scan and Trivy pipeline as VULN-01 to VULN-07, pointed at the control assets · patch audit and image inventory for the rebuilt WIN-LAB02 image and the soc-prod namespace images
items.logic:
CONTROL PURPOSE: a vulnerability report where everything fails is as suspect as Project 8's dashboard without CLD-08 or Project 10's without K8S-08. This entry re-runs the project's exact methods against the assets maintained on the new cadence — the rebuilt WIN-LAB02 workstation image (current patch ring, spooler disabled, no SMBv1) and the soc-prod container images (refreshed base, pinned digests from Project 10) — and requires the evidence to come back clean on the same bars the other findings failed: (1) zero critical and zero high scanner findings; (2) zero CISA KEV entries at any severity; (3) zero missing cumulative cycles; (4) no end-of-life OS or runtime; (5) TLS enumeration matching the VULN-07 baseline.
PASS = all five, evidenced the same way a FAIL would be.
items.ev:
Control evidence (same scan run, 2026-11-20):
Rebuilt WIN-LAB02 image: credentialed patch audit — 0 missing security updates; Print Spooler disabled; SMBv1 absent; scanner totals 3 informational items only (banner disclosures, recorded and accepted).
soc-prod images (4 workloads): Trivy totals — 0 critical, 0 high, 6 medium/low with fixes available in the next scheduled base refresh and named in the tracker; 0 KEV at any severity.
TLS check against the soc-prod dashboard copy: TLS 1.2/1.3 only, no 3DES, valid internal-CA certificate with 212 days remaining.
VERDICT: PASS. The target state for the whole estate already exists inside it — VULN-01 to VULN-07 are not knowledge gaps; they are the assets that were never brought onto the cadence these control assets are on.
items.triage:
1. Use these assets as the remediation template: VULN-06's patch ring copies the rebuilt image's build checklist, and VULN-05's rebuild copies soc-prod's base-refresh pattern — fixes copy a working example instead of improvising per asset.
2. Re-run this control with every scan cycle: the day a control asset shows a KEV entry or slips a patch cycle, the cadence itself — not one host — is the finding.
3. Protect the control's honesty: it is produced by the same scan, same credentials, same plugins as the failures, never by a separate friendlier scan.
4. Record the pass with its date and evidence exactly like a failure — an undated 'the new image is clean' is how controls quietly rot (the CLD-08 / K8S-08 rule).
5. No remediation tickets from a pass: the 6 medium/low image items ride the already-scheduled base refresh, named in the tracker, and that is the whole action list.
items.fp: A clean scan is a point-in-time claim with strict limits, stated in the report: it means these scanners, with these plugin feeds, on this date, found nothing at or above the stated bars on these assets. It does not mean 'secure' — zero-days, configuration flaws (Projects 8 to 10's territory), and anything the credentialed scan cannot see are outside the claim. The control would stop passing on any one of its five bars, which is why it is re-run by the same collection path as the failures instead of trusted from the rebuild notes.

writeup.problem: Projects 1 to 10 found intrusions, misconfigurations, and weak identities one assessment at a time. Project 11 asks the maintenance question underneath all of them: what is simply unpatched and known-vulnerable on the systems the lab already owns? Every asset here is authorized lab scope — the Windows hosts, the LAB.LOCAL domain controller, the file server, the Linux host, and the container images Project 10 pinned by digest. The problem a vulnerability management lab solves is not 'run a scanner'; any scanner prints hundreds of rows. The problem is turning scanner output into a short, honest, prioritized list a manager can fund and an analyst can execute: which findings are real, which are reachable, which are being exploited in the wild right now, what gets fixed this week versus this quarter, and how anyone proves the fix worked. That pipeline — authorized scope, credentialed scanning, validation, prioritization, reporting, remediation, rescan — is the project.
writeup.methodology: Scope, defined in writing before any scanning: WIN-LAB01, WIN-LAB02, DC-LAB01, and FILE-LAB01 (Windows), LINUX-LAB01, and the lab-k8s container images at the digests pinned in Project 10. Nothing outside the lab was scanned. Tooling: Nessus/OpenVAS for credentialed (authenticated) host scans — the scanner logs in and audits patch and package state directly, which is what makes Linux backports and Windows cumulative state readable at all; Nmap SMB and TLS scripts and testssl.sh for network-side verification; Trivy for image scans. Prioritization model, applied to every finding and recorded in its entry: CVSS base score, plus CISA KEV membership (exploited in the wild), plus exploit maturity, plus exposure (internet, lab-network, or local-only, and whether the vulnerable code path is actually reachable — VULN-05's curl is the worked example of a 9.8 that drops), plus asset criticality (the domain controller multiplier in VULN-02). Method per finding: (1) scanner flags it, (2) validate by hand against patch, package, or configuration evidence before it is reported — scanner output alone never becomes a finding, (3) check for prior exploitation in the Projects 1 and 2 logs where the finding allows it, (4) remediate or mitigate, (5) rescan, and close only on rescan evidence. Reporting: three artifacts — a one-page executive summary (counts by priority, the top risks in plain language, the cadence ask), the technical report (these eight entries with evidence), and a remediation tracker (owner, SLA by priority: Priority 1 critical/KEV/reachable 7 days, high 30 days, medium 90 days, and a rescan date per item). Safe-proof standard throughout: version, patch, and configuration evidence; no exploit was run against the domain controller or the dashboard.
writeup.findings: One scan cycle, eight reported items: 2 critical, 4 high, 1 medium, and 1 passing control — consolidated from several hundred raw scanner rows after validation removed duplicates and false positives (the raw count and the reported count are both stated in the executive summary, with the gap explained: superseded patches, the same CVE from two scanners, and banner-based hits that patch evidence cleared). Critical: VULN-01, Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228, CVSS 10.0, KEV) in the threat-intel dashboard's log4j-core 2.14.1, reachable through the indicator strings the dashboard exists to log; VULN-02, DC-LAB01 three patch cycles behind with the Zerologon fix (CVE-2020-1472, CVSS 10.0, KEV) absent — on the Tier-0 host Project 9 just finished hardening. High: VULN-03, SMBv1 enabled and MS17-010 missing on FILE-LAB01, proven by both patch audit and network enumeration; VULN-04, sudo vulnerable to Baron Samedit (CVE-2021-3156) on LINUX-LAB01, ranked above its 7.8 by Project 2's history on that host; VULN-05, 87 Trivy findings in the siem-ingest image (4 critical) consolidated into one rebuild finding, with the 9.8 curl CVE honestly demoted on reachability and the loaded OpenSSL library kept high; VULN-06, the pattern underneath half the report — WIN-LAB01 and WIN-LAB02 three cycles behind with KEV-listed PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) exposed through a Print Spooler neither host uses. Medium: VULN-07, TLS 1.0/1.1, a SWEET32 cipher, and an expired self-signed certificate on the SIEM dashboard, verified by direct enumeration. Control: VULN-08 passed on all five bars — the rebuilt workstation image and soc-prod containers scan with zero critical, zero high, and zero KEV. Remediation status at report time: spooler disabled and Log4j stopgap applied day one; DC and file server patched and rescanned clean; sudo upgraded; ingest image rebuilt (79 of 87 cleared) and redeployed; TLS fix and the monthly patch ring — every host plus container base images, one named owner, this scan as its verification — stood up as the cycle's durable output.
writeup.challenges: Four honest difficulties. First, scanner noise is the project's central labor problem: the raw output ran to hundreds of rows, and validation — checking each critical and high against patch audits, distribution backport notices, and reachability — was most of the work and is the entire difference between this report and a scanner dump; one OpenSSH banner hit on LINUX-LAB01 died at exactly this step, cleared by the Ubuntu backport evidence, and is recorded as a validated false positive rather than deleted quietly. Second, prioritization forces judgment calls that a score cannot make: a CVSS 9.8 in unreachable code (VULN-05's curl) versus a 7.8 local escalation on a host with a proven foothold history (VULN-04) — the model (KEV, exposure, reachability, asset criticality) makes those calls defensibly, but they remain calls, and each entry writes its reasoning down so a reviewer can dispute it. Third, remediation has blast radius and sequencing: the DC cannot be patched casually, SMBv1 cannot be disabled until its clients are proven absent, and the ingest image rebuild had to keep logs flowing into the SIEM the whole time — fixes were ordered and tested, not batch-applied. Fourth, the limits: this is a point-in-time scan of a small lab — plugin feeds age daily, a clean rescan means 'nothing these tools could see on this date' (VULN-08 states its own limits), authenticated scanning depends on the scan account's access staying valid and scoped, and the method says nothing about zero-days or the configuration flaws Projects 8 to 10 cover. Vulnerability management is a cadence, not an event, which is why the patch ring matters more than any single finding in this report.
writeup.learned: Prioritization is the skill; scanning is the commodity. Anyone can produce 400 rows — the analyst's work is the defensible eight: validated against real patch evidence, ranked by whether the flaw is exploited in the wild, reachable in this estate, and sitting on an asset that matters, with the reasoning written where a reviewer can challenge it. Credentialed scanning is non-negotiable: the unauthenticated pass missed the cycle's worst finding entirely (Log4Shell has no banner), and Linux patch state is simply unreadable without the distribution's backport context. The estate's deepest lesson repeats Projects 8, 9, and 10 in a new key: nothing here was a knowledge gap — the control assets (VULN-08) prove the team can build clean, and every failure is an asset that fell off a cadence nobody owned. A monthly patch ring with a named owner and a rescan as its report card prevents more findings than any scanner upgrade. Reports are what make the work real: the executive summary got the cadence funded, the technical entries gave analysts evidence to work from, and the tracker with SLAs and rescan dates is what turns 'we should patch' into closed findings. And closure means rescan evidence, never a ticket status — the same evidence-first rule as forensics in Project 7 and the cloud fixes in Project 8. Next: Project 12, Web Application Security Lab, takes the dashboard services this project scanned from the outside and tests them from the application layer in.

soc.title: Web Application Security Lab
soc.desc: Build a testing workflow and document vulnerabilities.
steps: Set up a deliberately vulnerable practice app locally
Build your testing workflow: intercept, enumerate, test, record
Work through the common vulnerability classes methodically
Document each finding with reproduction steps and impact
Stand up the testing workflow end to end: Burp proxy and browser configured, ZAP and Nikto for breadth, two lab accounts per role, and a test log that records every request, response, and verdict
Enumerate the app before testing it: crawl and directory discovery, technology and version fingerprinting, an endpoint and parameter inventory, and the role-by-object access matrix

Work the OWASP Testing Guide classes in order (injection, XSS, access control, authentication and session, tokens, misconfiguration, SSRF) and hand-confirm every scanner lead before it becomes a finding
Remediate one finding at a time against the soc-prod template, retest with the exact original requests, and file the before/after evidence so every finding closes on a retest

items.title: SQL injection in the indicator search: authentication bypass and UNION extraction
items.src: Burp Suite Proxy + Repeater (manual) and sqlmap in lab-only mode against WEB-LAB01 · application access log + database query log on the lab app host · OWASP ZAP baseline scan for breadth
items.logic:
WORKFLOW: (1) Intercept the login and indicator-search requests in Burp, (2) fuzz each parameter by hand first — single quote, boolean pairs (' OR '1'='1 / ' OR '1'='2), and time delays — before any automation, (3) confirm with sqlmap --level=1 against the lab copy only, (4) record the exact request, response difference, and database evidence for every claim.
TEST: POST /login username parameter and GET /search?q= on the practice app both concatenate input directly into the SQL query (code review of the lab app confirms string-built queries, no parameterization). A boolean-true payload returns rows, boolean-false returns none, and a UNION SELECT enumerates the users table columns. The same pattern was checked and NOT found on the soc-prod front end (WEB-08).
FIX: parameterized queries / prepared statements everywhere, an ORM or query builder that does not allow raw concatenation, least-privilege database account (the app account must not read the users table's password column), and input validation as a second layer — never as the only layer.
items.ev:
Evidence (lab app, WEB-LAB01, authorized test account analyst-a):
Baseline: POST /login username=analyst-a&password=wrong -> 200, 'Invalid credentials', 0 rows.
Boolean test: username=analyst-a' OR '1'='1' -- -&password=anything -> 302 to /dashboard, logged in as analyst-a without the password. The paired false case ('1'='2) returned Invalid credentials — the true/false difference is the proof, not a scanner label.
Search: GET /search?q=test' UNION SELECT username,password,3 FROM users -- - -> 200, result table listed 4 lab user rows including password hashes (lab-only accounts, hashes recorded by prefix only in the report).
Database log on the app host shows the injected query text verbatim in the same second — app evidence and DB evidence agree.
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — critical. Authentication bypass plus data extraction from one root cause.
items.triage:
1. Contain the pattern, not just the page: grep the lab app codebase for every string-built query — the login and search shared one helper, so fixing one endpoint and missing the other is the classic half-fix. Both were fixed together.
2. Rotate what was exposed: every lab password whose hash was enumerable gets reset, and the app's database account is rescoped so the web user cannot SELECT the password column at all.
3. Check for prior exploitation in the access and DB logs Projects 1 and 2 already collect: search for quote/UNION patterns and logins with no matching failed attempt — none found in the retained window, recorded as checked with that window stated.
4. Fix with prepared statements, rebuild, and retest with the exact requests in this entry: true/false pair must behave identically (both fail) and the UNION request must return a normal empty search.
5. Add the regression to the workflow: these three requests become a standing retest script run after every app change.
items.fp: Scanner FPs on SQLi are common: ZAP flags error-based hints on apps that return database errors for ordinary bad input without being injectable. The confirmation standard here is the boolean pair (true returns data, false does not, same everything else) plus the DB log showing the injected text — a 500 error alone is never reported as SQL injection in this lab. The reverse trap also occurred: one endpoint returned identical responses for true and false because results were paginated past the injected rows; time-based confirmation was used there and is recorded in the test notes rather than forcing a verdict from the first test.

items.title: Stored cross-site scripting in the incident note field: payload persists for the next analyst
items.src: Burp Suite Repeater + browser verification with two lab accounts (analyst-a author, analyst-b viewer) · app rendering review · ZAP reflected/stored XSS alerts as leads only
items.logic:
WORKFLOW: (1) map every field whose content is shown to a DIFFERENT user later — incident notes, indicator comments, display names — stored XSS lives there, not in search boxes; (2) submit a unique inert marker first to prove persistence and locate every place it renders; (3) submit the lab payload (<script> and an event-handler variant) and view the page as the second account; (4) check the rendering context (HTML body, attribute, or script block) because the fix differs by context.
TEST: POST /incidents/42/notes stores the note without encoding; the note renders inside the incident page's HTML body for any viewer. A payload stored by analyst-a executed in analyst-b's browser session on view — proven with a lab-only alert/document.domain proof, no session data was taken.
FIX: context-aware output encoding on render (the framework's auto-escaping, never bypassed with raw-HTML helpers), a strict Content-Security-Policy as the second layer, and HttpOnly on session cookies so a successful XSS cannot read the token (pairs with WEB-04).
items.ev: Evidence (lab app, two-account test): Step 1 — marker: analyst-a posts note 'XSS-TEST-7f3a hello' on incident 42; analyst-b sees it verbatim on GET /incidents/42 — persistence and cross-user rendering confirmed before any payload. Step 2 — payload: note body stored 201; analyst-b's view of /incidents/42 fired the handler (lab browser, screenshot and Burp history retained as evidence IDs in the test log). Step 3 — context: view-source shows the note inserted unencoded in the page body; a second field (display name on the profile page) encoded correctly — the bug is one template bypassing auto-escaping, not the whole app. VERDICT: CONFIRMED — high. Stored, cross-user, and in the incident workflow analysts open during an active case (Projects 1 and 2's timeline pages are the real-world twin).
items.triage:
1. Find every render site for the same data: the note also appears in the incident list preview and the PDF export — all three templates were checked; the list preview encoded correctly, the incident page and export did not.
2. Remove the raw-HTML bypass and rely on framework auto-escaping; where rich text is genuinely needed, sanitize with an allowlist library — never hand-rolled tag stripping.
3. Purge stored payloads: search the notes table for script/event-handler patterns from the test window and remove the test entries (evidence copies retained in the lab report, not in the live table).
4. Add CSP (default-src 'self', no unsafe-inline) and verify the app still works; CSP is defense in depth, recorded as such — it does not close the finding, the encoding fix does.
5. Retest as the second account with both payload variants; closure requires no execution in either rendering context.
items.fp: Reflected-XSS scanner alerts frequently die on manual test because the payload lands inside an attribute or a JSON response where it cannot execute — two ZAP reflected alerts in this app were exactly that and are recorded as validated non-findings with the rendering context as evidence. Stored findings need the opposite discipline: a payload that fires only for its own author is self-XSS and is reported at lower severity with that limit stated. This entry is cross-user by the two-account proof, which is why it carries high.

items.title: Broken access control: IDOR on incident reports — change one number, read another analyst's case
items.src: Burp Suite with two lab accounts at different roles (analyst-a, analyst-b, plus a read-only viewer account) · Autorize-style comparison and manual ID enumeration · server-side authorization code review of the lab app
items.logic:
WORKFLOW: (1) build an access matrix before testing: for each role, list which objects it SHOULD reach; (2) capture a legitimate request for your own object, then replay it with another object's ID and with the other account's session — the two replays separate IDOR from missing authentication; (3) test the write verbs too (PUT/DELETE on another user's object), not just reads; (4) check the API endpoints behind the UI, which often skip checks the pages have.
TEST: GET /incidents/{id} checks that the caller is logged in but never checks that the caller owns or is assigned the incident. IDs are sequential integers. analyst-b read analyst-a's incident 42 by requesting it directly, and the JSON API (GET /api/incidents/{id}) had the same flaw plus a working PUT from the viewer role that should be read-only.
FIX: server-side authorization on every object access (ownership / assignment / role), indirect references or unguessable IDs only as a supplement — never as the control — and deny-by-default route middleware tested by the access matrix.
items.ev:
Access matrix result (lab app, excerpts):
Owner (analyst-a) GET /incidents/42 -> 200 (expected).
Other analyst (analyst-b) GET /incidents/42 -> 200 with analyst-a's full case notes (NOT expected — no assignment relationship exists).
Viewer (read-only) GET /api/incidents/42 -> 200; PUT /api/incidents/42 {status: closed} -> 200 and the status changed (verified, then reverted in the lab).
Enumeration check: IDs 40-45 all returned 200 to analyst-b; the app has no per-object check to enumerate against — sequential IDs just make the walk trivial.
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — critical. Confidentiality and integrity both fail: read any case, alter any case, as any logged-in user. In a real SOC tool this is case evidence an attacker (or a curious insider) can rewrite.
items.triage:
1. Treat scope honestly: because IDs are sequential and the check was absent entirely, assume every incident object was reachable for the app's whole life; the access-log review for cross-user GETs is part of remediation, and its retention limit is stated in the report.
2. Implement the authorization check in one shared middleware/helper used by both the page route and the API — the API being missed the first time is how this bug class survives a fix.
3. Re-run the full access matrix as the retest: every cell, every role, both verbs — the matrix is filed with before (6 failures) and after (0 failures) results.
4. Add negative tests to the workflow: the retest script logs in as analyst-b and asserts 403 on analyst-a's objects, so a future refactor cannot silently drop the check.
5. Keep sequential IDs if the business wants them, but record the decision: the authorization check is the control; unguessable IDs alone would only have slowed the walk in this entry, not prevented it.
items.fp: The common FP is intended sharing mistaken for IDOR: some objects in this app (published indicators) are deliberately visible to all analysts, and direct access to them is correct behavior. Each object type was checked against its stated sharing rule before being called a finding — incidents are assignment-scoped by the app's own documentation, indicators are shared; only the assignment-scoped objects are in this entry. Tune: an IDOR claim must name the authorization rule it violates, evidenced from the app's roles or docs, not just 'I could change the number'.

items.title: Broken authentication and session handling: no lockout, no session rotation, logout does not invalidate
items.src: Burp Suite Intruder (lab accounts only, throttled) for lockout testing · session token comparison across login/logout in Burp history · app authentication configuration and code review
items.logic:
WORKFLOW: (1) test the login like Project 1's brute-force rules assume an attacker will: 50 failed attempts against a lab account and watch for lockout, throttling, or CAPTCHA; (2) capture the session token before login, after login, and after a privilege change — it must rotate; (3) log out and replay the old token — it must be dead; (4) review cookie flags (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) and idle timeout.
TEST: all four checks failed on the practice app. No lockout or delay after 50 failures (the exact gap Project 9's AD-03 fixed on the domain side, alive here at the app layer). The session ID issued to the anonymous visitor was kept after authentication (fixation). After logout, replaying the previous token still returned 200 on /dashboard. Cookies lacked HttpOnly and SameSite.
FIX: rate limiting plus lockout/backoff on the login, session rotation at authentication and privilege change, server-side invalidation at logout, and hardened cookie flags with an idle timeout — tested as a set, because each one covers a different theft path.
items.ev:
Evidence (lab app, test account brute-target created for this check):
Lockout: 50 POST /login failures in 2 minutes — every response identical timing and body, attempt 51 with the correct password succeeded instantly. No control fired.
Fixation: anonymous GET / set session=LAB-8f31; after POST /login success the session value was still LAB-8f31 (same token, now authenticated).
Logout: POST /logout -> 302; replaying GET /dashboard with session=LAB-8f31 -> 200 with the dashboard content. The token died only at its 24-hour expiry.
Cookies: Set-Cookie: session=...; Path=/ (no HttpOnly, no Secure, no SameSite in the lab's HTTP test config).
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — high. Any one of these is a finding; together they mean a stolen or fixed token is a durable logon, which is Project 2's valid-account pattern (T1078) at the web layer.
items.triage:
1. Fix server-side first: invalidate the session record at logout and rotate the ID at login — client-side cookie deletion alone leaves the replay in this entry working.
2. Add login throttling (progressive delay, then lockout with an analyst unlock path) and verify it against the Project 1 brute-force sample pattern: the web login should now generate the failures the SIEM rule can see, and then stop.
3. Set HttpOnly, Secure (on the HTTPS deployment), and SameSite=Lax on the session cookie; re-check WEB-02's impact note — HttpOnly is what keeps a stored XSS from becoming a stolen session.
4. Invalidate existing sessions on deployment of the fix: every token issued under the old rules is assumed live until expiry, so the fix ships with a forced re-login.
5. Retest all four checks with the same Burp sequences and file the four after-responses (429/lockout message, new token value, 401 on replay, flagged cookie) as closure evidence.
items.fp: Two honest nuances. First, 'no lockout' is sometimes a deliberate design paired with strong MFA and monitoring; this app has neither, and the finding says so — the verdict is about the missing combination, not the single checkbox. Second, the Secure flag's absence was observed on the lab's HTTP test instance and is recorded as a deployment check for the HTTPS instance rather than counted twice. Tune: brute-force testing runs only against designated lab accounts at throttled rates — the same test against shared accounts would lock out real users in a fixed app and pollute the Project 1 detections in an unfixed one.

items.title: JWT handling failures: none algorithm accepted and a weak signing secret cracks offline
items.src: Burp Suite (token capture and tamper replay) · jwt inspection by hand (base64 header/payload) · offline dictionary test against the lab token's HMAC secret using the lab wordlist
items.logic:
WORKFLOW: (1) identify the token type and algorithm from the header before trusting any claim about it; (2) tamper tests in order: change the payload role claim with the original signature (must fail), set alg=none with no signature (must fail), flip the algorithm RS256->HS256 where applicable; (3) if HMAC is used, test the secret's strength offline against a standard wordlist — against lab tokens only; (4) review expiry and issuer/audience validation.
TEST: the API's JWT failed two independent tests. A token with header alg changed to none and the signature removed was accepted, returning analyst data for an arbitrary user ID in the payload. Separately, the HS256 secret for genuine tokens was recovered by the offline dictionary run (a short dictionary word — value not reproduced in the report) — meaning anyone holding any one token can mint tokens for any user, including the admin role claim the API trusts.
FIX: pin the expected algorithm server-side and reject none outright, use a long random secret (or asymmetric keys) held in the secrets store Project 10 moved credentials into, validate exp/iss/aud on every request, and keep token lifetimes short.
items.ev:
Evidence (lab API, tokens for test accounts only):
Genuine token header: {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}; payload role: analyst, sub: analyst-b.
Test 1 — payload tamper, original signature kept: role->admin returned 401 (this check PASSED — signature verification exists).
Test 2 — alg=none, signature stripped, sub changed to analyst-a: GET /api/me -> 200 returning analyst-a's profile. The verifier honored the header's algorithm choice.
Test 3 — offline dictionary run against a captured lab token: secret recovered in under a minute with the standard lab wordlist; a self-minted token with role: admin was accepted by GET /api/admin/users (200, lab user list).
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — critical, by two independent paths. Either one alone is full authentication bypass; together they show the token layer was never given a threat model.
items.triage:
1. Rotate the signing secret immediately and invalidate all outstanding tokens — every token minted under a crackable secret stays forgeable until it expires, so rotation plus a version/issuer bump is the containment.
2. Pin the algorithm in the verification library configuration (an allowlist of one), reject none explicitly, and add the three tamper tests from this entry as automated negative tests.
3. Move the new secret into the managed secrets store (the Project 10 pattern) — a secret that lives in a config file in the repo is how the weak one got chosen and committed.
4. Shorten token lifetime and confirm the API checks exp on every route, including the admin routes tested here.
5. Retest: none token 401, dictionary run against a new token fails, self-minted admin token 401 — all three after-responses filed as closure.
items.fp: JWT findings are often overstated from a decode alone: seeing readable claims in the payload is NOT a vulnerability (that is how JWTs work), and a long random secret will not fall to a dictionary run — the FP discipline here is that both claims were proven by acceptance: the server accepted the none token and accepted a token signed with the recovered secret. A token the server rejects, however ugly its construction, is a hardening note, not a critical finding, and two such notes from this workflow are recorded that way in the test log.

items.title: Security misconfiguration: stack-trace errors, directory listing, a live debug endpoint, and missing security headers
items.src: Nikto and ZAP baseline scans for breadth · manual verification of every scanner claim (request the listing, the debug route, and a forced error by hand) · response-header review in Burp
items.logic:
WORKFLOW: (1) run the breadth scanners (Nikto, ZAP baseline) and treat every line as a lead; (2) hand-verify the four classes that matter: error behavior (force a 500 and read what it discloses), directory listing on known paths, debug/admin routes left enabled (/debug, /actuator, /.git), and the security-header set on real responses; (3) rate the bundle by what the disclosures ENABLE, not by scanner count.
TEST: the practice app returned full stack traces (framework version, file paths, a SQL fragment — which is how WEB-01's query structure was first hinted), listed /uploads/ contents, and answered a debug route that dumps environment keys (names recorded, values redacted in the report). Responses carried none of: Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options / frame-ancestors, or Referrer-Policy.
FIX: generic error pages with detail logged server-side only, directory listing off, debug routes removed from the deployed build (not just hidden), and the standard header set applied at the app or reverse proxy — then re-verified by the same manual requests.
items.ev:
Evidence (lab app, manual requests):
Error: GET /search?q=%27 -> 500 page containing the framework stack trace, the absolute path /srv/labapp/search.py, and the SQL statement fragment from WEB-01.
Listing: GET /uploads/ -> 200 index page listing 14 lab files including two incident-export names (the exports themselves tie back to WEB-03's scope question).
Debug: GET /debug/env -> 200 JSON of environment variable NAMES (DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET present as names; values redacted in this report and the route removed in the fix) — the route's existence, not its output, is the finding.
Headers on GET /login 200: Server banner only; CSP, XCTO, frame, and referrer headers all absent. Clickjacking proof: the login page framed cleanly in a lab test page (no frame protection).
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — medium as a bundle. No single item here hands over the app; together they hand an attacker the map (versions, paths, query shape, file names) that makes WEB-01 to WEB-05 faster to find.
items.triage:
1. Remove, do not obscure: the debug route is deleted from the deployed build and the upload directory is served through the app's authorized download path (which also closes the listing's tie to WEB-03).
2. Set the app to production error mode: generic error page to the user, full trace to the server log the SIEM already collects — the analyst keeps the detail, the attacker loses it.
3. Apply the header set at the reverse proxy so every route inherits it, then verify on five representative responses (login, dashboard, API, error page, static file) — headers set only on the homepage are a recurring half-fix.
4. Re-run Nikto/ZAP and hand-check the same four requests; closure is the four after-responses (generic 500, 403/404 on listing, 404 on debug, headers present), not a quieter scanner.
5. Add a build check: the deployment pipeline fails if a debug route or directory listing is detected in the staging check — this misconfiguration class returns by copy-paste, like Project 10's vendor manifests.
items.fp: Scanner header and config output is the noisiest class in web testing: Nikto reported 31 items for this app, of which 9 were real, several were duplicates of the four issues above, and the rest were banner guesses the manual requests disproved (including a claimed backup file that returned the app's catch-all 404 page with a 200 status — a soft-404, recorded as a validated non-finding). The rule applied throughout Project 12: a configuration finding exists when the manual request demonstrates the disclosure, and the scanner's raw count never appears in the report as a finding count.

items.title: Server-side request forgery in the URL enrichment fetcher: the server can be aimed at internal services
items.src: Burp Suite Repeater against the enrichment endpoint with lab-internal targets · app host outbound connection log + the Project 2 firewall view for corroboration · allowlist/denylist code review of the fetcher
items.logic:
WORKFLOW: (1) find every feature where the server fetches a user-supplied URL — this app has one with a familiar face: the indicator enrichment fetcher carried over from Project 5's dashboard design, which fetches a URL to preview it; (2) test in order: an external lab URL (expected to work), a loopback target, a lab-internal host by name and by IP, and a redirect from an allowed URL to an internal one; (3) test the bypass set for naive filters: decimal/octal IP forms, DNS names resolving internally, and 0.0.0.0-style variants — recorded at the level of what was tried, with the internal responses kept to status and length.
TEST: the fetcher followed the supplied URL server-side with no allowlist. Loopback and the lab app host's internal metadata-style test endpoint both returned content to the requester through the preview response, and an external lab URL that redirected to an internal address was followed — the filter, such as it was, checked the first URL only.
FIX: an allowlist of fetchable destinations by scheme and host, resolution-time checks that reject private/loopback/link-local results (and re-check after redirects, or disable redirects), no fetching of raw IPs, and the fetcher running with no route to internal services where the design allows (Project 10's NetworkPolicies are the cluster-side twin of this fix).
items.ev:
Evidence (lab app, internal targets are lab-only test services):
Baseline: POST /enrich/preview {url: http://lab-external.example/page} -> 200, preview shows the external page title — the feature working as designed.
Loopback: {url: http://127.0.0.1:8080/health} -> 200 preview containing the app's own internal health JSON (a service never exposed through the UI).
Internal host: {url: http://web-lab01.lab.local:8080/internal/status} -> 200 with the status body; the app host's outbound log and the firewall both show the server-initiated connection, corroborating server-side fetch rather than browser behavior.
Redirect: external lab URL answering 302 to the loopback health address -> followed, internal content returned. Initial-URL-only validation disproven.
VERDICT: CONFIRMED — high. In this lab the reachable internal surface is test services; the same fetcher pattern in front of a cloud metadata endpoint is the Project 8 IMDSv1 lesson (CLD-07) at the application layer, and the report rates the pattern, with the lab's actual reach stated.
items.triage:
1. Decide the feature's real need: enrichment previews only ever need a small set of public intel sources — replace free-form fetching with that allowlist, or remove server-side preview entirely if the need does not survive the question.
2. Implement validation at resolution and on every redirect hop (or disable redirects): parse the URL, resolve the host, reject any private, loopback, or link-local result, then fetch — and pin the validated address so DNS cannot change between check and fetch (TOCTOU/rebinding is named in the fix notes).
3. Egress-control the fetcher: where the app runs in the cluster, a NetworkPolicy that denies the workload access to internal service ranges makes the next fetcher bug a failure instead of a pivot (Project 10's control namespace already models the policy shape).
4. Review the fetch logs for the exposure window: which non-allowlist destinations were requested historically, stated with the log retention limit.
5. Retest the full set from this entry — loopback, internal name, internal IP, redirect, and encoded-IP variants must all fail closed while the allowlisted intel source still previews correctly.
items.fp: SSRF testing has a real FP shape: a fetcher that returns a generic error page for every failure can LOOK like it fetched internally when it did not. Confirmation here required the internal service's distinctive content in the response plus the server-side connection in two independent logs — status codes alone were not accepted. The scope honesty also matters in the other direction: the lab has no cloud metadata endpoint, so the report claims the internal test services it actually reached and names the metadata scenario as the pattern's risk, not as a demonstrated result.

items.title: Control check (passes): the hardened soc-prod web front end refuses the same workflow end to end
items.src: The identical Project 12 workflow pointed at the soc-prod web front end: Burp manual tests, two-account access matrix, token tamper set, fetcher tests, Nikto/ZAP breadth scans with manual verification
items.logic:
CONTROL PURPOSE: a web assessment where everything fails is as untrustworthy as Project 8's dashboard without CLD-08 or Project 11's report without VULN-08. This entry re-runs the project's exact tests against the hardened front end that serves the soc-prod namespace (Project 10's control) and requires each WEB-01 to WEB-07 test to fail closed on evidence: (1) boolean SQLi pair indistinguishable and UNION rejected as a normal empty result; (2) stored payload rendered encoded and inert for the second account; (3) access matrix 0 failures across roles and verbs; (4) login throttled, session rotates at login, logout replay returns 401; (5) none-alg and tampered tokens rejected, secret held in the managed store; (6) generic errors, no listing, no debug route, full header set including CSP; (7) fetcher allowlist rejects loopback, internal, and redirect-to-internal.
PASS = all seven, evidenced by the after-responses themselves.
items.ev:
Control evidence (soc-prod front end, same test scripts):
SQLi pair: true and false payloads both returned 'Invalid credentials' / empty search; UNION request returned a normal empty result set; the app log shows the inputs bound as parameters.
XSS: the WEB-02 payload stored by analyst-a rendered for analyst-b as visible text (<img...>) — readable, inert; CSP header present as the second layer.
Access matrix: 0 of 24 cells failed — cross-user GET 403, viewer PUT 403, API routes identical to page routes.
Session: token value changed at login; logout replay 401; login attempts throttled after 10 failures in the test window.
Tokens/fetcher/headers: none token 401, tampered role 401; loopback and redirect fetches rejected with the allowlist error while the approved intel source previewed; headers present on all five sampled responses including the error page.
VERDICT: PASS. The target state for the practice app already exists inside the same lab — WEB-01 to WEB-07 are remediation work against a working template, not research.
items.triage:
1. Use this front end as the remediation template for the practice app: its data-access helper (WEB-01), template defaults (WEB-02), authorization middleware (WEB-03), session configuration (WEB-04), token verification settings (WEB-05), proxy header block (WEB-06), and fetcher allowlist (WEB-07) are copied deliberately, one finding at a time, with the app retested after each.
2. Re-run this control with every assessment and after every app release: the test scripts are the control — if a future change reopens a cell, this entry flips to FAIL and that flip is the regression alarm.
3. Protect the control's honesty: it is produced by the same accounts, payloads, and scripts as the failures, never by a reduced test set for the hardened target.
4. Record the pass with its date and evidence exactly like a failure — an undated 'prod is hardened' is how controls quietly rot (the CLD-08 / K8S-08 / VULN-08 rule, kept for the fourth project running).
5. No remediation tickets from a pass: the action list is the copying work in step 1, already owned by WEB-01 to WEB-07.
items.fp: A pass is a point-in-time claim with the same limits as the earlier controls: these seven test families, with these payloads, on this date, failed closed. It does not certify the front end against vulnerability classes this workflow does not test — business-logic flaws beyond the access matrix, race conditions, and anything in the API surface not exercised here are outside the claim and are named as the next workflow's scope. The control would stop passing on any one of its seven checks, which is why it is re-run by the same scripts as the failures instead of trusted from the build notes.

writeup.problem: Projects 1 to 11 looked at the SOC platform from the network, the host, the directory, the cluster, and the patch level. Project 12 looks at it the way an attacker with nothing but a browser does: through the web application itself. The lab's web tier matters twice over — it is a real attack surface (the dashboards hold the incident data, the enrichment fetcher makes server-side requests, and the session token is a logon), and it is where the earlier projects' lessons either hold or evaporate at the application layer: Project 9 fixed lockout in the domain while the web login had none, Project 8 flagged IMDSv1 while the app's own fetcher could be aimed inward, Project 11 scanned these services for known CVEs but never tested what the application itself does with hostile input. The problem this lab solves is building a repeatable testing workflow — intercept, enumerate, test by class, record evidence, remediate, retest — and documenting real vulnerabilities with the proof standard the earlier projects set: a finding exists when the request and response demonstrate it, not when a scanner prints it.
writeup.methodology: Scope, authorized and written down before testing: the deliberately vulnerable practice app and the lab copy of the SOC web tier on WEB-LAB01, plus the hardened soc-prod front end as the control. Nothing outside the lab was tested, and brute-force and extraction tests ran only against designated lab accounts and lab data. Tooling: Burp Suite (Proxy, Repeater, Intruder) as the primary instrument — every critical and high finding was proven by hand in Repeater before any automation touched it; OWASP ZAP and Nikto for breadth scanning, treated strictly as lead generators; sqlmap in lab-only mode as confirmation for WEB-01 after the manual boolean proof; browser-based two-account verification for stored XSS and access control; and the app and database logs (already flowing into the Project 1/2 SIEM) as corroborating evidence. The workflow, run in this order and recorded in a test log: (1) enumerate — crawl, directory discovery, endpoint and parameter inventory, technology fingerprinting; (2) build the role-by-object access matrix before testing authorization; (3) test by OWASP Testing Guide class — injection, XSS, access control, authentication and session, token handling, misconfiguration, SSRF; (4) for every lead, hand-confirm with a discriminating test (a boolean pair, a second account, a tampered token the server must reject); (5) remediate one finding at a time against the soc-prod template and retest with the exact original requests, filing before/after evidence. Findings are mapped to OWASP Top 10 (2021) and CWE, with ATT&CK tactics noted where the web flaw feeds the intrusion chain from Projects 1 and 2.
writeup.findings: 8 entries recorded: 3 critical, 3 high, 1 medium, and 1 passing control, from a workflow that hand-tested 7 vulnerability classes. Critical: WEB-01, SQL injection in the login and indicator search — a boolean payload bypassed authentication and a UNION query enumerated the users table, proven by the true/false pair and the database log; WEB-03, broken access control — an IDOR on sequential incident IDs let any logged-in analyst read any case and let a read-only viewer modify one through the API, 6 failures in the access matrix; WEB-05, JWT handling — the API accepted an alg=none token for an arbitrary user and its real HMAC secret fell to an offline dictionary run, two independent paths to minting an admin token. High: WEB-02, stored XSS in incident notes executing in a second analyst's browser (two-account proof, one template bypassing auto-escaping); WEB-04, authentication and session failures as a set — no lockout after 50 failures, no session rotation at login, logout leaving the token valid on replay, and unflagged cookies; WEB-07, SSRF in the URL enrichment fetcher — loopback and internal test services reachable, redirects followed past the initial-URL check, corroborated in the app and firewall logs, the application-layer twin of Project 8's IMDS finding. Medium: WEB-06, misconfiguration as an enabling bundle — stack-trace errors that disclosed the WEB-01 query shape, a directory listing, a live debug route, and a missing security-header set, consolidated from 31 noisy scanner items into 9 hand-verified issues. The control, WEB-08, passed all seven test families against the soc-prod front end with the same scripts: parameters bound, output encoded, access matrix clean, sessions rotated and invalidated, tokens strict, headers complete, fetcher allowlisted. Remediation in the lab followed the template: prepared statements and a rescoped database account, the escaping bypass removed and stored test payloads purged, shared authorization middleware for pages and API, session and throttling fixes with a forced re-login, a rotated JWT secret in the managed store with the algorithm pinned, production error mode with the debug route deleted and headers applied at the proxy, and an allowlist fetcher with redirect re-validation — each closed by retesting the original requests.
writeup.challenges: Four honest difficulties. First, scanner noise is worse on web apps than anywhere else in this series: ZAP and Nikto together produced well over a hundred alerts for one small app, and the majority died on manual verification — soft-404s reported as backup files, reflected payloads landing in contexts where they cannot execute, header complaints with no exploitable path. The hand-confirmation discipline (a discriminating test for every claim) was most of the labor, exactly as patch validation was in Project 11. Second, several findings are only provable with restraint: the SQLi extraction stopped at lab accounts, the JWT dictionary run used lab tokens, the stored XSS proof took no session data, and the SSRF proof read only test-service responses — the report demonstrates reachability and impact class without performing the harmful version, and says so in each entry. Third, fixes interact: adding login throttling changes what Project 1's brute-force detection sees, HttpOnly cookies change WEB-02's impact rather than its existence, and the authorization middleware had to cover the API and the pages in one change or WEB-03 would have survived its own fix — remediation was sequenced and retested as a system, not as seven independent tickets. Fourth, scope limits: this workflow covers the OWASP classes it lists against a small lab app; it does not test business-logic abuse beyond the access matrix, race conditions, WebSocket behavior, or the full API surface, and the SSRF result is bounded to the lab's internal test services — the cloud-metadata scenario is named as the pattern's risk, not claimed as a result. A clean retest means these tests, on this date, the same honesty rule as every control check since Project 8.
writeup.learned: Web testing is the earlier projects' lessons at one layer up, and seeing the same failures recur is the education: the web login's missing lockout is AD-03, the fetcher's inward reach is CLD-07's IMDS problem, the JWT secret in a config file is K8S-04's committed credentials, and the scanner-noise problem is VULN-05 and VULN-06's validation labor wearing a Burp badge. The transferable skill is the workflow, not any single payload: enumerate first, build the access matrix before testing it, prove every scanner lead with a test that can distinguish true from false, and close on retest evidence. Two-account and true/false testing are the highest-value habits in the pack — they convert opinions ('this looks injectable') into verdicts, and they are what separate this report's eight findings from the hundred-plus raw alerts it started from. Authorization emerged as the deepest class: injection gets the headlines, but the IDOR's ability to read and rewrite incident cases is the failure a SOC tool can least afford, and it was invisible to every scanner in the run — only the matrix found it. And the control check remains the project's most useful output: soc-prod's front end proves the fixes are ordinary engineering (bound parameters, framework escaping left on, one authorization helper, strict token settings), so remediation is copying a working template inside the same lab, not inventing one. Next: Project 13, AI Phishing Detection Project, the final build — classifying the suspicious emails that started this whole incident chain back in Project 1's lure.

soc.title: AI Phishing Detection Project
soc.desc: Develop a basic system to classify suspicious emails.
steps: Collect a sample set of phishing and legitimate emails
Decide your signals: headers, links, language, attachments
Build the classifier and test it on held-out samples
Report accuracy honestly: false positives and false negatives

Build the feature pipeline end to end: header auth and alignment, sender and lookalike-domain checks, URL extraction with sandbox redirect resolution, TF-IDF language features, and attachment type and macro inspection
Train the logistic-regression classifier against the rules-only baseline, tune the quarantine and review thresholds, and lock the 60-email held-out test set before final scoring
Score the held-out set and record the confusion matrix with every error named: both false negatives and all three false positives read by hand and written up

Wire the classifier into the merged SOC: verdicts stamp a score header for Project 2 hunting, flagged domains and URLs go to Project 5 enrichment, attachments go to the Project 6 sandbox, and the preserved .eml joins the Project 7 evidence set

items.title: Header authentication: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC failures with misaligned sender domains
items.src: Email gateway Authentication-Results header (SPF / DKIM / DMARC) · parsed .eml headers in the classifier pipeline (Python email + authheaders) · Project 5 domain enrichment for the sending domain
items.logic:
FEATURES: spf_result, dkim_result, dmarc_result (pass/fail/none each), dmarc_alignment (From domain vs SPF/DKIM domains), from_vs_returnpath_mismatch, from_vs_replyto_mismatch, received_chain_hops, first_received_ip_is_free_or_bulk_sender.
SCORING: this family is the classifier's strongest single signal. DMARC fail with a credential or payment keyword in the subject is a HARD RULE: the email is raised to at least the review band (0.50) regardless of the model score, because a legitimate sender almost never fails its own DMARC on a password message. Full alignment pass does the opposite work: it caps how far language features alone can push a score (see PHISH-08).
THRESHOLDS (system-wide): score >= 0.85 quarantine, 0.50-0.84 analyst review, < 0.50 deliver with the verdict stamped in a header.
items.ev:
Sample email PH-014 (held-out test set, labeled phishing):
From: "Microsoft 365 Support" <support@micros0ft-secure.example>
Return-Path: <bounce@bulk-mailer-77.example> Reply-To: <reply@micros0ft-secure.example>
Subject: Action required: your password expires today
Authentication-Results: spf=fail; dkim=none; dmarc=fail (From domain micros0ft-secure.example does not align with either)
Features: dmarc_fail=1, alignment=0, returnpath_mismatch=1, replyto_mismatch=0, hops=4
Classifier: header family contributes the largest positive weight; combined score 0.94 -> QUARANTINE. Ground truth: phishing (credential harvest, PHISH-03 has its link). Verdict: TRUE POSITIVE.
items.triage:
1. Read the Authentication-Results, not the From line: the display name is free text, the auth results are the gateway's measurements. A DMARC fail on a password or payment message goes straight to the phishing queue.
2. Preserve the original .eml with full headers before any gateway rewriting — the Received chain and auth results are Project 7 evidence if the mail was delivered anywhere else.
3. Pivot the sending domain and first Received IP into Project 5 enrichment and check the gateway for every other recipient of the same campaign (same From domain or same URL domain in the last 7 days).
4. If any copy was delivered: treat clicks as Project 2 work — hunt the URL domain in proxy and DNS logs, and force a password reset for anyone who submitted credentials.
5. Block the From domain and the URL domain at the gateway, and add the pair to the classifier's known-bad list so the next variant starts from a raised score.
items.fp: Legitimate mail fails auth more often than intuition says: forwarded mail breaks SPF, mailing lists that modify bodies break DKIM, and a vendor sending through a new marketing platform can fail alignment until their DNS is fixed — two of the corpus's legitimate emails failed SPF for exactly the forwarding reason. That is why a bare SPF fail is a weighted feature, not a verdict: the hard rule needs DMARC fail PLUS a credential/payment subject, and every FP in this family in the test set came from a third-party sender whose alignment was fixed by adding their real sending domain to the allowlist with an expiry date, not by weakening the rule.

items.title: Sender spoofing: lookalike domains and display-name impersonation
items.src: Parsed From / display name in the classifier pipeline · Levenshtein and homoglyph comparison against the lab's protected-domain list (own domain, IdP, bank, Microsoft/Google) · Project 5 enrichment: domain first-seen date
items.logic:
