FEATURES: display_name_matches_protected_brand (the name says Microsoft / the CEO / IT Support while the address is unrelated), edit_distance_from_domain to the nearest protected domain (micros0ft, rnicrosoft-style homoglyphs, added words: -secure, -support, -verify), punycode_in_domain, from_domain_first_seen_days (enriched), sender_is_free_mail_with_corporate_display_name.
SCORING: edit distance 1-2 from a protected domain is a heavy positive weight; distance 0 with a passing DMARC (PHISH-01) zeroes this family out, which is what keeps the real IT notices in PHISH-08 deliverable. An external sender whose display name matches an internal executive is the BEC hard-rule trigger (PHISH-07).
items.ev:
Sample email PH-031 (held-out test set, labeled phishing):
From: "IT Helpdesk" <helpdesk@lab-secure-support.example>
Subject: Mailbox quota exceeded - verify within 24 hours
Features: display_name_brand_match=IT Helpdesk (internal name, external domain), edit_distance to the lab's real helpdesk domain = not close (borrowed trust comes from the NAME, not the domain), from_domain_first_seen = 6 days before receipt, free of any prior mail history with the lab
Classifier: sender family + young-domain feature score strongly; combined 0.89 -> QUARANTINE. Ground truth: phishing. Verdict: TRUE POSITIVE.
Contrast from training data: the real helpdesk sends from the lab domain with DMARC pass — same display name, opposite verdict. The name is the lure; the domain and auth are the tell.
items.triage:
1. Compare three things side by side: display name, actual From domain, and the domain's history with the organization. Impersonation always breaks at least one of the three.
2. Check first-seen: a protected-brand lookalike or a 'support' domain created days before the campaign is a campaign indicator — search the gateway for the domain's full recipient list.
3. For executive display names, switch to the BEC playbook (PHISH-07): verify the request out of band before anyone acts, whether or not the mail also carries a link.
4. Add confirmed lookalike domains to the protected-domain watchlist so the edit-distance feature catches the next spelling at intake.
5. If the impersonated identity is internal (CEO, helpdesk), notify the impersonated team — they will get the confused replies, and their warning is part of containment.
items.fp: False positives here are mostly legitimate lookalikes of each other: a real vendor whose name genuinely resembles a protected brand, a recruiter using a personal free-mail account with a company display name, and the lab's own test and staging domains, which are young by definition. The tuning that held: first-seen age is a weight, never a rule (new legitimate vendors exist), and the display-name feature only scores when the domain does NOT align with the claimed identity — a real Microsoft notice from a real Microsoft domain scores zero in this family no matter what its display name says.

items.title: URL analysis: anchor mismatch, redirect chains, and credential-harvest destinations
items.src: URL extraction from body (HTML and plain text) in the classifier pipeline · redirect resolution inside the Project 6 sandbox (no live clicks from analyst machines) · Project 5 enrichment: URL domain reputation and first-seen
items.logic:
FEATURES per URL (worst URL wins): url_count, anchor_text_vs_href_domain_mismatch (the text says the IdP, the href goes elsewhere), href_is_ip_literal, href_is_punycode, url_shortener_used, redirect_chain_length (resolved in the sandbox), final_domain vs sender_domain mismatch, final_domain_first_seen_days, url_contains_credential_keywords (login, verify, secure, update in path), url_has_at_sign_or_encoded_host_tricks.
SCORING: a mismatched anchor whose final domain is young and unrelated to the sender is the single heaviest URL weight in the model. Shorteners and redirects are weights, not verdicts — legitimate marketing mail uses both (see the false positives). No URL at all zeroes this family, which is exactly the BEC blind spot PHISH-07 exists to cover.
items.ev:
Sample email PH-014 continued (the PHISH-01 password lure):
Body link: anchor text 'https://login.microsoftonline.com' -> href 'http://micros0ft-secure.example/redirect?u=...' 
Sandbox redirect resolution: hop 1 the lookalike domain, hop 2 'http://198.51.100.44:8080/session/verify' (IP literal, non-standard port), final page is a credential form cloning the IdP login (screenshot filed with the sandbox run).
Features: anchor_mismatch=1, ip_literal=1, redirects=2, final_domain_age = none (IP literal), credential_keywords=2
Classifier: URL family alone scores this email into quarantine before language is even counted; combined 0.94. Verdict: TRUE POSITIVE, and the final IP:port joins the Project 5 IOC list next to the Project 2 beaconing address family it resembles.
items.triage:
1. Never click from the analyst workstation: resolve redirects in the sandbox and screenshot the landing page there. The landing page's shape (cloned IdP, form action to a third domain) is evidence.
2. Extract every URL and every final destination, not just the first href — campaigns hide the harvest page two redirects deep.
3. Hunt delivery and clicks separately: gateway logs say who received it, proxy/DNS logs (Project 2) say who resolved or visited the final domain. Only the second group needs credential resets.
4. Block the full chain at the gateway and proxy: shortener link, lookalike domain, and final IP — blocking only the first hop loses to the next variant.
5. Send the final domain and IP to Project 5 for enrichment and to Project 1 as a DNS-detection candidate if the domain starts resolving from endpoints.
items.fp: This family produced the most instructive false positive in the test set: a legitimate marketing newsletter scored 0.52 (review band) on shortener + 3 redirects + tracking domain mismatch — every URL feature firing honestly on normal marketing infrastructure. It was released on review because its headers fully aligned (PHISH-01) and its final domain was an established sender. The lesson baked into the weights: URL tricks raise a score, but aligned headers plus an established final domain can talk it back down — except when the anchor itself lies about the destination, which no legitimate sender in the corpus ever did.

items.title: Language classification: TF-IDF text model with an urgency and credential lexicon
items.src: Email subject + body text in the classifier pipeline (scikit-learn TfidfVectorizer, 1-2 grams, trained on the 240-email training split only) · handcrafted lexicon counts reviewed by hand against the training corpus
items.logic:
MODEL: logistic regression over (a) TF-IDF of subject+body and (b) the handcrafted features from PHISH-01/02/03/05. Logistic regression was chosen over the random forest that scored 1 test email better, because its coefficients are readable: an analyst can see WHY a score moved, which is what makes a verdict defensible in triage.
LEXICON FEATURES (counts, not presence): urgency terms (urgent, immediately, within 24 hours, expires today), consequence terms (account suspended, access revoked, payroll held), credential terms (verify your password, confirm your login, sign in to continue), secrecy terms (do not discuss, keep confidential — the BEC bridge to PHISH-07).
TOP LEARNED WEIGHTS (phishing direction): 'verify your account', 'password expires', 'unusual sign-in', 'confirm your identity', 'mailbox quota'. Strongest legitimate-direction weights: thread history markers, meeting and scheduling vocabulary, the lab's own project names — context a phisher cannot fake cheaply.
items.ev:
Sample email PH-047 (held-out test set, labeled phishing):
From: "Security Team" <alerts@secure-login-center.example> Subject: Unusual sign-in activity detected
Body excerpt: 'We detected an unusual sign-in to your account. If this was not you, verify your identity immediately or your account will be suspended within 24 hours.'
Auth: DMARC fail (PHISH-01 fires). Language: urgency=3, consequence=2, credential=2; TF-IDF top contributors 'unusual sign-in', 'verify your identity', 'within 24 hours'.
Classifier: combined score 0.91 -> QUARANTINE. Ground truth: phishing. Verdict: TRUE POSITIVE.
Honesty note: this is the easiest language class there is — a template the training set had close cousins of. The classes the language model is WEAK on are named in PHISH-07 and the findings, not hidden behind this score.
items.triage:
1. Read the model's top contributing phrases before acting on a language-driven verdict: if the phrases are the user's real business (a genuine deadline notice), the score is explainable and the release is documented; if they are pressure tactics, the verdict stands.
2. Check the reply context: language scores drop sharply on genuine threads (quoted history, known correspondents). A high language score on a thread-starter from a new sender is the dangerous shape.
3. For released false alarms, record which lexicon terms fired — that list is the tuning input, and two releases on the same term pattern means the weight gets reviewed, not the analyst overruled silently.
4. Never tune the lexicon on a single complaint: one user's urgent-but-real mail is a data point; the held-out set is re-scored before any weight ships.
5. Feed confirmed phishing language back as training data monthly — templates rotate, and a frozen model quietly decays.
items.fp: The classic FP is real urgency: the lab's genuine IT password-expiry notice scored 0.58 (review band) — urgency 2, credential 2, and honestly similar wording to PH-014, because real security notices and phishing lures copy each other. What saved it: DMARC pass with full alignment and the real IdP domain in its link (PHISH-01/03 scoring near zero). It was released in review in minutes, and it is kept in the corpus permanently as the control case for this family: any future tuning that pushes the real notice into quarantine is a regression, full stop.

items.title: Attachment classification: the Invoice_Q3.docm lure, replayed through the finished system
items.src: Attachment extraction in the classifier pipeline (file type by magic bytes, not extension) · macro and embedded-object inspection (olevba-style static check) · detonation verdict imported from the Project 6 sandbox analysis of the same file
items.logic:
FEATURES: attachment_count, true_file_type vs extension mismatch, macro_present (vbaProject in an Office file), autoexec_macro (AutoOpen / Document_Open), embedded_executable_or_script, double_extension (invoice.pdf.exe), archive_nesting_depth, attachment_name_matches_incident_lure_patterns (invoice, payment, remittance + quarter/month tokens).
HARD RULE: a macro-bearing Office document from an external sender whose headers do not fully align is raised to at least review, and macro + DMARC fail quarantines outright — documents that run code on open do not get the benefit of a borderline text score.
This entry is also the merged system's loop-closure test: the exact lure file preserved by Projects 6 and 7 is replayed through the classifier as a regression case on every model change.
items.ev:
Sample: the original incident lure, preserved .eml from the Project 7 evidence set (ground truth: phishing, the delivery that started Projects 1 to 4).
From: external supplier-impersonation address Subject: Invoice Q3 - payment due Attachment: Invoice_Q3.docm (macro-enabled Word document)
Static inspection: true type = Word macro document, vbaProject present, AutoOpen macro present, macro contains a downloader pattern (URL fetch + shell execution strings — matching the Project 6 SBX analysis of the same file, which detonated it to the upd.exe chain).
Headers on the preserved copy: alignment fails (the gateway record agrees; Project 7 noted the gateway retention gap for the full original, stated honestly there).
Classifier: attachment family maximum weight + hard rule -> score 0.93 -> QUARANTINE at intake. In the merged system this email never reaches the workstation, and Projects 1 to 4's intrusion does not start. Verdict: TRUE POSITIVE, and the regression case for every future model version.
items.triage:
1. A quarantined macro document is not opened to 'check it': static macro inspection first, sandbox detonation (Project 6) if the verdict needs behavior, and the file's hash goes to Project 5 either way.
2. Search the gateway for the attachment hash and the filename across all recipients and the last 30 days — lures are never sent once, and the Project 7 timeline proved this one was part of a set.
3. If any copy was delivered in the past: assume the Project 1 chain is in play — hunt for the macro's child processes and the downloaded payload's hash with the Project 1 rules before anything else.
4. Release path for a wrongly held business document is analyst-only, after sandbox clearance, and the release is logged with the hash — a user request alone never releases a macro file.
5. Keep the lure as a permanent regression test: a model or rule change that lets Invoice_Q3.docm through fails the build, the same discipline as Project 12's retest scripts.
items.fp: Legitimate macro documents exist and one is in the test set: a new vendor's genuine invoice template with a macro scored 0.61 (review band) — attachment features firing correctly on a file that does run code. The sandbox cleared its behavior (formatting macro, no network, no shell), it was released once, and that vendor's signing domain was allowlisted for the attachment rule with the macro hash recorded. The FP cost is real and accepted: macro-bearing mail from new external senders waits for an analyst. The alternative — trusting documents that execute on open — is the incident this whole board documents.

items.title: Combined scoring and held-out evaluation: the confusion matrix, reported honestly
items.src: Classifier evaluation run (scikit-learn metrics on the locked 60-email held-out set) · rules-only baseline scored on the identical set for comparison · error review: every false positive and false negative read by hand
items.logic:
PIPELINE: parse .eml -> header features (PHISH-01) -> sender features (PHISH-02) -> URL features with sandbox redirect resolution (PHISH-03) -> TF-IDF + lexicon language features (PHISH-04) -> attachment features (PHISH-05) -> logistic regression score -> hard rules can raise (never lower) the band -> verdict: QUARANTINE >= 0.85, REVIEW 0.50-0.84, DELIVER < 0.50 with the score stamped in a header for the SIEM.
EVALUATION DISCIPLINE: the 60-email test set was locked before final training, shares no campaign with the training split (same-template near-duplicates removed), and every error was read individually — the two false negatives below are findings, not rounding.
BASELINE COMPARISON (same test set): rules-only (header + blocklist checks): TP 22, FN 8, TN 24, FP 6 — accuracy 76.7%, recall 73.3%. The model's margin over the baseline comes mostly from language + URL features on mail whose headers were merely absent (not failing).
items.ev:
FINAL SYSTEM, held-out test set (60 emails: 30 phishing / 30 legitimate):
True positives 28 · False negatives 2 · True negatives 27 · False positives 3
Accuracy 91.7% (55/60) · Precision 90.3% (28/31) · Recall 93.3% (28/30)
Quarantine band (>= 0.85): 24 emails, ALL phishing — zero legitimate mail was auto-quarantined. Every false positive landed in the review band, so the FP cost was analyst minutes, not lost mail.
FALSE NEGATIVE 1 (score 0.47, delivered): thread hijack from a genuinely compromised supplier account — SPF/DKIM/DMARC all pass, real thread history, only the reply's file-share URL domain was wrong. No header or language feature could see it; the URL's first-seen age nearly did.
FALSE NEGATIVE 2 (score 0.38, delivered): contact-harvest BEC — executive display name asking staff to 'send me your mobile numbers for the directory update'. No link, no attachment, and deliberately no payment vocabulary, so the PHISH-07 hard rule did not fire either.
Both errors are documented as open limitations in the findings, with the compensating controls named (user reporting path, out-of-band verification culture), not tuned away by quietly lowering the threshold and buying false positives.
items.triage:
1. Treat the bands as workload design, not just scores: quarantine is acted on in batch, review band is the analyst's queue (in the test set, 10 emails — a sustainable daily volume for a small SOC), delivered mail still carries its score header so Project 2 can hunt by score later.
2. Re-score the locked test set after EVERY model, lexicon, or threshold change and compare confusion matrices — a change that trades a false negative for three false positives is a regression for a SOC, whatever it does to accuracy.
3. Review errors monthly as a set: are the misses clustering in one class (BEC, thread hijacks)? A cluster becomes a new feature or hard rule; a scatter stays a known limitation.
4. Watch live drift: track the review band's confirmed-phish rate. If it falls steadily, templates have rotated and retraining is due — the metric is in the write-up, not in someone's memory.
5. Keep the baseline scored alongside: if the model ever stops beating the simple rules by a clear margin, the honest move is to say so and simplify.
items.fp: The 3 false positives, all review-band, none quarantined: (1) the genuine IT password-expiry notice (0.58, PHISH-04's control case — urgency language, saved by aligned headers); (2) the marketing newsletter (0.52, PHISH-03 — shortener and tracking redirects on an established sender); (3) the new vendor's macro invoice template (0.61, PHISH-05 — cleared by the sandbox). Pattern worth stating: every FP was a legitimate email honestly using a phishing technique (pressure, redirection, macros), and every one was resolved by a DIFFERENT family's evidence — which is the entire argument for a multi-feature classifier over any single check.

items.title: Business email compromise: no link, no attachment, nothing for the content features to catch
items.src: Classifier hard-rule layer (display name + external marker + request semantics) · gateway external-tagging · the human control: out-of-band verification, tested in the lab with a planted request
items.logic:
WHY THIS ENTRY EXISTS: BEC defeats the feature design — a three-line email asking for gift cards or a bank-detail change has no URL (PHISH-03 silent), no attachment (PHISH-05 silent), passes or sidesteps header checks, and its language is ordinary business vocabulary. The base model scored the sample below at 0.41: a clean miss, recorded as one.
HARD RULE (raises to review band, never auto-quarantines — the cost of a wrong block on an executive's real mail is its own incident): external sender AND display name matches an internal executive or finance role AND body contains a request pattern (gift cards, wire/payment change, bank details update, secrecy + urgency pairing). A second rule covers lookalike-domain executives (PHISH-02's edit distance on the CEO's name/domain).
The classifier's job in BEC is only to put the mail in front of a human fast. The actual control is procedural: payment and bank-detail changes are verified on a known number, every time — and that control is tested, not assumed (step 3).
items.ev:
Sample email PH-052 (held-out test set, labeled phishing):
From: "Daniel Reyes, CEO" <d.reyes@lab-exec-mail.example> (external; the real CEO sends from the lab domain)
Subject: Quick task Body: 'Are you at your desk? I need you to purchase gift cards for a client thank-you today. Keep it between us until I announce it. Send the codes when you have them.'
Features: urls=0, attachments=0, language urgency=1 + secrecy=1, credential=0; base model score 0.41 -> would DELIVER.
Hard rule: executive display name + external + gift-card request pattern -> raised to REVIEW at an effective 0.50 floor, with the rule name stamped as the reason.
Analyst verdict on review: PHISHING (confirmed by calling the CEO's known number — he sent nothing). Final system verdict: TRUE POSITIVE via the hard rule — and the write-up counts it honestly as a model miss the rule layer had to catch.
The FN-2 variant in PHISH-06 (directory-update request, no payment vocabulary) shows the rule's edge: it did not fire, and that gap is an open limitation, not a secret.
items.triage:
1. On any BEC-band mail: do not reply to the email (the reply goes to the attacker). Verify the request by phone or in person on a number from the directory, not from the message.
2. If money or codes moved: this is a financial incident, not a phishing ticket — notify finance and the bank immediately; recall windows are measured in hours.
3. Test the human control quarterly with a planted lab BEC (authorized, executives informed): the control passes when staff verify out of band, and the result is recorded like any other control check on this board.
4. Search for siblings: BEC is usually one-to-one, but check the gateway for the same display name and sending domain across all staff before closing.
5. Brief the impersonated executive and the targeted employee the same day — BEC targets trust, and the debrief is part of why the next one gets reported instead of actioned.
items.fp: The hard rule's false positives are real executive behavior: a genuine external mail from an executive's personal account, or a real urgent payment request, will land in review — by design, for minutes, with the reason stamped. The tuning line that matters: the rule raises to REVIEW only, never to quarantine, and never blocks — because a system that silently quarantines the CEO's actual urgent mail teaches the business to route around the classifier entirely. The residual risk is stated plainly: a patient BEC with no request vocabulary the rule knows (PHISH-06, FN-2) still gets through, and the defense there is the verification culture in step 3, not another feature.

items.title: Control check (passes): legitimate mail is delivered, with scores and reasons an analyst can audit
items.src: Classifier scoring on the legitimate half of the held-out set (30 emails) · the three false positives reviewed separately in PHISH-06 · allowlist register (sender domains with expiry dates)
items.logic:
CONTROL PURPOSE: a phishing classifier that only demonstrates catches is as untrustworthy as an assessment with no passing control (the CLD-08 / K8S-08 / VULN-08 / WEB-08 rule, kept for the fifth project running). This entry requires the legitimate side to be evidenced the same way: representative real mail, its feature scores, and WHY each family stayed quiet.
PASS = legitimate mail delivered without analyst touch at the rate the test set shows (27 of 30 untouched; the other 3 reviewed and released, none quarantined), with the score header stamped so any delivery can be re-examined later.
The control also guards the tuning process: the genuine IT password notice (PHISH-04) and the vendor macro invoice (PHISH-05) are permanent regression cases — a model change that quarantines either one fails this control and does not ship.
items.ev:
Control evidence (held-out legitimate mail, three representatives of the 27 clean deliveries):
LEGIT-04, the real IdP sign-in alert: DMARC pass + aligned, link domain = the IdP itself, language urgency=1. Score 0.22 -> DELIVER. The same WORDS as PH-047 at a fifth of the score: headers and destination did the work.
LEGIT-11, an internal project thread (Project 10 assessment scheduling): known correspondent, deep thread history, no URLs, no attachments. Score 0.08 -> DELIVER.
LEGIT-19, a supplier's routine invoice PDF (no macro, established domain, aligned headers, matches a known PO pattern). Score 0.31 -> DELIVER.
Aggregate: 27/30 legitimate delivered untouched, 3/30 reviewed and released (PHISH-06 lists them), 0/30 quarantined. VERDICT: PASS — the system is safe to put in front of real mail at these thresholds, with the review band as the honest price.
items.triage:
1. Keep this control in the evaluation set permanently and re-run it with every model change; a pass is dated evidence, not a property of the system.
2. Sample delivered mail weekly (a small random set plus every delivered email scoring 0.35-0.49, just under review) and hand-check it — the near-boundary band is where false negatives-in-waiting live, and PHISH-06's FN-1 scored 0.47.
3. Maintain the allowlist like the other projects maintain exceptions: named domain, reason, expiry date. An undated allowlist is a hole an attacker can rent by compromising one vendor.
4. Give users a one-click report path and treat reports as labeled data: a user-reported phish that scored low is the highest-value training example there is.
5. No action items from a pass beyond the standing checks: the control's job is to be re-run, not celebrated.
items.fp: The control's honesty limits, stated the same way as every control on this board: 30 legitimate emails from one lab corpus is a small sample — the 0-quarantined result would need a far larger live run to claim a production false-positive rate, and the write-up says the lab number, not a production promise. Legitimate mail also changes: a new marketing platform, a new vendor, or a real emergency notice can each move a score, which is why the review band exists and why allowlist entries expire. The control would stop passing the day a tuning change quarantines real mail to buy recall — that trade is named here so nobody makes it quietly.

writeup.problem: Every project on this board exists because one email got through. The Invoice_Q3.docm lure impersonated a supplier, carried a document that ran code on open, and started the chain Projects 1 to 4 detected, hunted, and investigated, Project 6 detonated, and Project 7 reconstructed artifact by artifact. Projects 8 to 12 then hardened everything the intrusion touched — cloud, directory, cluster, patch level, web tier. Project 13, the final build, goes to the front door: can a basic, honestly evaluated classifier score suspicious email at intake well enough to stop that chain before it starts, and can it say exactly where it fails? The problem is not building a model that demos well — it is building one whose errors are known, named, and priced, that a small SOC can actually run: a quarantine band it can trust, a review band sized to an analyst's day, and no silent loss of real mail.
writeup.methodology: Corpus: 300 labeled emails assembled in the lab — 150 phishing (sanitized samples from public phishing corpora and the lab gateway's caught campaigns, including the preserved incident lure) and 150 legitimate (lab project mail, real vendor and IdP notices, newsletters, and internal threads, with personal content removed). Split before training: 240 train / 60 held-out test (30/30), with same-campaign near-duplicates removed so the test set measures generalization, not memorization. Pipeline (Python, scikit-learn): parse each .eml and extract five feature families — header authentication and alignment (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), sender and lookalike-domain analysis (edit distance and homoglyphs against a protected-domain list, domain first-seen via Project 5), URL analysis (anchor mismatch, shorteners, redirect chains resolved inside the Project 6 sandbox, never clicked live), language (TF-IDF 1-2 grams plus handcrafted urgency, consequence, credential, and secrecy lexicon counts), and attachments (true file type by magic bytes, macro and autoexec inspection). Classifier: logistic regression over all features, chosen over a marginally better-scoring random forest because its coefficients are explainable in triage. A rules-only baseline was scored on the identical test set for an honest comparison, and hard rules (DMARC fail + credential subject; macro + misaligned headers; executive display name + external + payment request) can raise a verdict into the review band but never lower one. Thresholds: quarantine at 0.85, analyst review 0.50-0.84, deliver below 0.50 with the score stamped in a header the SIEM can hunt on.
writeup.findings: 8 classifications recorded, and the system they form scored, on the locked 60-email held-out set: 28 true positives, 2 false negatives, 27 true negatives, 3 false positives — accuracy 91.7%, precision 90.3%, recall 93.3%, against the rules-only baseline's 76.7% accuracy and 73.3% recall on the same set. The quarantine band earned its trust: 24 emails scored at or above 0.85 and every one was phishing, so no legitimate mail was auto-quarantined; all three false positives (a genuine urgent IT password notice at 0.58, a marketing newsletter with shortener redirects at 0.52, a new vendor's real macro invoice template at 0.61) landed in the review band and were released on evidence from a different feature family than the one that flagged them. By family: header authentication (PHISH-01) and URL analysis (PHISH-03) were the strongest signals — the PH-014 password lure scored 0.94 on DMARC failure, a lookalike sender, and an anchor whose text claimed the IdP while its redirects ended at a credential form on an IP literal. The loop-closure result: the preserved Invoice_Q3.docm lure (PHISH-05) scores 0.93 and quarantines at intake — replayed through the finished system, the incident that generated Projects 1 to 7 does not start. The two false negatives are reported as findings, not footnotes: a thread hijack sent from a genuinely compromised supplier account (0.47 — every header passed; only the reply's file-share domain was wrong) and a contact-harvest BEC with deliberately no payment vocabulary (0.38). The gift-card BEC in PHISH-07 is the model's third miss (0.41) that the hard-rule layer caught and the analyst confirmed by phone — counted honestly as a rule save, not a model success.
writeup.challenges: Four honest difficulties. First, the classes that matter most are the ones the features see least: BEC and thread hijacking carry no malicious artifact — no bad link, no macro, sometimes no failed header — so a content classifier has a structural ceiling there, and this project refuses to pretend otherwise; the compensating controls are procedural (out-of-band verification, tested quarterly) and architectural (the score header lets Project 2 hunt delivered mail later). Second, legitimate mail honestly uses phishing techniques — urgency, redirectors, macros — so precision is bought with a review band and analyst minutes, and the threshold is a workload decision as much as a statistical one: lowering it to catch PHISH-06's 0.47 thread hijack would have pulled roughly a fifth of legitimate mail into review at this corpus's ratios. Third, dataset limits: 300 lab emails with public-corpus phishing is a teaching-scale corpus — templates in the wild rotate faster, class balance in real mail is nothing like 50/50 (phishing is a small minority, which changes what 90.3% precision means at production volume), and the reported metrics are lab numbers, stated as such wherever they appear. Fourth, leakage and drift discipline: near-duplicate templates across the split would have flattered the score, so campaign-level dedup came before training, and the model is a snapshot — its review-band hit rate is the drift alarm, and monthly retraining on confirmed verdicts (including user reports) is part of the system, not maintenance debt.
writeup.learned: Classification is a SOC discipline before it is a machine-learning one. The features that did the work were not exotic: authentication alignment, where a link actually goes, whether a document runs code — the same evidence Projects 1, 5, and 6 already taught an analyst to read, made systematic. Explainability beat raw score: the random forest's one extra test email was not worth losing the ability to tell a user, in plain terms, why their mail was held. The confusion matrix is the deliverable, not the accuracy headline: knowing the system misses compromised-account thread hijacks and vocabulary-shy BEC, and exactly what stands behind those gaps, is what makes 91.7% a number an analyst can act on instead of a number a demo can hide behind. And with this project the board closes its own loop. The merged system now runs as one pipeline: Project 13 scores mail at intake; Project 5 enriches what it flags; attachments detonate in Project 6 and the preserved .eml becomes Project 7 evidence; verdicts and score headers feed Project 2 investigations and Project 4 hunts; Project 1 and Project 3 detections watch whatever still lands; and Projects 8 to 12 hold the cloud, directory, cluster, patch, and web posture that decides how much a single delivered email can still do. Thirteen projects, one SOC: the lure that opened the incident is now the regression test that guards the door.

ott.SITREP: Ottawa public safety snapshot, 20 November 2026. This is a published briefing, not a live dispatch feed. Police, 2025 preliminary: total crime excluding traffic is 51,360, which OPS labels as +1% against 50,610 in 2024. Shootings fell to 38 from 52. Homicide victims fell to 19 from 26. Robbery rose to 561 from 488. Theft under $5,000 rose to 21,050. The 2025 Annual Report rounds offences to 51,100 and cites about 381,000 calls and online reports. Those figures come from a different publication and should not be argued against the portal total. Fire, 2024: 34,372 incidents, including 1,408 fires, 8,307 medical responses, and 11,827 false alarms. Calls received (114,851), incidents (34,372), and apparatus responses (85,511) are not interchangeable. Paramedics: 121,461 calls in 2024, down from 127,107 in 2023. Level Zero, minutes with no ambulance available, was 73,060 in 2022, 11,372 in 2024, and 866 in 2025. Response time targets were met in 2024 for the first time since 2020. Statistics Canada puts the Ottawa CMA crime severity index at 53.8 in 2024, below Canada's 77.9. OPS reports its own index as 55. Do not average those series. Police 2025 counts are preliminary and can be revised.

BEATS.title: Police volume is almost flat. The mix is not.
BEATS.text: Total crime excluding traffic is 51,360, which OPS labels +1% on 50,610. Shootings fell to 38. Robbery rose to 561. Theft under $5,000 rose to 21,050.

BEATS.title: Fire demand climbed, and most of it is not fire.
BEATS.text: 34,372 incidents in 2024, up from 28,663 in 2022. Actual fires were 1,408. False alarms were 11,827. Medical responses were 8,307, reported up 18%.

BEATS.title: Paramedic availability is the operational change.
BEATS.text: Level Zero, minutes with no ambulance available, fell from 73,060 in 2022 to 866 in 2025. Response targets were met in 2024 for the first time since 2020.

CAVEATS.title: Do not argue 51,360 against 51,100
CAVEATS.text: 51,360 is the portal preliminary total, crime excluding traffic. 51,100 is the annual report rounded offence figure. Same year, two publications, two rounding rules.

CAVEATS.title: Do not rank the three services on one axis
CAVEATS.text: A police offence, a fire incident, and a paramedic call are different units. Direction inside each service is fair. A horse race between them is not.

CAVEATS.title: Do not treat a map dot as an address
CAVEATS.text: OPS geomasks locations so a point cannot be tied to a victim. Use wards and the Ottawa Neighbourhood Study for patterns, not for a house or a single street.

CAVEATS.title: Do not call 2025 police figures final
CAVEATS.text: They are preliminary. Late reports revise counts. Say preliminary every time you say 2025.

CAVEATS.title: Do not brief the overdose drop as the health outcome
CAVEATS.text: 810 is a police call count, down from 1,480. It belongs beside the ByWard Market paramedic unit and the Mental Well-being Response Team, not instead of them.

CAVEATS.title: Do not add fire's three big numbers
CAVEATS.text: 114,851 communications calls, 34,372 incidents, and 85,511 apparatus responses answer three different questions. One incident can send several trucks.

FINDINGS.title: Serious violence fell. Everyday crime did not.
FINDINGS.text: Homicide victims 19, shootings 38, crime guns seized 77. Theft under $5,000 is 21,050 and robbery is 561. That mix is the briefing, not the +1% headline.

FINDINGS.title: The fire service is now mostly alarms and medical aid.
FINDINGS.text: Actual fires are 4.1% of 34,372 incidents. False alarms and medical responses together are more than half. Call volume can rise without more fires.

FINDINGS.title: Availability, not only speed, is the breakthrough.
FINDINGS.text: Level Zero: 24,310 minutes in 2021, 73,060 in 2022, 52,995 in 2023, 11,372 in 2024, 866 in 2025. A system that almost always has a crew is a different system.

FINDINGS.title: The police call drop needs the paramedic context.
FINDINGS.text: Overdose calls fell to 810. The Mental Well-being Response Team and the ByWard Market unit, launched July 2024, sit in the same downtown picture.

FINDINGS.title: City totals hide neighbourhood differences.
FINDINGS.text: The Ottawa Neighbourhood Study builds safety views from police data by neighbourhood, offence type, and day versus night. This desk does not invent a ranking the sources do not publish.

FINDINGS.title: Ottawa sits below the national severity index.
FINDINGS.text: Statistics Canada: Ottawa CSI 53.8 in 2024, crime rate 4,298 per 100,000. Canada: 77.9 and 5,672. OPS reports its own CSI as 55. Do not average the two series.

WATCH.title: Robbery up, to 561
WATCH.text: From 488 in 2024, even as shootings and break and enter fell. Assaults also rose, to 4,630.

WATCH.title: Fire medical responses 8,307
WATCH.text: Reported up 18% under tiered response. Only 4.1% of fire incidents were actual fires.

WATCH.title: Level Zero nearly gone

SOURCES.title: Ottawa Police, Community Safety Data Portal
SOURCES.desc: Primary source. Crime map updated daily, shootings and firearm discharges, overdose calls, calls for service, crime by ward, hate crime, auto theft, bike theft, and homicides. Locations are geomasked.
SOURCES.kw: police crime map shootings overdose calls ward hate auto theft bike homicide

SOURCES.title: OPS, about the Community Safety Data Portal
SOURCES.desc: Official explainer: what is published, how transparency reporting works, and links into strategic plans, annual reports, surveys, and audits. The 2025 Annual Report notes 12,000 or more monthly portal visits and more than a million records.
SOURCES.kw: police portal annual report transparency survey audit

SOURCES.title: Open Ottawa
SOURCES.desc: Municipal open data. Public safety sets include Total Fire Incident Volume and traffic collisions, plus 311 requests. Detailed fire and paramedic incident records are not published here. They live in annual reports.
SOURCES.kw: open data fire incident volume paramedic traffic collisions 311 city

SOURCES.title: Ottawa Neighbourhood Study, Safety and Crime
SOURCES.desc: Neighbourhood patterns from Ottawa Police data: offence mix, change over years, and day versus night. This is the right lens when a city total is the wrong scale.
SOURCES.kw: neighbourhood safety crime ward place day night patterns study

SOURCES.title: ONS data stories
SOURCES.desc: Narrative explainers that put neighbourhood data in context. Read one before citing a place pattern in coursework or a portfolio piece.

SOURCES.title: City of Ottawa, council and committee reports
SOURCES.desc: Where fire and paramedic annual reports are received. Search Emergency Preparedness and Protective Services Committee documents for call volumes, response times, and incident data.
SOURCES.kw: fire paramedic annual report council committee response times call volume bylaw
